Cutting out family members and going “no contact” has become chic in some corners.

Op-eds with titles such as “I feel happier and healthier when not around my mother” litter outlets like The Guardian, #nocontact has garnered 1.9 billion views on TikTok, and searches for “no contact” on Google are up 191% since early 2020, per Google Trends.

Increasingly, the narrative has become: Is your family member stressing you out? Well, then simply cut them off entirely. And apparently people are doing just that.

“I have noticed a larger rush to terminate contact and relationships,” Driola Dega, a New York City-based therapist specializing in couples and families, told The Post. “[People seem less willing to accept] that challenges exist in any emotional bond, be it friendship or family or romantic partnerships.”

A shocking 38% of American adults say they are estranged from at least one close family member, according to a 2025 YouGov poll. Many report that their therapists are the ones suggesting they take such drastic measures.

“You carry all the turmoil, all the conflict, all the pain with you when you leave, and sometimes it intensifies,” Dr. Dee Apple, a psychologist based in Princeton, New Jersey, said. “But [no contact] has, nonetheless, taken off off in therapy.”

Annie Wright, a San Francisco therapist, considers going no-contact “often the only way to survive” in cases of “severe narcissistic or emotional abuse.” She told The Post that going no contact “reminds people that family ties come with conditions.”

But Wright, an outspoken proponent of the method, tells The Post that thinks it’s becoming too trendy in the world of therapy and self-help.

“What I do hear about and occasionally see is clients who say… a former therapist or social media account encouraged them to cut someone off very quickly,” she told The Post. “Recommending no contact casually? Yes, I think that’s a problem.”

In her own practice, the clients she’s most likely to pump the brakes with are those wanting to go no contact after a bad fight rather than an ongoing pattern, or before they explained to their parents what’s wrong. The clients who are too eager, she says, usually have a rosy understanding of “no contact” from social media.

“A 60-second video can make no contact sound like the obvious answer… People can go in and make that decision really unprepared for how hard the aftermath is,” she said. “Not every parent is a narcissist, and not every hurtful moment is trauma. If we use those words for everything, they stop meaning anything to people who really actually do need them.”

James Kerr, a British Columbia-based therapist with a specialization in estrangement agrees that the trendiness of “no contact” has made it feel too simple a solution.

“Unwittingly, many therapists only hear one side of the story, and they are saying, ‘Wow, if your mother is all that, I don’t think you should have them in your life.'”

Kerr — and all other experts interviewed for this article — agrees that sexual or physical abuse clearly justify “no contact,” but that more complex emotional situations should be handled with greater care.

According to a 2025 YouGov survey of American adults, 34% of those who had gone “no contact” with a parent had done so due to manipulative behavior, 31% for lies, and 34% for physical, emotional, or sexual abuse — a notably broad category.

Karl Pillemer, a professor of human development at Cornell University, has interviewed hundreds of people with estranged or once-estranged family members. He says the biggest challenge for therapists is the fact that “they can’t get both people in” their office to get to the bottom of the conflict.

His research estimates that 27% of American adults have cut off contact with a family member and only a “tiny minority” of them felt unambiguously good about the choice.

“Most of the estranged folks described being highly ambivalent about it,” he explained. “[They] report that estrangement carries real costs, even when it feels necessary, like broken attachment, chronic stress, grief, collateral damage to children and families.”

According to Pillemer’s research, only a small fraction of estrangement stems from trauma-based relationships. More people go no contact for “situational” reasons, like values differences or in-law issues.

“I’ll go out on a limb,” he said. “I think this no-contact craze has a lot of adult children deciding to cut off contact from parents who were reasonably good parents and with whom some kind of contact would be beneficial for them and for their parents.”

Another big change, he says, is more adult children using clinical language.

“There is an impact of the therapeutic language of trauma, boundaries, and toxic relationships, and that’s new as a mass cultural phenomenon,” he said. “You have adult children using terms and reinterpreting what everyone during their childhood thought was normal behavior as trauma, boundary violation, toxic relationships [and] you have parents not understanding what gaslighting and ghosting or being called a narcissist means.”

Dega, who studied psychology in Austria, sees another layer in the story: a distinctly American component to the no-contact trend, rooted in our hyper-individualistic culture that centers the self over family.

“Having lived in different countries, I’ve noticed that in the US, people tend to rely more on the ‘I,’ on the individual, rather than emotional connection and family systems,” she said. “That promotes actually more distance, rather than understanding.”

Apple agreed: “I think there’s more focus on individuals, what individuals need, without relationship context or family context, and it sort of fosters a narrow ‘do what you need to take care of yourself’ outlook…. I think people think that way more often now. ‘What do I need? What do I need? And to heck with everybody else.'”

By

The Associated Press

Paramedics work at the Wainwright Health Centre as injured military members are treated after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, outside of Wainwright, Alberta Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.
                
                    
                    John Ulan/The Canadian Press/ AP
                    
                
                hide caption

EDMONTON, Alberta — Canada's defense minister said Saturday that people were killed and injured in an incident at a military base in Alberta that caused a major fire, while reports said that large numbers of injured people were being transported to hospitals.

Fire crews scrambled late into the night as fierce winds whipped flames beyond Canadian Forces Base Wainwright and into the surrounding rural area.

It was not immediately clear how many people were killed or injured, but a doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, 180 km (120 miles) northwest, told Canada's national broadcaster that patients were being brought to hospitals across the city as health-care facilities around the base became "completely overwhelmed" by the number of people needing care.

"This number of patients would overwhelm the city of Edmonton," Dr. Warren Thirsk, an emergency department physician at the Royal Alexandra Hospital, told CBC News. "It is more patients than any of us want to count right now. It's a disaster. It's a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster."

The town of Wainwright, near the base, has about 7,000 residents.

Defense Minister David McGuinty said the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were involved in investigating the incident and described the situation as "very, very active and delicate." He said authorities were still working to determine what happened and expected to provide further information.

The Royal Canadian Mounted Police said officers were called shortly after 4 p.m. Saturday following reports of a fire in a training area at the base.

Emergency crews and military personnel are seen at the Wainwright Health Centre as injured military members are treated after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, outside of Wainwright, Alberta Saturday, Oct. 17, 2026.
                
                    
                    John Ulan/John Ulan/The Canadian Press/ AP
                    
                
                hide caption

Firefighters faced a volatile situation. Large areas of the province were hit during the day by a windstorm with gusts up to 100 kilometres an hour. The wind toppled some trees and sent signs flying and garbage cans rolling down streets.

By 11 p.m., the Municipal District of Wainwright said on social media the fire was being held and that property and critical infrastructure were protected. There was no evacuation order for residents.

Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said his province was sending assistance to Alberta but did not specify what resources were being deployed.

"Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected," Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier in a social media post.

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith described the fire as "significant and tragic" and said it was affecting many military personnel.

CFB Wainwright is one of Canada's busiest military training bases, where soldiers prepare for combat operations. It is home to the Canadian Manoeuvre Training Centre, which conducts realistic battlefield exercises, and the 3rd Canadian Division Training Centre, which provides military training.

Canadian Conservative opposition leader Pierre Poilievre said he had spoken with Carney and the defense minister to offer support to those affected by the fire.

"Pray for Wainwright, everyone," Poilievre said in a social media post. He urged people in the area to follow emergency instructions and keep roads clear for first responders.

The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday's referendum on whether Alberta should begin a process that could lead to independence from Canada. Elections Alberta said two polling locations, in Lloydminster and Vermilion, closed early Saturday and the ballots were transported securely.

Political commentator Brilyn Hollyhand discusses America's retreat from marriage as the number of single young men jumps 50 percent since 2000. Hollyhand explains how a lack of socializing is impacting young men.

America spends a great deal of time talking about what has gone wrong with young men.

They are falling behind in building families and in their careers. Too many lack direction, discipline, purpose and confidence. Many worry about pornography, loneliness, video games, declining marriage rates, anger, apathy and more.

Yet remarkably little attention is paid to a more fundamental question: Who should be forming boys to become men? For much of American history, the answer was men themselves.

DADS AREN’T OPTIONAL — AND AMERICA’S KIDS ARE PAYING THE BRUTAL PRICE

Before education became synonymous with brick-and-mortar classrooms, a boy learned first from his father, then from a career mentor, from older male relatives and from other leading men in his community. Education certainly included literacy and arithmetic, but also scripture, history, duty, courage, self-control and how a man was expected to conduct himself.

Boys might rarely encounter a male teacher in their first years in school. (Ridofranz)

At least until reformers such as Horace Mann came on the scene. Mann, known as "the father of American education," wanted standardized education across the country, which required enormous numbers of teachers. Women, who were up until then typically homemakers, became the answer.

Some argued women were naturally nurturing and morally suited to shape children. Still, others noticed something else. Finding inexpensive labor for the growing number of schools became a priority. Women at that time could be paid considerably less than men.

Mann asked in 1838 why communities should pay male teachers $25 or $30 monthly when women could do the job for roughly half the price. By 1870, nearly 90% of Massachusetts teachers were women.

Industrialization further transformed fatherhood. Boys who once watched their fathers work on farms, in workshops and running family businesses increasingly saw less and less of their fathers who began working elsewhere. Fathers became primarily breadwinners while others assumed responsibility for children’s formation.

The cultural division became this: Dad earned the money. Mom handled education.

TRADITIONAL TWO-PARENT FAMILIES VANISH FROM BIG AMERICAN CITIES AS 'MARRIAGE DESERTS' EXPAND

Today we can see what Mann’s reform wrought.

Nearly 80% of America’s public school teachers are women. Meanwhile, approximately one in five American children, more than 15 million, live with their mothers but not the fathers.

ALEX BERENSON: GENTLE PARENTING CAN'T REPLACE THE STRENGTH OF A GOOD DAD

Based on the proportion of female elementary teachers, a simplified statistical model reveals nearly half of American children could complete kindergarten through fifth grade without ever being in a classroom led by a male teacher. This is not to suggest female teachers provide inferior education. Women stepped into a space too many men vacated and continue to carry an enormous responsibility educating both girls and boys. But a system offering boys almost no male role models is missing something essential.

Industrialization further transformed fatherhood. Boys who once watched their fathers work on farms, in workshops and running family businesses increasingly saw less and less of their fathers who began working elsewhere.

Consider then what happens when these two realities intersect. Millions of boys are growing up without a father in the home. And classrooms are overwhelmingly led by women. Some boys may go through their most formative years — during which they develop confidence, courage, resilience and the ability to handle frustration — without a consistent male role model in the places they spend most of their time.

BILL BENNETT: WHAT I TOLD MY SONS ABOUT THEIR FAITH, FAMILY AND AMERICA

This raises a serious question: Who is teaching America’s boys how to become good, responsible men? Should we really be surprised too many boys are struggling when good male role models are so scarce in their daily lives, especially in education?

Boys need meaningful exposure to good men who take intellectual and moral development seriously. Men who teach boys to turn aggression into protection, competitiveness into excellence, physical strength into service and eventually sexual desire into restraint, responsibility and commitment.

WE SHOULD TELL REAL AMERICAN ADVENTURE STORIES TO TEACH OUR BOYS ABOUT HEROES

Yet, influential men spend hours today discussing what’s happened to 25-year-olds while devoting remarkably little attention to boys at 7, 10 or 13. They discuss declining masculinity without discussing curriculum, history, character formation or what fathers should personally teach their sons.

We have become fascinated by repairing men while remaining strangely disengaged from making them. It's been said, after all, it's easier to build strong children than to repair broken men.

AMERICAN SCHOOLS COST MORE THAN EVER BUT OUR STUDENTS STILL KEEP FAILING

This boy crisis is indeed an education crisis. And nothing will be solved by a new bureaucratic policy or a government spending scheme. The heart of education is the human mind and important formation happens when boys are little.

How does a 10-year-old prepare for life’s challenges? Where does he find courage? Can he distinguish good from evil, control his emotions, tolerate rejection and understand his responsibilities to his family and to his neighbor?

Perhaps the most consequential change in America was when men gradually stopped believing educating children was central to how boys became men.

That is a cultural mistake we should correct.

Boys need meaningful exposure to good men who take intellectual and moral development seriously. Men who teach boys to turn aggression into protection, competitiveness into excellence, physical strength into service and eventually sexual desire into restraint, responsibility and commitment.

Boys need more male teachers and fathers who are involved in their children’s schools and learning journeys. America’s boys need more intellectuals who take childhood education as seriously as geopolitics. And they need more politicians who care as much about who helps form a child’s mind as who gets to formulate a school’s budget.

Here and now I hear my own father saying: "Stop complaining and do something about it."

EXCLUSIVE — Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes’ office repeatedly sought recruiting help from two prominent left-wing legal groups that spent years suing the state’s corrections department alongside Mayes’ top deputy, internal emails obtained by Fox News Digital show.

Chief Deputy Attorney General Daniel Barr sought recommendations from the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) and Berkeley-based Prison Law Office (PLO) for attorneys to handle Arizona Department of Corrections, Rehabilitation and Reentry (ADCRR) work inside the attorney general’s office and later for candidates to serve as ADCRR general counsel, according to the emails.

Barr already had a long history with both groups before joining Mayes’ office. Prior to his position in the Arizona Attorney General’s Office, he was a partner at Perkins Coie, where he spent years litigating alongside the ACLU and PLO in a federal case that ultimately resulted in a judge finding Arizona’s prison conditions to be constitutionally inadequate.

'THRILL KILLER' AND DESERT EXECUTIONER — MEET THE DOZENS OF CRIMINALS DEM AG BACKED FOR PAROLE: 'NO BRAINER'

Both groups advocate substantial changes to incarceration policy. The ACLU has pursued a nationwide goal of cutting jail and prison populations by 50% through reforms, including decriminalization, bail reform, shorter sentences and clemency and has called for reductions in immigration detention.

The PLO, meanwhile, says it works to reduce incarceration while also litigating on issues related to prison conditions, medical care, disability rights and solitary confinement.

Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes speaks at an Arizona AFL-CIO Get Out the Vote canvass launch with union members and supporters Nov. 2, 2024, in Phoenix, Ariz. (Mario Tama/Getty Images)

In November's general election, Mayes is slated to face Arizona state Sen. Warren Petersen, a Republican, as she seeks to defend her role as the top law enforcement officer in the state. Mayes won her 2022 race by just 280 votes, one of the narrowest margins in state history.

"Maybe FOX News should start with the facts: The ACLU has repeatedly sued Kris Mayes over issues where they disagreed with her," Delaney Corcoran, the campaign manager for Mayes' re-election campaign, told Fox News Digital when asked about the email correspondence.

"Mayes has consistently fought for funding for Arizona police and cartel task forces and stands shoulder to shoulder with Arizona sheriffs and police. Together, Mayes and law enforcement have seized 27 million fentanyl pills off of our streets, more than any other attorney general in state history."

Mayes has defended Arizona against lawsuits from the ACLU challenging laws that allowed state and local police to arrest people illegally entering the country between ports of entry and restricted when people could film police officers.

She later settled with the ACLU in the police filming case, agreeing to permanently prohibit the unconstitutional police recording law.

Though Mayes describes herself as a "moderate" and sparred with liberal legal groups, Barr, one of her top aides, repeatedly sought candidate recommendations from the progressive ACLU and PLO for corrections-related legal roles.

DRAG QUEENS, TRANS PASTOR, ABORTION RALLIES: INSIDE DEM GOVERNOR HOPEFUL'S PROGRESSIVE CHURCH

Arizona Senate President Warren Petersen speaks during a rally for vice presidential nominee JD Vance at Arizona Christian University July 31, 2024. (Imagn)

"I am looking to bring as much ADCRR work back in-house as possible in the Arizona AG’s office. To do that, I need to hire attorneys to represent ADCRR in numerous capacities. If you know of anyone who may be interested in helping to turnaround things around here, please let me know," Barr wrote to representatives of the ACLU and PLO in February 2023.

In April of that year, Barr again turned to the groups, this time seeking possible candidates for ADCRR’s top legal position.

"Let me know if you have any suggested candidates," he wrote, forwarding an email to PLO and ACLU representatives soliciting applications for ADCRR general counsel. When his efforts to fill the role of ADCRR’s top lawyer bore no fruit, he again turned to the two groups.

"Still no takers for the ADCRR general counsel job. If you have any suggestions, please let me know," he wrote to them May 11, 2023.

That same day, ACLU National Prison Project Director David Fathi responded, promising to "redouble" his efforts to find a candidate for Barr.

Among the priorities of the ACLU National Prison Project are "substantially reducing the incarcerated population" and promoting a criminal justice system in which incarceration is used only as a "last resort."

Fathi has also criticized relying on police and prisons to address drug problems, stating in one social media post that "we will never solve drug problems with police and prisons."

Corene Kendrick, the deputy director of the National Prison Project, responded to Barr's email that one of her possible recommendations was already "enjoying suing ADCRR in civil rights damages cases in her spare time of running her café in Carrizozo," showing that at least one prospective candidate being floated to Barr had experience suing ADCRR in civil rights cases.

SOCIALISTS SET SIGHTS ON THE GROUND FLOOR OF GOVERNMENT AS GOP WARNS OF BIGGER PLAN UNFOLDING

Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes is warning about cartel drones at the southern border, which a new bipartisan law aims to tackle. (Getty/iStock)

Fox News Digital only obtained email records, not call transcripts or in-person meeting minutes, so it’s unclear what further assistance, if any, the PLO and ACLU gave the Arizona Attorney General’s Office. ADCRR ultimately hired Ashley Oddo to serve as its general counsel.

Before joining ADCRR, Oddo led Arizona State University’s Academy for Justice and backed several criminal justice positions associated with the left, including addressing systemic racism in policing and pardoning people convicted of nonviolent federal marijuana offenses.

Oddo has no institutional affiliation with the ACLU or the PLO nor was her name mentioned by either organization in email communications with Barr.

Other communications obtained and reviewed by Fox News Digital show a cordial relationship between Barr and staffers working for the ACLU and PLO. Fathi, for instance, requested a phone conversation with Barr in February 2023, and Barr responded two minutes later.

Fathi disclosed in another email that the director of ADCRR reached out to him "to schedule a call about working together on ADCRR issues."

Don Specter, a longtime PLO attorney, also reported having a "productive meeting" with the head of ADCRR in June 2023.

To reduce incarceration, the PLO has pursued litigation that contributed to court-ordered reductions in California’s prison population, supported credit systems that can advance release or parole eligibility and advocated reentry programs allowing eligible people to serve portions of their sentences in the community.

The organizations Barr turned to for recruiting assistance have taken positions on policing and incarceration that differ sharply from Mayes’ public law-and-order posture.

ARIZONA DEM AG BLASTED FOR 'DANGEROUS' CLAIM RESIDENTS CAN SHOOT ICE AGENTS UNDER STATE LAWS

The FBI is investigating the incident, which occurred Tuesday in Phoenix. (Davel5957 via Getty Images, File)

"As Attorney General, Mayes has been a partner to law enforcement, delivering millions of dollars in funding and resources so border sheriffs and Arizona police can keep us safe," her campaign website reads.

"She has locked up drug cartel members, seized more than 27 million deadly fentanyl pills off our streets and gone after criminals trying to take advantage of our kids."

The ACLU, meanwhile, has explicitly advocated defunding or divesting from police departments and redirecting resources toward other community services, publishing blogs with titles such as "Defunding the Police Will Actually Make Us Safer" and "Local Officials: Pledge to Divest from Police and Reinvest in Black Communities."

Additionally, the legal advocacy group has urged Congress to cut federal police funding while also calling on state and local leaders to reduce law enforcement spending.

The PLO likewise advocates reducing incarceration, expanding release opportunities and increasing community-based alternatives.

Those positions differ sharply from Mayes’ stated position on police funding. During her 2022 campaign, Mayes responded with "a resounding no" when asked whether she supported defunding the police.

What began last month as a small protest over teacher shortages at a school in the Créteil suburb of Paris has become a full-on national revolt, with various leftist unions and other organisations also taking to the streets in cities across the country on Saturday, with an estimated 550,000 demonstrators.

At a press conference in Paris, Minister of the Interior Laurent Nuñez said that unlike other protests, where rioters wait until the end of the event to turn violent, the violence on Saturday “started right from the beginning”, Le Figaro reported.

Nuñez specifically blamed the “radical left” for stoking the riots, saying that “groups of several hundred or thousands of rioters, clearly instigated by the far left, attacked the police,” leaving at least 60 officers injured. He said that around 400 people, mostly adults, have been arrested. However, the minister noted that “the day isn’t over yet.”

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu also pointed to “ultra-left groups” being behind the demonstrations and having “organised violence in several French cities”.

“Peaceful demonstrations have their rightful place in our Republic. Prime Minister Lecornu expressed his support for the so-called vandals pay legislation, which would force those involved in rioting to pay for the damage caused, whether they personally engaged in destruction themselves or not. “Public money is scarce: it must fund our public services, not endlessly repair what vandals destroy. According to the prefect of Haute-Vienne, the building was “largely lost”.

Mayor of Nice Éric Ciotti lamented that the fire which ravaged Limoges town hall was an “allegory of our republic”. “We will not let our country die without reacting. We are millions who refuse chaos. We will prevail!” he vowed.

Two people are in police custody after occupying an offshore Woodside gas platform about 200 kilometres off Western Australia's coast to protest against the company's gas operations.

"Special police forces landed a helicopter on the [platform] at around 11:30am AWST," Greenpeace said.

"The activists safely removed themselves from their equipment before being taken into police custody around 1pm."

"Pre-commissioning activities at Scarborough have been paused as part of routine procedures following the unauthorised access," a spokesperson said.

Scott Reef is Australia's largest standalone oceanic reef and a refuge for thousands of aquatic creatures and shorebirds — Woodside's plans have been heavily contested by environmental groups opposed to gas developments in the area.

Vegan, shmeygan — red meat in all its bloody glory is the king of New York taste.

While the media hype a mostly imaginary craving for plants, seeds, obscure global delicacies and 10-seat omakase counters, the numbers tell the real story about what New Yorkers are paying to eat.

Why the disconnect between popular taste and politicized shilling for plant-based diets?

Max Tucci, a partner in Delmonico’s chuckled, “New York never lost its appetite for steak — it’s just the headlines that  went elsewhere.”

More than 15 new steakhouses of all kinds opened in the Big Apple over the past three years, many of them 200-plus-seat giants. As many launched between 2019 and 2023.

Nearly all are thriving, notwithstanding publicity for supposedly healthier fare. Only a tiny handful closed over the same period, most notably Porter House and a single Wolfgang’s branch out of five.

The new, thundering herd included the uptown edition of Korean-style Cote; Las Vegas-inspired Golden Steer and Carver Steak; Monte Carlo-born Beefbar; Argentine-inspired Graciela and Baires Grill;  Mexican-style Cuerno; and La Tete D’or from French-born Daniel Boulud.

Elder is based on British-Indian menus; Fogo de Chao brought its Brazilian style to  the World Trade Center; and Amasa goes Latin at the Kimpton Era Hotel.

The most recent global tide was preceded by Salt Bae’s Nusr-Et (Turkish), Hawskmoor (English), and Carne Mare (Italian).

There’s no slowing the momentum. Last year brought instantly successful Palladino’s at Grand Central Terminal. This year  saw the Manhattan debuts of Atlantis Prime, Vinyl Steakhouse and Dynamo Room.

Coming soon are one of next year’s most anticipated openings, Delmonico’s Reserve on midtown Sixth Avenue. Also coming soon are Jack D’s and Maple & Ash from Chicago, which promises to be the first  “experiential steakhouse.”

Meanwhile, old-school beeferies like Peter Luger, Smith & Wollensky, Sparks, Wolfgang’s, Empire Steak and Knickerbocker Bar & Grill continue to prosper.

Michael Stillman’s company Quality Branded includes the original Manhattan Smith & Wollensky, which has seen a 5-10% increase in business over the past two years — “a big number for a 50-year-old place,” he marveled.

Realization that New Yorkers love red meat more than ever even prompted some famous chefs and owners to change course.

Vegan-heaven Eleven Madison Park added beef and chicken to its menu for the first time early this year. Jose Andres turned his Baazar at the Ritz-Carlton Nomad into Bazaar Meat — a steakhouse. Simon Oren’s Monterey originally identified as an American brasserie; it’s now proudly “a modern steakhouse.”

Mark Bucher, a National Restaurant Association board member who founded the Medium Rare empire including a Manhattan outpost, recalled that the great French chef Paul Bocuse advised young chefs, “Give customers what they want — not what you want.”

For Americans and for most New Yorkers, “Meat and potatoes are the center our diets” notwithanding exotic passing fads, Bucher said.

For sure, Big Apple steakhouses now offer first-rate seafood, pasta and salads as well. And the beef’s never been as good, from USDA Prime to Japanese Wagyu blends.

Today’s steakhouses “are more elevated,” said Sebastien Silvestri, CEO of Daniel Boulud’s Dinex Group.

At Boulud’s elegant La Tete D’or, where the most popular cuts  are filet mignon, porterhouse, cote de bouf and New York strip, “Daniel sources the best meat from around the globe and uses French techniques on it.”

Its success came as no surprise to Silvestri. When he previously worked at several Las Vegas casino hotels, “We had the  best chefs in the world, like Daniel, Thomas Keller and Charlie Trotter.

“And out of 40 restaurants the four top-grossing ones were all steakhouses.”

By

Kate Bartlett

A mass funeral is held in Sharpeville, South Africa, on March 30, 1960, for 69 people killed by police during an anti-apartheid protest. More than six decades later, victims' families are renewing their fight for justice.
                
                    
                    AP
                    
                
                hide caption

SHARPEVILLE, South Africa – Paulina Mathinye gestures with anguish at the rows of garbage-strewn graves, overrun with weeds, in the cemetery where her father is buried.

"Look at that, where they sleep," she says of the dozens of Black protesters buried here, all of whom were killed when police opened fire on March 21, 1960 in what became one of the bloodiest days in apartheid history.

"Why are they dirty? It's a disgrace," says the 71-year-old grandmother, who wears a floral dress and a smart sunhat.

The cemetery, like much else in this visibly poor township about an hour's drive from Johannesburg, has been left to decay. But Mathinye notes that for one day a year at least, when South Africa's political elite descend to commemorate the massacre, the graveyard is spotless. The anniversary is a public holiday known as Human Rights Day.

"I'm still angry. My anger comes out because that's the day my father was shot," says Mathinye, who was just five years old at the time.

She says her father's part in what became a turning point in the struggle against apartheid has not been sufficiently recognized by the current democratic government.

And she says she wants justice – however delayed.

Paulina Mathinye stands at her father's graveside at a cemetery in Sharpeville, South Africa, on 23 September, 2026.
                
                    
                    Kate Bartlett/NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

That's why she's signed up to take part in a potential class action lawsuit 66 years later, along with Sharpeville survivors and the families of Sharpeville victims.

At least 69 people were shot by police that day. They had been demonstrating against the country's pass laws – which restricted black people's movements and where they could live and work.

While it's unclear if any perpetrators are still alive, those taking part in the case hope it could lead to reparations.

But first, the group's lawyers must challenge an apartheid-era law that continues to block their efforts to seek legal redress. The law remains in force decades after apartheid ended and a Black-majority government took power.

In September they filed an application in the Gauteng High Court challenging the continued existence of the Indemnity Act 61 of 1961. If the court finds the law unconstitutional, and also certifies a class action for survivors and dependants of those killed, then claims for individual damages could follow.

Mathinye says the repercussions of that day in 1960 have affected her whole life.

Without her father, the main breadwinner, she couldn't finish school. That, in turn, affected the lives of her children and grandchildren.

"So we struggled a lot. And we are still struggling now, because nothing has been happening," she told NPR.

If the case goes ahead and succeeds, Mathinye says she'll use any money from reparations to fix up her modest home and pay for her four grandkids' educations.

The Sharpeville case is just one in a new wave of legal efforts that are seeking truth, accountability and reparations for apartheid-era crimes before it's too late.

"It's crucial that these issues of deep injustice are properly dealt with and that South Africa confronts them and does not sweep them under the carpet," says Daniel Leader, an international human rights lawyer advising the South African legal team representing the Sharpeville survivors and families.

Other cases include a court ruling last year that found South Africa's first Nobel Peace Prize laureate, Chief Albert Luthuli, was beaten to death by apartheid police in 1967.

Luthuli, the former leader of the African National Congress — Nelson Mandela's party — had previously been ruled to have died after being struck by a train. The new ruling overturned the finding of an earlier inquest.

The inquest into the 1985 killings of four anti-apartheid activists known as the "Cradock Four" has also been reopened. The activists were abducted and killed by apartheid security forces near the Eastern Cape town of Cradock. Although the officers involved are all dead, the victims' families hope the inquest will establish who ordered the killings.

And the inquest into the torture and death of Steve Biko, the iconic Black Consciousness leader who died in police detention in 1977, has also returned to court.

"It's very clear that the murder of Steve Biko was exactly that, murder," Biko's son Nkosinathi told media in September at the reopened inquest. "We hope that this inquest will eventually get to this very certain, unambiguous finding."

The family of Steve Biko, South African Black Consciousness leader, await the start of an inquest into his prison death in Pretoria, Nov. 14, 1977.  From left to right:  his older brother Kaya Biko; his widow Nontsikelelo Biko; his sister Nobanile Mvovo; and his mother, Alice Biko.
                
                    
                    Anonymous/CAPE ARGUS/AP
                    
                
                hide caption

The original inquest in 1977 heard from members of the security branch who said Biko had fallen and hit his head in a "scuffle with security police."

The Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), a court-like restorative justice body set up in the 1990s to uncover the truth about human rights violations during apartheid, re-examined the Biko case.

It denied amnesty to security officers who testified, saying they hadn't been truthful. That essentially cleared the way for possible prosecutions, but they never happened.

In fact, hundreds of the TRC's recommendations for prosecutions were delayed or never pursued. Last year, President Cyril Ramaphosa established a formal inquiry to investigate whether the recommendations were deliberately shelved.

The inquiry is looking into whether there was a secret deal between the old leaders of the apartheid regime and the country's new Black leaders not to prosecute cases in the interests of reconciliation. Its findings are due in December.

Back at the Sharpeville cemetery, Paulina Mathinye and three other descendants of those killed in the massacre, pause in front of a memorial plaque before exiting the graveyard.

Vincent Thamae, from the NGO, Voices of Sharpeville which works with survivors and descendants asks that they take leave of the dead.

"We ask of those who are sleeping here to be with us as we pursue justice for them," he says.

Bridgeport Democrats trying to stave off Amtrak’s attempt to move maintenance operations into the neighborhood find themselves in a rare bind — fighting both longtime union allies who support the project’s promised trade jobs and the rail company they are convinced advanced its plans for years without their full knowledge.

Gov. JB Pritzker entered the fray Friday, saying via a spokesman Amtrak pulled a “bait and switch” on government officials and neighbors in its rollout. And the governor’s office suggested a state-owned easement in the Bridgeport property could complicate Amtrak’s efforts to move ahead without state support.

A Wednesday City Council hearing with Amtrak exposed those tensions — with Bridgeporters booing union members and aldermen grilling company officials about their transparency around the evolving project.

Public records reviewed by the Tribune reveal some early awareness of Amtrak’s Bridgeport plans by local officials, though questions remain about how much they knew about its scope.

The standoff has unfolded in the 11th Ward — a longtime center of local Democratic strength, home of the White Sox and, historically, a neighborhood full of union workers.

Amtrak says its current facilities at 14th Street in the South Loop are outdated and too small to service its fleet. Upgrades would benefit Amtrak’s national network and speed trips through Chicago.

A modern facility on an existing rail yard next to the Sox’s Rate Field, Amtrak officials argue, would not only be a safer workplace for employees, but would also get finished more quickly and at less cost than alternatives, including renovating its current site. Trade unions are in strong support, citing some 3,000 new construction and roughly 400 permanent jobs it would bring.

But despite the touted economic benefits, union jobs and promised upgrades to crumbling viaducts, the neighborhood is largely siding against Amtrak and Justin Ishbia. The private equity investor is in line to switch from minority to majority owner of the Sox as early as 2029, depending on owner Jerry Reinsdorf’s decisions about the team, and is pitching in $125 million to the Amtrak project through his development partner, Canal Edge.

The majority of the Chicago City Council and entire Cook County Board are taking up residents’ cause in opposition to current plans, echoing neighborhood concerns about potential pollution and noise, and demands for more information.

To local Ald. Nicole Lee, the company has been hiding the ball in the run-up to Ishbia’s plan to help develop the Canal Street rail yard as part of a larger effort to move the team from Bridgeport to Amtrak’s existing South Loop site, across from the in-progress Chicago Fire stadium. Lee’s home is a stone’s throw from the new proposed maintenance facility. Hers and thousands of others’ homes, several schools and Armour Park would be within hundreds of feet of the site.

If Ishbia successfully moves the team, Bridgeport would be left with an empty stadium and declining property values for nearby homeowners, opponents worry.

Though an Amtrak attorney argued in a September letter to the Chicago Law Department that the project “is not subject to state or local zoning, building permit, planned development, subdivision, site plan, design review, or other land use or development approval requirements,” the company agreed to a council hearing last week where it was grilled by aldermen.

Many questions revolved around what Amtrak knew and when. Amtrak maintains its plans to move to the Canal Street Yard haven’t been a secret: At least as far back as 2023, a state planning document showed intent to purchase Union Pacific’s yards for equipment storage. Since then, various public presentations on a broader set of upgrades known as the Chicago Hub Improvement Program, or CHIP, also mentioned Amtrak’s intent to put maintenance operations there.

It has also sought federal grants to upgrade its aging facilities. Between November 2025 and February 2026, city, county and state transportation officials all wrote in support of federal funding for a new maintenance campus at Canal Street, including commitments to match some funding. Amtrak said it no longer needed public matching dollars because of Ishbia’s funding pledge.

“Major infrastructure projects evolve over time, and we recognize that some stakeholders have questions” about those changes and how they were communicated, Amtrak spokesperson Marc Magliari said in a statement, pledging to ensure “stakeholders have the information they need.”

Canal Edge maintains the Bridgeport and South Loop projects are separate and argued “the only thing that has changed” at Canal Street is its own involvement as developer and funder.

It’s not entirely clear how recently local elected officials learned about plans to conduct a 24-hour maintenance operation just west of Rate Field, let alone the Ishbia-backed stadium. Aldermen are used to some level of ring-kissing any time a development is proposed for their ward. But Amtrak officials referred repeatedly to federal — not local — regulatory hoops during the hearing, with little deference toward “aldermanic privilege” to steer and shape ward projects.

Lee asked when Amtrak’s plans evolved beyond the “storage” referenced in that 2023 report to the round-the-clock maintenance operations. Steve Segerlin, Amtrak’s head of commercial development, suggested storage was shorthand for a variety of operations. “The wording in some of these documents gets very truncated to not be fully inclusive to all the elements of the yard,” he said, and plans for the site evolved as the company sought and secured funding.

Amtrak’s team pledged to follow up with more information later, as well as the environmental review submitted to the Federal Railroad Administration.

Because the project is happening at an existing rail yard on land already in railroad use and doesn’t add more trains, Amtrak said the FRA granted it a “categorical exclusion” from more stringent environmental reviews. Amtrak officials agreed to release the noise and vibration, air quality, and traffic studies it submitted to federal officials and come back for another hearing to discuss them.

Until then, they noted moving operations indoors would have a smaller environmental imprint and be less busy than in 2019, when Union Pacific used the site for freight operations. Ald. Andre Vasquez, 40th, told the Amtrak team he was skeptical of any environmental sign-off given by the Trump administration.

Documents obtained by Bridgeport residents William Boyle and Jack Byrnes and shared with the Tribune paint a complicated picture of city and state knowledge and involvement in the project. Boyle and Byrnes, who are opposed to the project in its current form, received the documents via public records requests.

Illinois Department of Transportation records indicate that as far back as December 2024, the state knew that Amtrak planned to use the Canal Street Yard to provide storage and transition to “a satellite maintenance facility over time.”

IDOT acknowledged it had previously committed state matching funds to an Amtrak proposal that included building a new yard at Canal Street while still operating at 14th Street.

But in a statement Friday, Pritzker spokesman Matt Hill said Amtrak’s current proposal “is significantly different from the project the state originally supported.”

Amtrak, Pritzker’s office said, “planned and executed a bait and switch on state, federal and local officials as well as community members.”

In January, U.S. Senators Dick Durbin and Tammy Duckworth and others in the Illinois Congressional delegation wrote to the U.S. Department of Transportation in support of Amtrak’s plans for Canal Street with Canal Edge, including “a new mechanical and inspection facility, service and cleaning yard, new storage tracks, a new car wash” and maintenance machinery.

Only after the letter was sent, aides for the senators said, did information about the impact on the White Sox and what they described as Amtrak’s lack of communication with local officials emerge.

Canal Edge, however, said it did inform both senators in December 2025 meetings that it was under contract to purchase the 14th Street Yard. A future development there could potentially be anchored by a Sox ballpark, they said, with the caveat that Reinsdorf still retained control of Sox-related decisions.

Aides for Durbin and Duckworth, however, maintain they were not informed about the Sox aspect of the plans in meetings with Canal Edge. The senators have since joined calls for transparency.

Lee said there was a meeting with Canal Edge officials in February and she was informed the project was now a public-private partnership. While she was told about a three-story structure between parking lots next to Rate Field, she said they were given no site plans, traffic studies, or any of the materials a developer would typically share. At that time — and given the Trump administration’s slow rolling of other transportation projects — she said she believed funding would be slow to arrive.

A Canal Edge spokesperson said officials at that meeting presented documents to Lee and Cook County Commissioner John Daley showing the project’s scope. They said they also floated a potential White Sox ballpark, with the same caveat about Reinsdorf.

Lee and Daley denied there was any mention of a new ballpark. It “would have set off some other alarm bells for us,” Lee said.

Daley and Pritzker’s office both suggested Amtrak’s plans might cross onto access points at Sox parking lots around the proposed maintenance yard owned by the Illinois Sports Facilities Authority. ISFA CEO Frank Bilecki acknowledged he met with Amtrak officials earlier this month and told the Tribune “both sides are working through historical information to better understand the history of the property.”

Mayor Brandon Johnson’s spokesperson Griffin Krueger acknowledged the city’s Department of Transportation had also previously indicated its ability to provide funds for Amtrak improvements in Chicago, though he said matching funds weren’t committed to any grant application involving the acquisition of the Canal yard, and that the expression of support “did not commit the City to appropriating funds.”

The mayor, Krueger said, wants transparency from Amtrak, a thorough and publicly-released environmental review and “substantive” community engagement.

In April, Amtrak participated in a webinar held by the University of Illinois Chicago’s Urban Transportation Center.

During the event, Joe Shacter, director of project management at Amtrak, gave a presentation about the CHIP program (the Canal Street yard program, Amtrak says, is no longer part of CHIP).

Shacter also said Amtrak hoped to get the Canal Street yard acquisition done soon.

Shacter said Ishbia approached Amtrak in August 2025 with his desire to acquire the 14th Street yard “for commercial development,” and referenced March 2026 reporting in Crain’s Chicago Business that the billionaire was angling to build a new Sox stadium.

At the top of the webinar, a UIC official noted the presentation would be recorded and posted online afterward. But emails shared with the Tribune by Boyle and Byrnes show Amtrak officials asked UIC staff to take webinar materials down after Crain’s reached out to UIC about the presentation.

Within hours, Shacter wrote to UIC’s Edward Bury: “we need you to pull the deck I used on Wednesday from the UIC website ASAP, please.”

University staff complied, and Amtrak officials continued to flag other posts for removal late into the night. The emails indicate university staff ultimately deleted the PowerPoint and posts about the event from Linkedin, Facebook and Box, an online document storing system.

After Crain’s story referencing the UIC event was published — including what sources told Crain’s were inaccurate renderings of a new stadium — Amtrak’s Magliari thanked Bury “for your work to protect our brand.”

Asked why Amtrak had requested the webinar info be deleted, Magliari said Shacter was not the “subject matter expert” on the Canal Street Yard. The presentation, he said, had an “incomplete/obsolete” layout for the 14th Street site and inaccurate references to a second phase.

The offices of Republican Sens. Ted Cruz and Susan Collins received envelopes Friday containing a “white powder,” putting the number of lawmakers targeted by the suspicious mailings at more than dozen.

The FBI, US Postal Inspection Service and Capitol Police are investigating the letters, some of which have been intercepted before reaching their destination.

“This afternoon, my Houston office received a suspicious piece of mail containing a white powder substance,” Cruz (R-Texas) wrote on X. “The FBI, Houston Police and Fire Department, and U.S. Capitol Police responded swiftly.”

Cruz called the incident “deeply concerning,” and added that the “attempts to intimidate your political opponents have no place in our country.”

A similar letter addressed to Collins (R-Maine) arrived at her Portland office, prompting an evacuation and emergency response. A separate letter was also mailed to Collins’ Washington, DC, office but was intercepted by US Capitol Police.

“Thank you to the Portland police, the Portland fire department, the hazmat team, and the FBI their quick and courageous response,” Katie Brown, the senator’s chief of staff, said in a statement to local outlets. “This was the fourth attack targeting Sen Collins’ office or home in the past two months.

“Despite escalating political rhetoric and harassment, we will continue our work for the people of Maine.”Cruz and Collins are both locked in close midterm reelection battles.

Senate offices received a warning about the letters on Thursday from Capitol Police, which included an image of what the suspicious envelopes looked like.

Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said his staffers did not open a “suspicious piece of mail”  that arrived at his office in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, on Friday because of the law enforcement warning.

“I am grateful for the U.S. Capitol Police, who intercepted other letters and sent out a warning allowing my team to recognize this letter before opening it, and to the Sioux Falls Police Department,” Rounds wrote on X. “I am also grateful for all of my team members, who work tirelessly on behalf of South Dakotans despite the risks involved.”

The senator added, “This situation is deeply concerning and follows a trend of intimidating tactics that impact our team members. This has no place in our nation. America is better than this.”

The Senate warning included a photo of one of the suspicious envelopes that was postmarked “DSA” and gave a return address at the same Financial District building — 75 Maiden Lane — that the Democratic Socialists of America formerly listed on their membership forms.

“DSA has not occupied this office address since 2013,” a rep for the organization said in a statement. “We are also no longer headquartered at 75 Maiden Lane.”

Apart from the three GOP Senate offices that received letters Friday, at least 15 offices of congressional Democrats and some 26 state election offices have also been targeted, according to NBC News.

New York Reps. Laura Gillen, Tom Suozzi and Ritchie Torres, and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) are among the Democratic lawmakers that have confirmed having received letters.

The FBI has not said what the white powder inside the envelopes is, only describing it as “an unknown substance.”

Congressional offices have been targeted in the past with contaminated letters, most notably in a series of anthrax attacks in 2001 that sent the deadly bacteria to Senate offices.

One of those letters arrived at then-Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle’s (D-SD) office in October of that year, forcing staff to seek treatment while an entire building was later decontaminated.

The mailing spree killed five people and sickened at least 17.

Letters containing ricin, a poison, have also been mailed to Senate offices in the past, but didn’t result in any deaths.

The European rabbit is a common sight in the British countryside today. Yet it was not always so. They are not native to the British Isles and are one of the most devastating invasive species.

The early history of rabbits in the British Isles tells the captivating story of social change in medieval England. From a rare luxury gifted by kings and the Norman aristocracy, rabbits became more commonplace after the living standards of the poor improved in the years after the Black Death (1346 to 1353).

The satirical depictions of rabbits found in medieval books reveal a gallows humour for social inversion that would not feel out of place today.

Once thought to have been introduced by the Normans, archaeologists have since uncovered a rabbit bone from Roman Britain. However, documentary evidence of rabbits in the British Isles has only been found from the Norman period onwards.

One of the earliest references survives from the Scilly Isles in the form of a tithe, which was a tenth of produce given to the church as an offering. In 1176, the landowner Richard de Wyka admitted that he had withheld paying tithes on his rabbits because he had believed that “tithes were not payable on things of this kind”. His confusion suggests that rabbits were a novelty.

Rabbits continued to be sufficiently rare to warrant the king’s care and attention in the 1200s. In 1235, Henry III gave a gift of ten live rabbits to Geoffrey Despenser, the English landowner and Lord of Martley in Worcestershire, out of his park at Guildford.

A few years later, the king sent men to catch 30 or 40 rabbits in his Guildford park. They were told only to collect them if the warren was well stocked, indicating that the king didn’t want the colony to be depleted.

At the time, rabbits were kept for their meat and fur. Henry III sent out orders for the supply of venison, boars, fish, swans, peacocks, hens, eggs, and hares for various feasts in the early 13th century. It had not been until his Christmas feast of 1240 that he added rabbits to his requisition list.

Rabbits were an expensive delicacy, costing four or five times as much as chickens. Their owners guarded their warrens against poaching and predators to the point that watchtowers and stone lodges were built to protect them.

Yet rabbits did not remain the preserve of the aristocracy. The Black Death (1346 to 1353), which killed between a third and two-thirds of the European population, led to improving living standards for the survivors. Land became more freely available. Labourers could also charge more for their work. And many adopted the lifestyles of those higher up the social ladder.

Legislation was introduced in 1363 to restrict what people could wear according to their social status. Its introduction was explained because of “the excess of dress of people beyond their estate, to the very great destruction and impoverishment of the land.”

Rabbits reflected this social change. They became more commonplace during the 14th and 15th centuries as their meat was eaten by wealthier peasants and their furs worn by aspiring craftsmen.

The fur of the common grey rabbit was used for warmth, but some warrens specialised in rarer silver-grey or black rabbits. Rabbits were still fit for a king and Henry VII had night attire tailored with black rabbit fur.

As rabbit numbers increased through breeding, so too did the number of complaints about the destruction caused by them. Manorial accounts included repeated protests about the loss of crops and damage to land caused by the lord’s rabbits.

At the same time, hunting rabbits and other game was seen as potentially subversive. In 1390, following the Peasants’ Revolt of 1381, parliament introduced legislation against poaching and hunting by labourers and artisans. It was feared that, under the guise of hunting, such people would “make plots and conspiracies of rebellion” against the king.

The king consented to the legislation, extending the ban to the use of “hounds and ferrets, hays, nets, hair-pipes, cords and all other devices to take or destroy beasts of the forest, hares or rabbits, or other sport of gentlefolk”.

Rabbits and hares also reveal the satirical humour of medieval society. The Killer Rabbit of Caerbannog, the fictional and deceptively deadly rabbit from Monty Python and the Holy Grail (1975), is but a modern adaptation of this ironic imagery associated with medieval rabbits.

Rabbits adorn the margins of medieval manuscripts. Playful portrayals of rabbits jousting on the backs of snails point to a gentle self-mockery that pervades medieval culture – in this case of chivalric ideals. More in line with the killer rabbit myth, some went even further, depicting rabbits as violently attacking people and seeking retribution.

The Smithfield Decretals, a manuscript illuminated in London in the 1340s, contains one of the most elaborate of such examples. In it, rabbits are portrayed as turning the tables on their hunters, capturing them, holding them trial, and then executing their human and greyhound hunters.

Such examples fit well within the medieval culture of inverting society – the world turned upside down – for comedic relief. Similar examples include the practice of electing a boy as the bishop for the day in Durham or electing a “lord of misrule” during May Day games.

By 1555 the Swiss naturalist Conrad Gesner could write that “there are few countries wherein coneys (rabbits) do not breed, but the most plenty of all is in England”.

Associate Professor of Medieval History, Durham University

Inflation Has Escaped the Gas Station

September’s inflation reports came drenched in gasoline. Unfortunately, there are signs that inflation is heating up outside of the energy complex.

The Labor Department said Thursday that the producer price index jumped 1.3 percent last month, the biggest increase since March 2022, and is up 6.3 percent for the year. Coming a day after the consumer price index showed inflation rising to 3.7 percent, that’s enough to give people unwelcome flashbacks to the Bidenflation years.

Prices for goods in the producer price index rose 2.6 percent in September and are up 9.8 percent from a year ago. To be sure, more than 80 percent of that increase came from energy, where prices jumped 10.8 percent. Gasoline alone accounted for half the goods increase, with prices soaring 20.3 percent. Diesel prices for intermediate demand rose 21.0 percent, helping explain why the transportation and warehousing price index climbed 3.4 percent in September alone. For the year, transportation and warehousing prices are up 16.0 percent.

But even if we strip food and energy prices out of the producer price index’s goods measure, the monthly increase was still a too-high 0.3 percent. For the year, core goods are up 5.1 percent. The year-over-year core goods index has been above five percent for five straight months.

Prices for durable consumer goods are up 3.6 percent from a year ago and rose 0.3 percent in September, according to the PPI. The CPI report released Wednesday showed even more inflation on this front last month, with durables rising 0.9 percent for the month (although it has durables flat year-over-year).

The PPI also tracks a special index for personal consumption goods excluding energy. This jumped 0.4 percent in September, although it is only up 1.7 percent from a year ago.

Services prices rose 0.8 percent last month, and they are up 4.9 percent from a year ago. Excluding trade services, transportation, and warehousing brings the monthly services increase down to 0.3 percent. For the year, this is running at 3.8 percent.

Core PPI, which excludes food and energy, rose 0.7 percent, more than double the 0.3 percent economists expected. The measure excluding food, energy, and trade services increased 0.5 percent and was up 5.0 percent over the year.

In short, we have an inflationary oil spill that is now contaminating the broader economy.

Estimates following the CPI and PPI releases have September’s personal consumption expenditures price index rising around 0.51 percent, according to the Wall Street Journal‘s Nick Timiraos. That would be a big jump from August’s 0.31 percent. Core PCE prices are forecast to rise around 0.34 percent for the month, up from August’s 0.25 percent. That would lift the PCE inflation annual rate to about 3.6 percent and the core rate to 3.1 percent.

We won’t get these numbers until the day after the Federal Reserve’s next meeting, but the Fed officials won’t have to wait for the announcement to know where their index is headed.

The high price of gasoline has not deterred American shoppers. Retail sales rose 0.8 percent in September and were up 6.3 percent from a year earlier. Using the monthly CPI increase as a rough adjustment suggests real sales rose about 0.2 percent.

Of course, a big part of that was gas station sales. Excluding gas stations, retail sales rose 0.2 percent in September and are up 4.5 percent from a year ago.

There’s some impressive strength beneath those figures. Grocery store sales picked up 0.5 percent even though grocery prices fell a tenth of a point according to CPI. Furniture store sales jumped 1.3 percent despite furniture and bedding prices falling 0.8 percent. Electronic store sales rose 0.6 percent. Health and personal care store sales rose 0.7 percent. Sales at bars and restaurants jumped 1.1 percent, easily beating the 0.2 percent price increase recorded in CPI.

The regional Fed factory surveys are also showing continued expansion. The Empire State manufacturing index jumped to 25.5 from 7.6, its strongest reading in nearly five years, with new orders rising markedly. The Philly Fed’s index remained solidly positive at 20.9, although it declined from September, and new orders slowed. Factories are feeling the strain without collectively retreating.

This strength, however, probably will make it easier for the Fed to decide to hike rates. An energy shock accompanied by collapsing demand would give policymakers a clearer reason to wait. Continued spending and factory expansion will likely give them more confidence that the economy can withstand higher rates.

For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule.

It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies.

Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10-to-15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference.

“The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.”

Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.”

Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.”

He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said.

Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added.

Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid.

Serial paedophile Dennis McKenna was the warden at St Andrew's Hostel in Katanning.  (ABC News)

A freshly unearthed allegation against one of WA's worst serial paedophiles who molested dozens of teenage boys is under scrutiny by authorities, just weeks out from a decision on his release from prison after 15 years.

Dennis McKenna abused students in the 1970s and '80s while he was the warden at St Andrew's Hostel, a boarding lodge in the town of Katanning, 290 kilometres south-east of Perth.

McKenna used a combination of favouritism, intimidation and threats to abuse teenage boys under a veil of secrecy at the hostel.

Justice Marcus Solomon is weighing up what life will look like for McKenna when his sentence of more than 15 years expires later this year.

But in an extraordinary development outside court on Friday, McKenna's victims claimed there may be at least one more abuse survivor who complained to police.

Tony Buti says High Risk Serious Offender applications are conducted independently by the State Solicitor's Office. (ABC News: Courtney Withers)

Attorney-General Tony Buti has confirmed to the ABC that information about the complaint had been provided to the State Solicitor's Office.

"They are considering it," he said.

Prosecutors have sought to declare McKenna a high-risk serious offender, which could have him jailed indefinitely or see him face tough restrictions for the rest of his life upon release.

"Dennis McKenna's offending against children is abhorrent, and I condemn his behaviour in the strongest possible terms," Mr Buti.

"If anyone has allegations against Mr McKenna I would strongly encourage them to go to the police so the allegations can be properly investigated."

McKenna's brazen and repetitive offending of hostel students was revealed over the course of four separate court cases between 1991 and 2015.

Dennis McKenna has spent more than 15 years behind bars.  (ABC News)

McKenna was jailed in 1991 but released after a year and 10 months on parole. Police laid further charges in the late 2000s and he was jailed in 2011 for a 15-and-a-half year term.

Expert evidence given to the court by a forensic psychologist and psychiatrist pointed to a lack of offending between 1993 and 2011 as a reason that McKenna would be a low risk of committing a serious offence in the future.

But Maggie Dawkins, a whistleblower who worked in Katanning during McKenna's period of offending, said today that she knew of a police report made in 2004 or 2005 by a man who claimed he was assaulted by the paedophile.

Maggie Dawkins (right) says another man claimed to have been assaulted by McKenna.  (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

McKenna was not charged in relation to that matter, meaning it was not disclosed or taken into account in the proceedings.

But Ms Dawkins questioned how a decision about McKenna's release could be made based on the belief he had not offended between 1993 and 2011, given the police report.

"We know that this man went to the police and made a police complaint. There is an incident number," she said.

"The expert witnesses haven't had a chance to even know that information."

Maggie Dawkins hugs a supporter outside court. (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

That complaint is the one now under consideration by the State Solicitor's Office.

Justice Solomon is deciding whether to declare McKenna a high-risk serious offender, which would see him face tough restrictions as to where he could go and who he could socialise with.

He could impose a continuing detention order, meaning McKenna would be locked up for life, but state prosecutor Brett Tooker and McKenna’s lawyer Joel Grinceri said a restriction order would be more appropriate.

Joel Grinceri is representing McKenna in court.  (ABC News: Jake Sturmer)

The court heard from various experts about McKenna's capacity to reoffend. Among them was forensic psychiatrist Peter Wynn Owen, who considered the risk low, primarily due to his advanced age and lack of offending between his 1991 and 2011 jail sentences.

Demolition has begun at the site of one of state's worst cases of institutionalised child sexual abuse, where dozens of boys were harmed by paedophile Dennis John McKenna.

But Dr Wynn Owen said the serial paedophile continued to "categorically" deny any offending after 1981.

"[He] attributes blame to victims, suggests victims in fact instigated aspects of the offending," he told a hearing in July.

"If an individual is denying offending, it suggests they are not going to be able to engage with treatment."

Dr Wynn Owen said McKenna continued to hold distorted views that, in his mind, minimised or justified his offending.

"This distortion … enabled him to continue to offend over a long period of time," he said.

Justice Solomon's decision is due to be handed down in November, weeks before McKenna’s sentence is due to expire.
