Labor has a problem with Anthony Albanese. It also has a problem with Jim Chalmers. 'Two for the price of one', as one unimpressed Labor MP put it to the Daily Mail.

And the uncomfortable truth for a government searching for someone to blame is that getting rid of either one would do precious little to absolve the other of the same fate: 'They're tied at the hip now.'

Behind the public declarations of unity, two currents of discontent are running through Labor at once.

Some Labor figures believe the Prime Minister is politically spent: that voters have stopped listening, and that another carefully staged announcement won't bring them back. Albo's age, 65 by the time of the next election, doesn't help.

Others are increasingly frustrated with the much younger Treasurer, whose economic explanations keep coming while the promised improvement in people's lives keeps being pushed further over the horizon. 'He's the problem,' a former Labor strategist says.

The various complaints overlap, but they don't necessarily lead to the same conclusion about who should go, who should stay, or who could possibly fix the mess.

'People are losing faith in Albo, but that doesn't mean they think Jim is the answer,' a second Labor MP argues.

Dissatisfaction with Albanese doesn't automatically translate into enthusiasm for Jim Chalmers. Nor does frustration with Chalmers mean the PM has escaped responsibility for the government he leads.

A Labor colleague says: 'You can't have a Prime Minister claiming he fixed something and expect nobody to ask who stuffed it up in the first place.' That's what happened this week

Labor's problem is that its two most important figures are both the cause of the drift that colleagues are complaining about.

There is a qualification to all this. Labor has 94 MPs in the lower house. That landslide brought in people defending seats the party doesn't normally hold, including inexperienced MPs who have never endured a serious reversal in political fortunes before.

Approaching the halfway mark of Labor's second three-year term, some panic is entirely predictable, even with the right wing of politics fractured.

An MP fearing the loss of their seat isn't necessarily offering a dispassionate assessment of the national interest.

Nor does a huge parliamentary majority mean every individual sitting behind the Prime Minister feels safe. Some worry about the opposition recovering. Others have more immediate reason to worry about One Nation.

Albanese's reassurance that Labor will be 'kicking with the wind in the fourth quarter' is wearing thin for some.

The latest Newspoll offers little comfort either. Labor's primary vote is 29 per cent, barely ahead of One Nation on 28 per cent, with the Coalition on 20 per cent. Sixty per cent of those polled are dissatisfied with Albanese personally.

The weakness of Angus Taylor's opposition is a cushion for the PM. But it's also an indictment: Labor is struggling against an opponent who is polling just 20 per cent.

'It's easy to tell people to hang on when you're not the one wondering whether you'll lose your seat,' a first-term MP declares.

The Australian Taxation Office credit card fiasco has supplied a particularly revealing glimpse of the government's workings.

Small Business Minister Anne Aly and Communications Minister Anika Wells: two frontbenchers who have copped flak this week

A decision threatening a small business cash flow lifeline produced confused ministerial messages, mounting anger and a taxpayer-funded delay.

Then came the scramble over who deserved credit for the retreat.

At a business dinner, Albanese presented himself as the man who responded to an appeal from business and got things moving. Chalmers subsequently insisted the pair had shared the same view and were already working on an intervention.

By Question Time, the Prime Minister was stressing collective agreement. Even the fix became another story about the government's dysfunction.

For Chalmers, the political damage is obvious. When business appeals directly to the Prime Minister and he publicly celebrates his own intervention, the Treasurer looks diminished, whatever the sequence of conversations that took place.

For Albanese, the difficulty is just as real. He can't keep claiming credit for rescuing people from decisions made on his watch without inviting questions about why his government keeps needing rescuing.

'You can't have a Prime Minister claiming he fixed something and expect nobody to ask who stuffed it up in the first place,' a colleague says. It's a fair point.

The state of the economy makes those questions even harder to brush aside.

The Reserve Bank's September increase took the cash rate to 4.6 per cent, its fourth rise this year and the highest it's been in 15 years. The Middle East conflict is adding to inflation, but Governor Michele Bullock has been clear that domestic capacity pressures were already a problem.

Her assessment that productivity was 'doing nothing' was especially uncomfortable for a Treasurer last month. Chalmers has made lifting productivity a central ambition.

There is a tempting suggestion that Albanese could solve his economic problem by replacing his Treasurer. He could, in theory, but with who?

He can point to international shocks, some spending restraint and a better budget position than earlier forecasts suggested all that he likes.

But they don't settle the political question confronting his colleagues: when does an explanation become an excuse?

A household for which mortgage repayments have gone up again is unlikely to be consoled by a comparison with an old Treasury forecast. It's inside the beltway stuff.

The budget squeeze exposes the competing demands on the Albo-Chalmers partnership. The PM constantly wants more cost-of-living help.

Chalmers must somehow reconcile that with pressure for budget savings and the fight against inflation.

'We keep explaining why things are difficult. People want to know when we're going to make them better,' a Labor backbencher says.

Which brings us to the tempting suggestion that Albanese could solve his problem by replacing his Treasurer. In theory he could but that doesn't mean that he will.

Sacking Chalmers would be an admission that a key appointment, and years of defending the government's economic management, had gone badly wrong.

It would also invite an obvious follow-up question: if the Treasurer's performance warrants dismissal, what does that say about the Prime Minister who handpicked him for the role in the first place?

A new treasurer could hardly offer a convincing fresh start while being required to defend the same spending commitments, political promises and prime ministerial decisions. Who would even be in line for the job?

Chris Bowen has done it before, but he's hardly a popular figure. Tony Burke might fancy himself, but few others would. Richard Marles as party deputy has a right to pick his portfolio, but he knows his own limitations. Mark Butler is a close ally of Albo, but the factional right is unlikely to tolerate two left-wingers in the top two roles.

And a wounded former treasurer on the backbench would scarcely make life more comfortable for Albo.

The safer immediate calculation is to keep Chalmers in place. But keeping him also means continuing to share responsibility for whatever failure comes next.

Chalmers faces the reverse predicament. Any argument that Labor needs renewal has to confront his own prominent role in producing the record from which it would be renewing itself.

Being younger than the Prime Minister doesn't make him a fresh start if the decision is made that Labor needs one.

And the broader talent pool hardly justifies the confidence of those imagining a change of leader would transform the government's fortunes.

Some of the behind-the-scenes grumbling we're starting to see is self-serving: a search for somebody else to blame, without much evidence that the people doing the complaining could do any better.

'There's plenty of criticism of the leadership. There's a lot less agreement about who would actually do better,' one Albo supporter claims.

That might buy Albanese (and by extension Chalmers) more time, but it hardly amounts to a vote of confidence. Labor MPs can spend the rest of the time between now and the next election arguing over who is the bigger problem. Meanwhile, voters struggling to pay their bills might decide that the easiest way to settle the debate is to just get rid of both of them.

Media boss Antony Catalano has denied swinging a clothes iron at his wife as he launched a fresh legal bid for a plea deal over domestic violence assault charges.

Catalano, 59, is accused of the drug-affected assault of his wife Stefanie at their Melbourne penthouse in St Kilda on March 13, when he allegedly held the iron to her head and dragged her by her hair.

Ms Catalano has since stopped cooperating with Victoria Police and lodged a detailed statement of no complaint, signalling she no longer wants the prosecution to proceed.

On Friday,  her lawyer Sarah Pratt told Melbourne Magistrates' Court she was liaising with the Office of Public Prosecutions on Ms Catalano's behalf.

As well as the 'statement of no complaint', Ms Catalano has also lodged a police ethical standards complaint about her treatment in the months since her husband’s arrest, alleging authorities were seeking to 'destroy' him.

Catalano made no comment as he finally appeared in court in person after previously attending hearings by videolink.

He is now being represented by top Melbourne barrister Dermot Dann, KC,  the man who launched a successful appeal for alleged killer Greg Lynn.

Police allege Catalano swung a clothes iron at his wife’s head, unlawfully imprisoned her in their St Kilda apartment, threatened to stab her to death, and choked or strangled her.

Dermot Dann, KC (left) and Antony Catalano (centre) make their way into court on Friday

Ms Catalano was admitted to hospital with a fractured tailbone.

CCTV footage showing common areas adjacent to the Catalanos’ apartment is part of the police case against him, with Ms Catalano also providing a statement shortly after the incident.

Mr Dann said that CCTV may never be admissible should the matter proceed to trial.

'There are charges that we have grave difficulty with. There's an allegation of strangling that we say in simple viewing of the CCTV demonstrates (it never happened),' he said.

'There's an allegation that's been widely reported of swinging an iron at his wife's head. We say the same thing: Look at the CCTV; didn't happen.'

Mr Dann described the legal situation as ‘unusually delicate’ before warning the court he intended to make a variety of applications should it proceed as intended by the Crown.

'From our client's point of view, he certainly wants to avoid the drama and time associated with all that,' he said.

Mr Dann suggested there were two ways that could be avoided: 'withdraw the charges or explore a plea'.

Catalano and wife Stefanie have since apparently reconciled following the alleged incident

The couple hope to travel overseas to escape the media spotlight

'He hasn't shut the door to that either,' Mr Dann said.

'We have been in discussions with my learned friend. We've even nominated a charge, which we say will suitably resolve the matter.'

The prosecution of Catalano has been handed to barrister Jane Warren, who was central in leading the case against mushroom killer Erin Patterson.

Ms Warren told the court she was in 'meaningful discussions' with Mr Dann, but she needed more time to come to a position.

The court heard Catalano had since reconciled with his wife and moved back into the family home in Byron Bay.

On Friday, The Age reported Catalano had received planning approval to expand his family’s Byron Bay compound and build a third home in the Wategos Bay enclave, creating an estate worth more than $67million.

Mr Dann asked for Catalano’s bail restrictions to be softened further to allow him to travel overseas with his family to avoid ongoing media scrutiny.

Ms Catalano is reportedly already overseas and tuned into Friday’s hearing remotely.

The St Kilda apartment complex where the alleged assault took place

Magistrate Donna Bakos agreed to the change, allowing Catalano to travel overseas.

Catalano's bail was extended to December 14 when he is expected back in court.

After the criminal charges Catalano said he was struggling with significant mental health and substance abuse issues.

'I am deeply ashamed and humiliated,' Catalano told the Australian Financial Review in March.

'Those close to me have been urging me to seek professional help for some time and there have been interventions by close family and friends.

'I regret not heeding their advice and I continued to believe I could hide my mental health issues.

'I allowed shame and pride to prevent me from confronting these problems and seeking treatment earlier.'

TYLER, Texas (KLTV/Gray News) - A Chilean flamingo at Tyler’s Caldwell Zoo is recovering from a soft tissue injury to his ankle joint with the help of a custom-built brace.

Queenie, 9, got spooked and ran while on exhibit, tearing ligaments in his ankle. Bird Department Supervisor Nichole Moore said keepers noticed him lagging behind.

“He sustained this injury on exhibit. We saw him lagging behind his flock. And then we decided since he’s so tactile, we’d be able to get him in hand and really help him,” Moore said.

The injury first showed up in 2021. Medicine did not fully fix the problem, so the zoo worked with Ben Guenther, an orthopedist who typically builds braces and prosthetics for people. Guenther designed a brace for Queenie.

“This was the best opportunity for him because we would be able to put a brace on him and work with him and make sure it would really work so he would be able to live a really long life,” Moore said.

Flamingos use their legs for more than walking. They also use their feet to stir up food so they can filter through it.

“It is really important for us to be quick when assessing injuries, especially on long-legged birds like this, they utilize their feet quite a bit when they’re moving around,” Moore said. “They also use their feet to kind of stir up the the food, to really like move things around for them to filter through. So it’s just such a really important thing for them to have function in both legs. So yeah, it’s really important for us to really make sure that we’re able to take care of them as quick as we can.”

Chilean flamingos can live into their 60s.

Moore said the brace provides joint support Queenie’s leg cannot provide on its own. He will wear it for life, and it will be checked weekly for swelling or irritation.

“Now that he’s quite used to it, we see such a change in him. He puts full weight on that leg. He’s around with the rest of the flock. He’s taking baths with the flock and running around,” Moore said.

There is no timeline yet for when Queenie will fully rejoin the rest of the flock.

Most companies use AI agents to ship products faster or to speed up workflows. Apate.ai sends them undercover to get scammed.

Founded in 2024 on the basis of research done in Macquarie University in Sydney, the Australian startup deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims. The agents can answer scam calls, respond to shady messages and emails, follow phishing links, and join social media groups to bait fraudsters. They pretend to be people of all stripes, sporting different ages, genders, and accents, and speak various languages as they try to keep scammers engaged long enough to learn something useful.

The company says its fleet of agents has so far wasted 17 years of scammers’ time across 2.5 million conversations. More importantly for Apate’s customer base of banks, telecom companies, government agencies, and utilities, the undercover agents try to get scammers to reveal things about themselves that are usually learned only after a victim has been scammed: bank accounts, crypto wallets, phone numbers, malicious websites, the brands they’re impersonating, and other details about the scams they’re running.

Apate, one of the finalists at this year’s Startup Battlefield 200 at TechCrunch Disrupt, then feeds that information to its customers, who use it to inform their anti-fraud measures and initiatives. (The company will pitch a panel of VC judges at Disrupt, which is taking place this week at Moscone West in San Francisco through Thursday, October 15.)

It’s a curious evolution of scam-baiting, but it’s not so surprising given how much AI has empowered scammers and hackers. The FBI received more than 22,000 complaints of AI-related crimes in 2025, which resulted in about $893 million in losses. More than $632 million of that came from investment scams, in which the FBI says fraudsters use AI to run conversations, and deepfake the voices and appearances of celebrities, executives, and trusted figures.

For a long time, people have made a hobby out of deliberately stringing scammers along — sometimes hilariously, like getting scammers to read aloud entire books, or even to get ridiculous tattoos. Now, with AI growing increasingly capable, the tables are turning.

Curiously, the idea behind Apate was sparked by a real scam call.

Several years ago, Apate’s founder and CEO Dali Kaafar was at a family picnic when he got a call from an unknown number. Realizing it was a scammer on the line, he decided to play dumb for the benefit of his kids and managed to keep the call going for 44 minutes.

Everyone had a laugh, but Kaafar noticed that those were 44 minutes the scammer had not spent calling a real victim. It was also 44 minutes of his wasted time, which led him to wonder: Could he automate it, and in the process, learn something useful?

That idea eventually led to research work at his job at Macquarie University, where Kaafar and his colleagues used machine learning and natural language processing to uncover the content of scam calls, and develop better ways to detect and prevent scams.

“Most of the industry works after the fact. Telcos block numbers, but scammers just get new ones. Banks watch transactions, but by then the scammer has already reached the customer. We go to the scammer directly and get the information before anyone gets hurt,” Brad Joffe, co-founder and chief commercial officer, told TechCrunch. “Our AI agents talk to tens of thousands of scammers every day across calls, messages, email, and the web. What we offer our customers is what comes out of those conversations, and what they can do with it.”

Joffe said Apate uses both frontier models and its own fine-tuned models to power its agents and analysis. The company trains its models on conversations its agents have had with scammers, as well as the research Kaafar did at Macquarie.

In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get access to an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more. Customers can even assign these agents particular missions, such as obtaining a bank account number or crypto-wallet address. Its text agents can search forums, investment groups, and social platforms for potential scam activity, and can then enter conversations with a fabricated identity to surface scammers’ details.

The startup’s customers include Commonwealth Bank of Australia, TPG Telecom, as well as other utilities, telcos, and government agencies. Joffe said TPG has diverted nearly 590,000 calls to Apate’s agents, Commonwealth has seen a 76% drop in publicly reported scam losses, and an unnamed Australian bank the startup works with has used its outbound agents to disrupt 22 scam campaigns.

Investors are betting there is money to be made from fooling scammers, too. Apate raised $8.15 million in seed funding in August from Lobby Capital, OIF Ventures, Investible, Concept Ventures, and Baobab Ventures. Joffe said the 20-person company has raised just under $10 million in total and plans to spend the latest round on its product and international expansion, including opening an office in London and building a larger presence in the U.S.

“Apate is named after the Greek goddess of deception, which felt appropriate given what our agents do,” Joffe said, adding that the startup even features scammers swearing at the bots in its pitch material.

“We track that as a sign of frustration and every swear word gets celebrated by us at Apate. We are probably one of the only businesses in the world that celebrates when people swear at our product.”

Former Jets quarterback Mark Sanchez has struck a tentative deal to settle a civil lawsuit over a bloody brawl with a 69-year-old truck driver he allegedly attacked in Indianapolis last year, according to court documents.

The proposed deal comes after Sanchez agreed to plead guilty last month to charges stemming from his alleged beatdown of Perry Tole in October 2025.

Tole claimed he was left “permanently disfigured” from the battering he took from the ex-Fox Sports TV analyst, according to the lawsuit.

Sanchez, Tole and Fox Corporation — which employed the former athlete at the time of the assault — reached an agreement in principle on Oct. 3, court papers filed in the Southern District of Indiana on Oct. 6 show.

Tole’s attorneys are expected to file a motion to dismiss the case by Jan. 8, 2027, once the settlement is signed. Details of the deal were not immediately known.

The lawsuit stemmed from Tole being body slammed and beaten by Sanchez when he parked his truck in an alley to collect cooking oil from an Indianapolis hotel on Oct. 10, 2025.

The truck driver stabbed Sanchez multiple times after he attacked him.

Footage captured a bloodied Sanchez, who cops said reeked of booze, clutching his wounds while staggering from the alleyway into a nearby bar.

Grisly photos after the pummeling showed Tole in a neck brace in his hospital bed with deep wounds to his cheek and jaw.

Sanchez, a onetime standout quarterback at USC, was hit with a slew of charges, including battery resulting in serious bodily injury, battery resulting in bodily injury, unauthorized entry of a motor vehicle, and public intoxication.

Sanchez’s attorneys and Indiana state prosecutors filed a joint motion on Sept. 2 asking that a judge vacate a Sept. 8 trial date and “set this matter for a guilty plea and sentencing hearing.”

But it was not clear which criminal charges Sanchez plans to plead guilty to.

Sanchez’s legal advisor told The Post in a statement last month that they were “encouraged by the constructive conversations taking place regarding the related civil matter.”

“There is real momentum toward bringing this entire chapter to a close,” Nick Sanchez Jr., said.

Matt Golitko, an attorney for Tole, previously said discussions with Sanchez’s legal team have created a “positive path” for moving forward.

“Our discussions have been productive, and we’re on a positive path toward an agreement that will allow the parties to move forward,” Golitko said in a statement last month.

“Mr. Tole appreciates the progress we have achieved and looks forward to an amicable resolution.”

Attorneys for Sanchez and Tole did not immediately respond to The Post’s request for comment.

Inside NBC4’s Universal City studios, Bass appeared relaxed and confident as the candidates faced off before an in-person audience.

Raman, referring to prepared notes, invoked Ronald Reagan’s famous question, “Are you better off today than you were four years ago?” She accused Bass of being “MIA” during the city’s biggest crises and argued that Angelenos were struggling with homelessness, housing costs and public safety on her watch.

But the sharpest exchange came when NBC4 political correspondent Conan Nolan, citing Raman’s previous remarks to The California Post, demanded a straight answer.

“For clarity, will you replace the chief before the twenty-eight Summer Olympic Games in LA?”

“I wanna replace the police chief. I’ve been very open about that. I’ve been very clear about that,” Raman insisted. “I don’t believe this chief has met the moment. I believe he’s lost the trust of Angelenos, especially in response to the ICE raids.”

But she wouldn’t commit to a deadline.

“It is not a unilateral decision by the mayor,” Raman said, pointing to the Police Commission and City Council.

Nolan pressed again, raising the security stakes surrounding the Games. “Will you replace the chief before twenty twenty-eight?”

“It will depend on these other factors, on other decision-making bodies,” Raman responded.

Bass pounced. “It is absolutely in the power of the mayor to fire the police chief,” she countered, warning that replacing McDonnell before the Olympics could disrupt the department’s preparations.

New to The Nation? Subscribe

Print subscriber? Activate your online access

The government’s sweeping crackdown on the LGBTQ community is an escalation of a decades-long pattern.

Turkish police detain dozens of LGBTQ rights protesters in Ankara, on September 15, 2026.

Between September 12 and 14, in coordinated overnight raids across five cities, Turkish police targeted seven LGBTQI+ rights organizations, two groups supporting people living with HIV, and 13 bars and clubs where queer people gather. Board members of some of the country’s oldest LGBTQI+ associations, including Kaos GL and Lambda Istanbul, were taken from their homes. Human Rights Watch reports that at least 112 people were arrested and that 82 remain in detention by court order. Courts also ordered the blocking of dozens of websites and social-media accounts belonging to LGBTQI+ groups and activists; when people gathered outside Istanbul’s main courthouse to protest, more than a hundred were detained as well. The alleged offenses were “obscenity,” “prostitution”, and crimes against “public morality.”

Justice Minister Akın Gürlek named the operation “My Family Is Safe” and placed it squarely within President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s “Decade of Family and Population,” a 10-year programme launched this year to reverse Turkey’s falling birth rate and defend what the government calls “national and moral values.” That framing is the most important aspect of the raids. Homosexuality has never been a crime in Turkey. What this month showed is a state that has found other ways to criminalize queer life and now presents such measures as family policy.

This didn’t come out of nowhere. Istanbul’s Pride march has been banned every year since 2015, on the grounds of public safety, and police have detained hundreds of people who tried to march anyway. But those detentions were fleeting. Marchers were picked up on the street and, for the most part, released within hours. This month’s operation was different in kind. It did not target a march; it targeted the infrastructure of a movement, including its offices, leadership, health services, websites, and social spaces, in five cities at once. It relied on criminal law rather than public-order powers, and courts have kept dozens of people in pretrial detention. And it was announced not as a policing matter but as the enforcement of a government program.

To understand how Turkey arrived here, it helps to know how the family became the organizing principle of the state’s politics, and how much of that politics follows a script written transnationally.

Same-sex relations have been legal in Turkey since 1858, earlier than in most of Europe. Yet LGBTQI+ people have never enjoyed equal citizenship in practice. As with other minority groups, including ethnic and religious minorities, the state’s approach to LGBTQI+ people was long defined primarily by denial, repression, and nonrecognition. This decades-old policy began to shift after the neoliberal-Islamist Justice and Development Party (AKP) came to power in 2002, but not toward greater equality. Instead, LGBTQI+ people increasingly became targets of explicit political, administrative and legal action, driven by the party’s conservative gender politics. This is not to say that queer people had been free from state harassment or the “indirect” violence of the law before then. What distinguishes the AKP era is the increasingly overt use of law, administrative power and state institutions to act against LGBTQI+ visibility, organization and public life.

Earlier manifestations included, among others, the removal of sexual orientation from the antidiscrimination provision of the draft 2004 Penal Code during its drafting; repeated fines imposed on trans women under the 2005 Misdemeanours Law; persistent impunity for police violence; the requirement that gay conscripts “prove” their homosexuality to obtain an exemption from military service; the use of “unjust provocation” to reduce sentences for men who killed gay or trans people; legal proceedings seeking the dissolution of Lambda İstanbul, one of Turkey’s oldest LGBTQI+ organizations; and the declaration by the minister responsible for women and family affairs, Selma Aliye Kavaf, that “homosexuality is a disease.”

The turning point came in June 2015, when the Istanbul Pride march was banned for the first time and dispersed with water cannons. It has been banned every year since, and activists who defy the ban face mass detentions each June. Repression did not stop the movement from growing, though. By the mid-2010s, LGBTQI+ organizing had become a visible, consolidated social and political force, with organized marches drawing tens of thousands. That visibility changed what came next. After the attempted coup of July 2016 and the authoritarian consolidation that followed, restrictions on LGBTQI+ activism became part of a broader campaign against any social movement the government saw as a challenge to its authority.

Sporadic bans and moralizing statements hardened into coordinated institutional repression. Under the post-coup state of emergency, the governor of Ankara imposed an indefinite ban on all LGBTQI+ events in the province in 2017. By 2020, the restrictions had reached the regulatory state: The broadcasting authority imposed sanctions on programs depicting same-sex relationships, and the Ministry of Trade required rainbow-themed products sold online to carry an 18+ warning.

In 2021, institutional repression and political rhetoric fused. Erdoğan declared that there was “no such thing” as “LGBT.” Weeks later, his government justified Turkey’s withdrawal from the Istanbul Convention—the Council of Europe treaty on preventing violence against women—on the grounds that it had been used to “normalize homosexuality.

From 2022 onwards, “LGBT” became an organizing theme in government politics. Official discourse now casts the LGBTQI+ movement, and increasingly LGBTQI+ people themselves, as a threat to the family, social values, and the national order. Government policy has also moved beyond state institutions into organized public mobilization, most visibly through so-called “Great Family Gatherings” held in opposition to LGBTQI+ visibility. The resulting dichotomy places queer existence outside the family altogether, as if queer people neither belonged to families nor formed families of their own. That is the framing Gürlek invoked when he called the September raids “My Family Is Safe.”

None of this is a purely Turkish story. The government is working from the script of the transnational “anti-gender” movement, so called because it organizes against what it labels “gender ideology,” a catch-all for feminism, LGBTQI+ rights and any loosening of traditional gender roles. What makes this movement international is not merely that similar ideas circulate across borders. Rather, a shared political repertoire, built around a heterosexual, cisgender ideal of the “traditional family,” is translated into local vocabularies and written into law and institutions.

Across many countries, LGBTQI+ people have come to be portrayed as incompatible with, or a threat to, the “traditional family,” and that rhetoric is used to justify exclusionary policies and, in some places, criminalization. Coalitions such as the Political Network for Values and the Group of Friends of the Family have carried conservative understandings of family, gender, and sexuality into international institutions, including the United Nations. The clearest example is the Geneva Consensus Declaration on Promoting Women’s Health and Strengthening the Family. Cosponsored by the United States alongside Brazil, Egypt, Hungary, Indonesia and Uganda, signed by 32 states in October 2020, and later transmitted to the UN General Assembly, the Declaration listed among its principal aims the defense of the family as “foundational to any healthy society,” described the family as the “natural and fundamental group unit of society” entitled to state protection, and insisted that abortion “in no case should be promoted.” (The Trump administration rejoined within days of returning to office in January 2025.) The family thereby becomes more than a social or legal category: It operates as a normative and political framework through which reproductive policy, gender, sexuality and LGBTQI+ rights are contested.

What is new in this politics, therefore, is not hostility toward LGBTQI+ people. Rather, previously distinct questions, including LGBTQI+ rights, feminism, reproductive rights, fertility and the protection of children, are folded into a single narrative about threats to the family, demographic continuity, and the national social order. In Turkey, that narrative has been expressed in an Islamic-nationalist vocabulary centered on the “traditional family,” falling birth rates, “national and moral values,” and resistance to supposedly foreign projects of “gender-neutralization.”

Jeet Heer

Sasha Abramsky

Books & the Arts
                                            
                            /
                        
                                                                        Emily Wilson

Sasha Abramsky

Erdoğan’s speech to the International Family Forum on May 23, 2025, illustrates how the translation from transnational to national works. He blamed individualism and changing family structures on globalization and “cultural imperialism”; described “gender-neutralization” as an organized global project “infiltrating the fabric of [Turkish] society” and threatening “national integrity”; and, within this narrative, cast LGBTQI+ people as “enemies of humanity, enemies of women, enemies of children.” He tied all of this to Turkey’s falling fertility rate, praised countries that had defined the family in law or Constitution as a union between a man and a woman, and promised that Turkey would take a “leading role” internationally on the issue. In the same speech, he called declining fertility a “disaster,” declared that “every abortion is a murder,” and announced that 2026–35 would be the “Decade of Family and Population.”

That agenda has since been embedded in the machinery of the state. On May 2, 2026, the Official Gazette published Presidential Circular No. 2026/4. The circular (the equivalent of a US presidential executive order) frames human rights and individual freedoms as a tool of what it calls “harmful movements” promoting “gender-neutralization”; treats changes to family and population structures as an “existential threat”; and calls for measures to protect future generations from “gender-neutralizing” trends, including laws to promote marriage and to protect what it terms “traditional marriage,” with the stated aim of “protecting and strengthening the family and population structure.” Four months later, police were raiding LGBTQI+ organizations under the banner “My Family Is Safe.”

Taken together, these developments show that anti-LGBTQI+ politics in Turkey cannot be reduced to hostile rhetoric or episodic repression. The family has become the framework through which demographic anxiety, gender and sexuality, national identity, and state authority are bound together. LGBTQI+ people are positioned not merely as a moral or cultural “other” but as a threat to the demographic and social order the state has set out to preserve. The Turkish case also shows what transnational anti-gender politics looks like on the ground: a narrative that circulates globally, is translated into a national political vocabulary, institutionalized through law and policy, and then enforced by the police.

It is LGBTQI+ people who pay the price: shrinking space for visibility and association, greater exposure to state and social violence, and an increasingly hostile environment in which our rights, our organizations and our presence in public life are under pressure. All of this unfolds against a legal framework that offered scant protection to begin with. Anti-gender politics does not merely reshape political discourse. It deepens the legal and social insecurity in which queer people in Turkey are required to live, an insecurity that, this month, was given a name.

Levent Pişkin is a Turkish human rights lawyer based in Scotland.

On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim?

Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants

Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.

He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities."

"I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.

Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.

On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.

Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.

Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".

On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.

Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured.

When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday, Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".

Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled".

"That war is a disaster if you see the numbers," he said.

For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure, disrupting energy supplies on both sides.

Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".

Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.

In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.

Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.

Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."

Supporters of the White House barely showed up in replies to its latest post about election fraud, as critics claimed its “bots” vanished after drones hit a Russian data center.

“Under President Trump, criminals who disrupt the integrity of America’s elections will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law,” the White House wrote on X Monday.

The post shared a Justice Department announcement of charges against 16 people accused of illegal voting, fraudulent voter registration and related election crimes.

A Raw Story review of the 176 most relevant replies Monday found that 138 opposed or mocked the White House. Only 19 backed it, and 19 more could not be classified.

“So Trump and Elon are going to jail?” one user asked.

“Hey! Where’d all the bots go?!?” another user wrote.

“Are you sad your RUSSIAN bot farms were destroyed?” a third user asked.

“Sixteen down, tens of thousands to go!” wrote one of the few users who backed the White House.

“Holy s— read the comments. The bots are completely gone,” Quadcarl, an X user with nearly 48,000 followers, wrote 22 minutes after the White House posted.

“Lmao usually these posts are filled with bootlicking bots….they’re all gone!” wrote the account Wu Tang is for the Children, which has more than 300,000 followers.

Their posts on X show the claim spread among popular accounts, but the posts are not evidence that it is true.

“Now that Russia data centers are getting pounded by Ukraine, your bots are going away,” another user replied to the White House.

Yandex, a Russian tech company sometimes called “Russia’s Google,” said Sunday that a drone attack completely shut down its data center in the Vladimir region, Reuters reported.

It was the third major Yandex data center knocked out in a few days, after strikes on sites in Sasovo and Kaluga, according to Reuters.

Yandex has blamed Ukraine for the Kaluga attack, but Ukraine has not officially claimed the strikes, The Deep Dive reported.

Automated traffic from Yandex’s network fell to near zero around the start of Oct. 11, according to Cloudflare Radar data cited by The Deep Dive. At one point that day, requests stood at 0.3% of the chart’s peak, compared with 88.2% at the same hour a week earlier.

The Deep Dive writer JP Alegre cautioned that knocking out so much of Yandex’s infrastructure would likely cut automated requests even if no influence operation ran there.

“The chart can’t separate fewer bots from fewer working servers,” Alegre wrote.

An artificial intelligence (AI) tool could help doctors predict a woman's risk of developing breast cancer years in advance, according to new research.

In a new study, published in the American Journal of Roentgenology, researchers at NYU Langone Health and its Perlmutter Cancer Center tested an AI model designed to estimate a woman's risk of developing breast cancer within five years.

The tool looks at several years of a woman's 3D mammograms to track changes in breast tissue over time, rather than looking only at the latest scan, according to the researchers.

giant_tortoise_aldabra_population_reboun:
A landmark survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has revealed the once-endangered species is now thriving.

The latest count of tortoises on the Seychelles atoll of Aldabra revealed that there are approximately 180,000 living on the islands.

This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of the Seychelles.

The team, led by the Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, analyzed five years of tortoise counts collected between 2018 and 2022.

It is the first update since the widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Aldabra Atoll (a ring of coral islands in the Indian Ocean east of Africa) is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises can be found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galapagos.

“More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve,” said Dr. Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF.

“This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises on the island.

But a recovery program meant the island became a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a UNESCO site in 1982.

Now, researchers are saying it’s one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it.

“Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring program is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr. Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

MORE FROM THE SEYCHELLES: Nearly 200-year-old Tortoise Becomes First to Contribute Extraordinary Epigenome to Research on Aging

“By modeling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, so the conservationists intend to be vigilant.

The study authors say that invasive mammals remain a key threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings.

The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

“These results are great news for the tortoises and testament to the fantastic work done in the field,” said Dr Dave Hudson, postdoctoral research associate at the University of Exeter, Cornwall.

“Hopefully we have provided the conservation managers the evidence they need to track future change and act early as the tortoises face increasing pressures from climate change, drought, and invasive species.”

Cybercrime losses reached nearly $21 billion last year, prompting Kurt Knutsson to warn of increasingly sophisticated AI scams. He joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to break down the FBI data, highlighting that investment fraud alone cost victims $8.65 billion. Knutsson hosts a free live class to teach families how to protect their money and secure accounts.

If you've ever wondered how much damage a scammer could really do with your name, phone number and home address, the answer is probably more than you'd expect.

Those three details are generally not enough by themselves to empty your bank account, take out a major loan or completely steal your identity. However, they can give a scammer a believable starting point. From there, the goal may be to trick you into revealing the more sensitive information they still need.

That is what makes seemingly basic personal information so useful to criminals. Here's what a scammer can actually do with those details, the warning signs to watch for and the steps you can take to make yourself a harder target.

Join us for a free CyberGuy LIVE class.

Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson shares practical ways to stay safer, smarter and more confident with technology. Explore classes on stopping spam, phone security, financial protection and using AI to get better health care . Each class is free, easy to follow and comes with a free printable checklist .

See the classes and register at CyberGuyLive.com

THE SECRET LIST THAT TELLS SCAMMERS YOU'RE AN EASY TARGET

Scammers can use your name, phone number and home address to create convincing phishing attacks, impersonate trusted companies and target your financial accounts. (Photo by Thomas Trutschel/Photothek via Getty Images)

Your name, phone number and address may already appear in public records, old directories, property records or data broker databases. As a result, people sometimes assume there is little risk if a stranger already knows them. The problem starts when those details are combined.

A scammer may add information from a data breach, social media account, people-search site or earlier phishing attempt. Suddenly, the person contacting you may know where you live, your phone number, the names of relatives or other details that make a fake story sound legitimate.

That is why a scam call can feel so convincing even when nobody has actually hacked your phone or bank account. Data brokers can also collect information such as current and previous addresses, phone numbers, approximate age and possible relatives. A scammer may use those details to learn more about you before making contact.

Here are some of the most common ways that information could be used.

A scammer who knows your name and address can pretend to represent your bank, utility company, delivery service or government agency. For example, hearing someone read your correct home address may make the call seem legitimate. However, knowing personal information does not prove that the caller is really from the company they claim to represent.

Once someone has your address, they can send fraudulent invoices, fake prize notices, counterfeit checks or other deceptive mail directly to you. Because the material arrives at your real address and may include your full name, it can look more credible than a random email or text.

Your phone number can also become part of a SIM-swap or account-takeover attempt. A phone number and address alone usually will not be enough to take control of your wireless account. Still, a criminal may combine those details with passwords, PINs or other information stolen elsewhere. If they successfully move your number to another SIM or device, they may then receive calls and text messages intended for you, including some verification codes.

This is where the risk can grow quickly. Perhaps one database exposes your phone number and address while another contains an old password or Social Security number. Criminals can combine pieces from multiple sources to create a much more complete profile. That information may then be used for identity theft, account takeovers or additional phishing attempts.

Personal details can also strengthen family-emergency scams. A criminal may know your relative's name, where you live or other information that helps support a fake story. With AI-generated voices making impersonation scams increasingly believable, personal details can make an already emotional call even harder to judge.

Some services still rely on personal details or knowledge-based questions during account recovery. A scammer may try information such as your address, phone number or other details to see whether they can get further into a password-reset or identity-verification process. They may still need additional information. However, every correct answer can move them one step closer.

Knowing your name, phone number and address does not automatically give someone access to your bank account. Those details alone are also generally insufficient for opening major financial accounts or taking out loans because financial institutions typically require additional identity verification.

However, I would not treat that as a guarantee. The bigger concern is that a scammer can use the information they already have to convince you to provide what they are missing, such as a password, verification code, Social Security number, bank account information or credit card number. In other words, your basic information may be the beginning of the attack rather than the end.

HACKER CLAIMS 7.49M CUSTOMER RECORDS STOLEN FROM AMERICAN UTILITY COMPANY

Your name, phone number and address may not be enough to steal your identity, but scammers can combine those details with information exposed in data breaches. (Photo by Silas Stein/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Suppose your phone rings and the caller immediately knows your full name and home address. Then they tell you there is suspicious activity on one of your accounts. That specificity can cause you to listen a little longer. Next, they may ask you to verify a code that just arrived by text, confirm an account number or transfer money to supposedly protect it. This is where I want you to be especially careful. A caller knowing something about you is not proof that the caller knows you. Personal information should never replace independent verification.

Watch for these warning signs:

One unusual call does not necessarily mean someone has stolen your identity. Still, several warning signs appearing together deserve attention.

A few precautions can make it much harder for someone to turn basic information into a successful scam.

Search your name, phone number and address and see what comes up. You may find people-search sites and data brokers displaying information you would rather keep private. Where possible, submit opt-out requests to have those listings removed.

Ask your wireless carrier what protections it offers against SIM swaps and unauthorized number transfers. Set a strong account PIN or password and enable any available port-out or number-transfer protection.

If an unexpected caller knows your address, bank name or another personal detail, do not assume that means the call is real. Hang up and contact the company directly using a phone number or app you already trust.

Turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) for important accounts. When possible, I prefer an authenticator app, passkey or physical security key over text-message verification for especially sensitive accounts. That reduces the damage a successful SIM swap could cause.

Choose a private family verification word or phrase that family members can use if someone calls claiming there is an emergency. Do not post it online or use something a stranger could easily guess.

Avoid confirming or correcting personal details during an unexpected call. If someone says, "You're still at 123 Main Street, correct?" you do not need to tell them your new address. End the call and verify the request independently.

Review bank and credit card activity for transactions you do not recognize. You should also check your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries. If you are concerned about identity theft, a credit freeze can make it harder for someone to open new credit accounts in your name. Credit freezes are free and can be placed with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.

Personal information tends to accumulate online over time. One breach may expose an email address while another exposes an old password. Meanwhile, data brokers may already have your address, phone number and information about your relatives.

An identity theft protection service can help you watch for signs that some of this information is being misused. Depending on the service and plan, that may include identity monitoring, credit monitoring, financial account alerts, data broker removal and help recovering from identity theft.

Identity and financial monitoring: Some services can alert you to certain suspicious activity involving your identity, credit or financial accounts.

Data broker removal: Some plans include tools that can help remove your personal information from supported data broker and people-search sites.

Scam support: Certain services offer access to specialists who can help you evaluate suspicious messages, calls or websites.

Identity restoration: If identity theft occurs, some providers offer restoration specialists who can help guide you through the recovery process.

Loss coverage: Depending on the provider and plan, you may also get insurance or reimbursement for certain eligible identity theft expenses or losses. Coverage limits, exclusions and availability vary, so read the terms carefully.

No identity theft service can prevent scams or guarantee that your personal information will never circulate online. However, monitoring and alerts may help you spot suspicious activity sooner.

Even with strong security habits, identity theft can still happen. Your Social Security number, financial information or other personal data may already be exposed without you realizing it. If you are concerned, consider using an identity theft protection service as an added layer of monitoring and recovery support. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at Cyberguy.com

It is also worth checking whether your email address or other personal information has appeared in a known data breach. Free breach-checking tools can help you identify exposed accounts so you can change affected passwords, turn on two-factor authentication (2FA) and take other steps to lock them down.

If you notice suspicious activity, act quickly. The first priority is to stop any potential damage and determine whether someone has gained access to your accounts.

Most importantly, do not let someone pressure you into making a quick decision. Scammers rely on urgency to keep you from checking whether their story is real.

SCAMMERS ARE COMING FOR YOUR MONEY. HERE’S THE ONE THING YOU MUST NEVER DO

Criminals can use basic personal information to impersonate banks, delivery services and government agencies in attempts to steal passwords and verification codes. (Photo by Silas Stein/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Your name, phone number and address may not seem like highly sensitive information, especially when some of it can already be found online. Still, those details can give a scammer enough material to build a much more believable story. I would pay less attention to how much a caller knows about you and more attention to what they want you to do next. If they ask for money, a password, a verification code or another sensitive detail, end the conversation and verify the request yourself. You probably cannot erase every trace of your personal information from the internet. However, you can reduce what is exposed, lock down important accounts and make sure a stranger cannot use a few correct details to earn your trust.

When Scott Golden and his wife Stephanie Cohen sold their Upper West Side condo in July, they thought they were done with New York’s sky-high taxes.

Instead, they were slapped with an additional $48,949 bill on the way out — roughly 25 times their regular property tax bill.

The Miami-based couple, who run an insurance brokerage firm, are among the thousands who were retroactively slammed by the state’s controversial new pied-à-terre tax on luxury second homes.

And now they’re teaming up with other homeowners and a New York City co-op in the latest lawsuit contesting the legality of a new state-imposed tax that was initially pitched by Gov. Kathy Hochul and socialist Mayor Zohran Mamdani as targeting billionaires — but also hits owners of less expensive second homes.

“I think it’s blatantly unfair that they are targeting and discriminating against out-of-staters,” the 63-year-old Golden told The Post.

“And there was no ability to plan in advance. If we had known, we would have sold earlier,” added Golden, who got $6.55 million for the Riverside Boulevard property.

The suit, filed Sept. 29 against the Hochul administration in state Supreme Court, alleges the second-home tax violates the US and state constitutions by unlawfully discriminating against nonresidents, imposing unfair burdens on homeowners and cooperative buildings and applying retroactively to Jan. 5.

That’s nearly five months before it was enacted on May 28 by Democratic-controlled state Legislature and Hochul at the behest of Mamdani to raise $500 million for the city budget.

Others who’ve joined the litigation include Kent Barwick, a New York City civic legend who previously headed the city’s Landmarks Preservation Commission and the Municipal Arts Society, and his wife, June.

Barwick purchased his co-op apartment on Mott Street in Little Italy in 1972 and lived there full-time until he and his wife moved upstate to Cherry Hill a few years ago. They kept the co-op, which the city values at nearly $2.1 million, as a part-time residence.

When the second-home tax kicked in, the senior couple was slammed with a whopping $83,603 bill on top of the $24,984 they must pay in normal property taxes — bringing the entire tab to $108,587.

“For us, for people of modest means, both retired, it meant suddenly getting a property tax bill that was four times higher than what we were paying,” said Barwick, 85. “Now we have to figure out a way to come up with an additional $80,000.”

June conceded they might have to sell the co-op if they can’t come up with the money.

The plaintiffs and others being slammed have to pay the new tax by January.

Mamdani vowed to forge ahead with the tax rollout two weeks ago even after a judge ruling on a related lawsuit ordered the city to go back to the drawing board and essentially start the process from scratch. Instead, the city opted to appeal the decision.

Jim Whelan, president of the Real Estate Board of New York, which is funding the lawsuit and vehemently opposes the new tax, said the perils raised by the plaintiffs show that the “second-home tax is hurting New Yorkers, not the out-of-state billionaires its supporters promised to target.”

“Their stories demonstrate why this tax is misguided, unconstitutional, and unfair to the very people who live, work, and invest in New York,” he said.

The Mayor’s Office did not return messages.

Hochul spokesperson Kassie White said, “While this lawsuit about the administration of the tax is a matter for the city and the courts to work through, the governor continues to believe that people who can afford a multimillion-dollar second home in New York City can afford to pay their fair share.”

Another death was reported in Jefferson County, Ala., which includes Birmingham.

As of 11:50 a.m. ET Saturday, about 780,000 power customers remained without power in Florida, Alabama and Georgia, according to the monitoring site Poweroutage.us. That figure had been closer to 900,000 earlier Saturday.

In Florida, the worst outages were in counties such as Santa Rosa; Holmes; Washington; and Walton – all of which had more than 80% of their residents without power, Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said in a morning news conference.

The governor said some 16,000 utility workers were busy trying to get power returned to homeowners.

"Last night in the wee hours of the morning, those crews began working as early as 3 a.m.," DeSantis said. He added that teams were also working to remove trees blocking main roads -- and that both I-10 and Route 98 were open as of Saturday morning, along with all state bridges.

Isaias made landfall near Destin, Fla., as a Category 2 hurricane around 8:30 p.m. local time Friday night, packing 105 mph winds, according to theNational Hurricane Center. It brought a storm surge of some 5 feet -- short of the 6 to 9 feet forecasters had said was possible if landfall coincided with peak high tide. It arrived roughly two hours before high tide in Destin.

Isaias was downgraded to a post-tropical storm hours after making landfall. By 5 a.m. local time on Saturday, its sustained winds had dropped to 35 mph, as the system sped its way through Alabama.

"Multiple trees and power lines are down across the county,"tweeted the emergency management agency in Jefferson County, Ala. It told residents to "avoid unnecessary travel if possible while crews clear roads and restore service."

CAIRO (AP) — The international airport in Saudi Arabia's capital, Riyadh, was attacked again Saturday as the kingdom faces an extraordinary series of assaults in the new front in the Iran war. President Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the U.S. should join Saudi strikes against the Tehran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen.

The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. On Saturday, a missile struck a complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights and many people were wounded, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to speak to the media.

"We may. We're going to look at it," Trump said of intervening. "We just found out about the recent attack. So we'll make a decision. We move very quickly."

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis. There was no immediate statement from the rebels, who earlier Saturday accused Saudi Arabia of striking Sanaa International Airport in the Houthi-held Yemeni capital.

Saudi civil aviation authorities said airport operations were suspended and the extent of injuries and damage was being assessed. An official notice to aviators said the suspension was through midnight. The airport had a heavy police presence, with all entrances blocked, and lights around the complex were dimmed.

Flights diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the United States, Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.

The attacks on Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, have rattled markets and the region. And yet the Saudi energy ministry hours after the latest one was still promoting a major international energy conference set to begin in Riyadh on Sunday.

Fighting in Yemen between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces has escalated, with the Saudi-led coalition providing air support for government forces attempting to reverse recent Houthi gains along the Red Sea. Those gains gave the rebels better surveillance of shipping on a corridor that is a crucial alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has been attacking ships.

Though the Houthis have told the AP and others they are only targeting Saudi shipping as part of a blockade in retaliation for one imposed on them, concerns about wider attacks persist. The Houthis previously attacked other ships after the war in Gaza began, calling it solidarity with Palestinians. A U.S. bombing campaign sharply limited that.

Saudi Arabia is running low on missile interceptors and has asked France, Britain, Pakistan and Egypt to deploy air defense support to the region, regional officials told the AP last month, with one noting that the U.S. has seen its own stock dwindle during the war with Iran.

Officials have said U.S. assistance has included intelligence sharing, target identification and planning for the latest offensive against the Houthis.

On Saturday, Saudi Arabia said its foreign minister and Omani counterpart spoke by phone about the importance of "supporting diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions" in the region. Oman, which lies across the Strait of Hormuz from Iran, has played a mediator role at times in the region.

Meanwhile, Saudi authorities warned the public this week that "filming, publishing or sharing information related to countering missiles and drones and their impact sites exposes you to legal liability."

The Houthis this week warned global airlines "for the last time" about the potential consequences of operating in Saudi airspace, which they described as a theater for their military operations.

At least 291 flights at the Riyadh airport had been canceled over the past 24 hours, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware. Before the latest attack, Air India, FlyDubai, Lufthansa Group and Pakistan International Airlines were among airlines suspending flights to and from Riyadh and other Saudi airports for varying periods.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency had expanded its guidance on Saudi airspace, noting the Houthis' ability to strike targets deeper inside the kingdom, including Riyadh, and a "greater focus on aviation infrastructure."

The missile and drone attacks and interception efforts "create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft," it said.

Two regional officials said Houthi attacks on the Riyadh airport on Thursday damaged three planes. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren't authorized to brief the media. The Saudi national carrier said one of its aircraft was damaged while it was on the ground, with no passengers on board.

This week, my wife and I are celebrating our 35th wedding anniversary. Of course, the inevitable question is, “Where would you like to go for dinner?” The ritualistic play then begins as my wife tells me she doesn’t care and asks me to choose. You can guess how the story proceeds from here. It is another example of the seeming ambiguity of choice: not necessarily knowing what we want but certainly knowing what we don’t want.

In previous essays, I’ve mentioned Jean-Paul Sartre’s Being and Nothingness, and today will be no exception. Sartre describes a man and a woman on a date. The man takes the woman’s hand. She can pull her hand away or grasp his hand firmly, with either action sending a clear signal to the man. But there is a third choice: she can do neither, leaving her hand where it is and behaving as though the situation were somehow outside her decision. That refusal to decide is itself a choice.
