The attacks on September 11, 2001, unleashed a wave of Islamophobia in the United States that resulted in widespread harassment and persecution of Muslim Americans. In addition to vigilante attacks targeting Muslims or those perceived to be Muslim, there was also state repression including police roundups, community surveillance, prosecutions on often flimsy terrorism charges and mass deportations. Meanwhile, the wars launched by the United States in the aftermath of 9/11 have killed close to 1 million people in Afghanistan, Iraq, Pakistan, Yemen and elsewhere, according to the Costs of War Project at Brown University.

“There were so many responses to 9/11. One was obviously fear and grief and shock, but another was rage. And so much of that rage was towards Muslims and those who looked like Muslims,” says award-winning journalist Rozina Ali, author of Seasons of Fury: Four Families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America.

We also speak with Fahd Ahmed, executive director of Desis Rising Up and Moving, or DRUM, a grassroots organization for South Asian and Indo-Caribbean immigrant workers and families in New York City. He says that much of the anti-Muslim retaliation came from law enforcement.

“In New York City and in New Jersey and across the country, … we saw these massive roundups of mostly Muslim men or people that were perceived to be Muslim, and this included citizens, green card holders and undocumented people,” says Ahmed. “There was at least 1,200 men that were picked up this way.”

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat.

ANJALI KAMAT: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, the city’s first Muslim mayor, will be attending the 9/11 commemoration ceremony this week along with the families of victims. Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani and former New York Governor George Pataki have led critics who say Mayor Mamdani should skip the ceremony.

Speaking on Newsmax, Giuliani criticized Mayor Mamdani for giving a symbolic pen to his chief legal counsel, Ramzi Kassem, during the signing of an executive order establishing September 11th as an official citywide day of remembrance and service. Ramzi Kassem previously represented several detainees at Guantánamo Bay. Giuliani then went on an Islamophobic tirade against Mayor Mamdani.

RUDY GIULIANI: Too many Americans fall for that Islamic propaganda, which is the reason they’re taking over certain parts of America and certain parts of Europe. They have every desire to take us over. This is not they want to be just another religion. They — they want to dominate us. That’s what they’re taught from the day they begin their extremist religious education. Mamdani is a clear — a clear supporter of that.

ANJALI KAMAT: A circulating online petition that expresses concern regarding Mamdani’s attendance at the ceremony has reached 100,000 signatures. This was Mayor Mamdani’s response to Giuliani’s remarks.

MAYOR ZOHRAN MAMDANI: What I want this week to be a focus on is on the families whose loved ones were stolen from them 25 years ago in the horrific act of terror of September 11th, and a focus also on the first responders who gave everything they could to this city and to the people who came together to try and help their fellow New Yorkers.

AMY GOODMAN: For more on Islamophobia after 9/11 and its impacts on communities here in the United States, we’re joined by two guests. Rozina Ali is an award-winning journalist, a New York Times contributing writer, author of the new book, Seasons of Fury: Four Families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America. She’s reported on the “global war on terror” from Egypt, Afghanistan, Iraq and Syria. And Fahd Ahmed is the executive director of DRUM. That’s Desis Rising Up and Moving, a grassroots group for South Asian and Indo-Caribbean immigrant workers and families in New York City. He also runs DRUM Beats, one of the first organizations to endorse Zohran Mamdani during his run for mayor.

We welcome you both to Democracy Now! Let’s begin with Rozina. You spent years writing this book. This is a sacred week here in New York, this 25th anniversary of 9/11. Talk about what happened after 9/11, the rise of hate against people of the Islamic faith.

ROZINA ALI: There is — there were so many responses to 9/11. One was obviously fear and grief and shock, but another was rage. And so much of that rage was towards Muslims and those who looked like Muslims. Around the country, we obviously saw a lot of hate crimes, violent killings of, actually, Brown people who were not Muslims, but they were actually Sikhs. There were also, in Bridgeview, outside of Chicago, a mass group of about 300 people who marched towards a mosque shouting “Death to Arabs!”

And I think what’s particularly fascinating, too, is what the government did, which was, in the weeks after, in the days and weeks after, they started arresting people. They started arresting Muslim and Brown men and boys from streets, from their homes, from their workplaces.

ANJALI KAMAT: I want to bring Fahd Ahmed into the conversation. Fahd, executive director of DRUM, Desis Rising Up and Moving, you’ve been a grassroots organizer with DRUM for over 25 years. Take us back to that immediate aftermath and that panic and fear that Rozina talked about. What was it like organizing? And what were people worried about? And what was going on?

FAHD AHMED: Yeah. Within a day or two after 9/11, we had printed a flyer and set up a hotline and said, “If you’re facing hate crimes, if you’re facing discrimination, if you’re facing targeting, please reach out to us.” And the calls that we started getting were largely related to people experiencing targeting by law enforcement. I remember one call being children calling us and saying, “My father left for work four days ago, and he hasn’t come home.” Women calling and saying, “The police burst down my door, and they grabbed my brother and my husband, and I don’t know where they are.” Workers called and said, “A black van pulled up and grabbed my co-worker and another guy off the street and just drove off with them.”

And so, in New York City and in New Jersey and across the country, but particularly in New York/New Jersey, we saw these massive roundups of mostly Muslim men or people that were perceived to be Muslim, and this included citizens, green card holders and undocumented people. In the beginning, it was just mass roundups. And then they held them, and then they tried to figure out: What is the reason that we’re holding them? And sometimes they would dig up, you know, false — like, they would make up some charges. But most of the time, they would be able to use immigration, immigrant status. And this was happening at — there was at least 1,200 men that were picked up this way.

AMY GOODMAN: I want to talk about one person. I want to talk about Mohammad Salman Hamdani, a New York City police cadet, trained as an EMT, who was headed to work at Rockefeller University with his Qur’an, then raced to ground zero — we only learned this later — attempting to save whatever lives he could at the twin towers, September 11, 2001. Democracy Now! spoke to his parents on the eve of the second anniversary of his death in 2003, as they joined hundreds in a quiet procession to ground zero. His mother, Talat Hamdani, remembered searching for him for days.

TALAT HAMDANI: The reality started to hit us at that moment. Something did happen to him. And the third day, we went down to the center that they had made for the families to come and write their — give the names of their loved ones. Armory, it was. Yes, it was the Armory. We went down there, and we registered his name, and we gave our swab samples for the DNA. And we made a flyer, searching for him. We put down his name as Sal Hamdani. My brother did not put down his name, the first name, Mohammad, for certain reasons. And we searched for him. Nobody had seen him.

AMY GOODMAN: So, while they searched for weeks through all hospitals, giving their own DNA samples, Salman’s parents, they then went to Mecca to pray. As they were there, the New York Post portrayed Salman as a possible terrorist. The Post article was headlined “Missing — or Hiding? — Mystery of NYPD Cadet from Pakistan.”

TALAT HAMDANI: You know, this is what the newspaper, the Post, printed, a very horrible heading, you know, “Missing — or Hiding?” And amongst the news that the way they presented it, it had, you know, insinuations that he was seen near the — at 11 a.m., he was seen near the Midtown tunnel. And is he really hiding? Most probably. Is he really missing? He’s not missing, but he’s hiding, and he could be one of the terrorists.

AMY GOODMAN: Talat Hamdani’s mother — Talat Hamdani told me how difficult it felt to be Muslim in the United States at the time.

TALAT HAMDANI: We have nieces and nephews in second and third grade, they were at that time. They were in second grade. And believe me, they changed their names. You know, Armeen became Amy, and one became Mickey, and the other one became Mikey, and the fourth one became Adam. And we asked them, “Why you change their names?” Then they said, “You know, because we don’t want to be called terrorists in the school. We are Muslims.” … So, it came at that moment, you know, like a year and half ago, like, “Islam” and “terrorism” were synonymous terms. And that is where I find myself defending myself, my faith, my people, my community, my fellow Americans who are Muslims. Islam and terrorism are not synonymous.

AMY GOODMAN: Talat Hamdani, the mother of Salman Hamdani. In fact, when she was looking for him in hospitals, she said his name was Sal, because she already knew there would be discrimination. The mayor would later apologize. The police commissioner would later apologize. He’s named in the USA PATRIOT Act. And the president, President Bush, would praise Salman for the hero that he was. How typical was this?

FAHD AHMED: It was quite, quite common. You know, a lot of the people that we were encountering in detention centers were people that were just picked out by other people who said that they look suspicious. And there was just a overall framework of anybody that looks Muslim is likely complicit, and let’s just round them up and figure things out.

And maybe just to give an example of to the extent, we heard about Talat searching for Salman. We found a Salman Hamdani in the detention center, and it turned out to be a 53-year-old man. And, you know, there was just tons of these stories of particular neighborhoods, and in particular, in New York City, Midwood and Bay Ridge, that there was just large numbers of men that just disappeared. And so — and it was really disappearance, because, as I mentioned, people would go to work and not come home.

And so, the campaign that we launched was Stop the Disappearances Campaign. And, you know, these people were held incommunicado, without access to lawyers, without being able to contact their families, some for six months, some for nine months. And there was almost, like, a whatever basic constitutional rights exist do not apply in this situation.

ANJALI KAMAT: Rozina, I want to go back to you. I know we’ve been talking about this post-9/11 dragnet and how many Muslim men were kind of caught in this. You’ve got the 1,200 men who were disappeared. But then you also had the special registration. So, talk about that and how many people were affected, and also how the Bush administration kind of used its immigration arm to deal with what they called preventing terrorism.

ROZINA ALI: So, we know one of the things that we have learned over the years is that one of the failures of 9/11, one of the reasons it happened, was because of an intelligence failure, not an immigration failure, except the Bush administration kept using immigration as a tool to clamp down on what they thought were terrorist threats.

What happened after the mass arrests of the 1,200 people was that the Bush administration thought that they should do something a bit more systematic and something perhaps a bit more orderly. And they created what is called the National Security Exit-Entry Registration System, NSEERS, which was basically a registry for men and boys of, you know, at least 15 years of age from about two dozen Muslim-majority countries. They had to register with the government. The result of that was that about 80,000 people registered. Thousands of them were deported, and not a single one was thought to — was found to have ties with terrorism. And there has been no apology about that.

And it’s interesting, because I actually — years later, I interviewed a few former officials, asking about the NSEERS system, and I found two responses. One main response was a lot of them didn’t remember that this — that the Bush administration had instituted this. It wrecked so many lives, but officials just have forgotten. But the other thing, the other response I usually get is, “We did what we had to do, and it was necessary. Civil rights may have been violated, but we did what was necessary.” The problem is, I don’t think it was necessary. My reporting has found that, actually, we didn’t find terrorists this way at all.

AMY GOODMAN: We’re going to go into the four families that you profile in Seasons of Fury, Rozina Ali, award-winning journalist, New York Times contributing writer. And we are also speaking with Fahd Ahmed, the executive director of DRUM, Desis Rising Up and Moving, on this week of the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attacks and what happened after. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN: “Jaano Jot” by Sonny Singh, performing in our Democracy Now! studio. This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report. I’m Amy Goodman, with Anjali Kamat. Our guests are Rozina Ali, author of Seasons of Fury: Four Families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America, and Fahd Ahmed, the executive director of DRUM, Desis Rising Up and Moving. Anjali?

ANJALI KAMAT: Rozina, you write about the long shadow of post-9/11 use of terrorism prosecutions and the material support laws. And you write — one of the families you write about is the family of Matin Siraj, and he was a young Pakistani immigrant. In 2007, Siraj, then just 24, was sentenced to 30 years in prison for plotting to bomb the Herald Square subway station in New York City. Attorneys for Siraj said he was set up by a police informant who pushed the idea of bombing. Democracy Now! spoke to his attorney, Martin Stolar, soon after the sentencing. If we could just go to that clip? Siraj — while they get that clip ready.

ROZINA ALI: So, Matin Siraj was living in New York City. He was living in Queens and working in Brooklyn at his uncle’s Islamic bookstore. And this was during the time of, obviously, the Iraq War. There was a lot of conversation about foreign policy and what the U.S. was doing. Matin was very vocally critical. And he was visited one day by a man who turned out to be an undercover NYPD informant, who befriended him over months and goaded him towards a plot to blow up Herald Square.

Now, it is worth remembering and recognizing that there was actually no details of the plot. There were no weapons. There was no date or time set for the plot. And perhaps most critically, Matin actually tried to back out of this plan multiple times. And yet he was still arrested by the NYPD, convicted and eventually sentenced to 30 years in prison.

ANJALI KAMAT: We have that clip ready. This is his lawyer, Martin Stolar, speaking to Amy Goodman back in 2007.

MARTIN STOLAR: This young man becomes the symbol of terrorism in the United States. In essence, what we have is the New York City Police Department creating a crime so they can solve the crime and claim a victory in the war on terror. That is not the way to investigate terrorism, as far as I’m concerned.

AMY GOODMAN: Is he recorded on tape saying, “I don’t want to do this. I’m going to talk to my mother”?

MARTIN STOLAR: Oh, yes. He’s recorded on videotape, saying, “Wait. I better not do this. I have to check with my parents to see if I really want to go forward with this.”

ANJALI KAMAT: So, he says he has to check with his parents. And the attorney for the case, and you, as well, talk about the use of informants. So, how prevalent was the use of informants at this time? And what did this do to the sort of, you know, community of Muslims in the U.S., who could be — you know, who were dealing with infiltration, being surveilled? Can you talk about how all of that was related to the prosecutions?

ROZINA ALI: So, what’s fascinating to me is the difference between the pre-9/11 era and the post-9/11 era. Before 9/11, law enforcement really did not have good or close relationships with the Muslim community, nor did they have a lot of knowledge about Islam or the Arab world. After 9/11, they were in desperate need of any ties to Muslims, and so they started recruiting informants. And they could recruit informants by paying them or by bribing them and saying, “We’re going to speed up your immigration status or application,” or they would use a stick approach and say, “If you don’t help us, we might make things more difficult for you.”

Eventually, the FBI amassed a base of about 15,000 informants, which is absolutely wild. But what’s so critical is that Muslims became scared of going to the mosque, of going to bookstores, of going to cafes, because these undercover informants were everywhere. They were infiltrating practically every restaurant and cafes, certainly in the Tri-State area, but also around the country.

You know, we have used informants in the past. The FBI certainly has. But in those cases, usually an informant has a tie to a mafia member or a gang member. After 9/11, the only tie that informants had to another Muslim was that they were Muslim.

ANJALI KAMAT: Fahd, you’ve worked with Matin Siraj’s family. What was the impact of his arrest and his being sentenced to 30 years in prison on the community? And, I mean, 25 years after 9/11, what’s changed for the communities you’re working with, working-class South Asian and Muslim communities?

FAHD AHMED: Yeah. We worked with the Siraj family for more than 20 years, and first and foremost, this has absolutely devastated the family. Every day that Matin has spent in prison, his mother and his family have been in prison with him. Every single day. The family, it becomes hard to find work. Your own family becomes afraid: Do I stay in contact with them, or do I not? If I stay — if I support them, will I get targeted? And that same dynamic plays out in the community. People that were your neighbors now are like, “I’m not sure who — should I talk to this family? Who should I talk to?”

And what we saw was the complete devastation of the social fabric in Muslim communities for many, many years, for almost two decades, to where people were afraid to have political conversations. And, you know, if you know anything about Muslim communities and masjids, like, it’s — that’s pretty much all people do, is you do the ritual, like, religious things, and then you sit around and talk about what’s happening back home, what’s happening here, what do we think about the war, what do we think about this. And there were large number of places where people said, “No political conversations allowed.” You know, there was like Muslim student associations that started putting up signs: “Political conversations here are not allowed.”

And all of this was happening at a time that several Muslim countries were being targeted by U.S., U.S. wars, while civil rights of Muslim communities were being violated. And so, our communities were in this difficult situation that at the very moment where people needed to defend themselves, there was a high level of uncertainty on: Can and should we talk, or should we not talk? Should we engage in political activism, or should we not?

AMY GOODMAN: And this, of course, all didn’t begin 9/11. Rozina, you write about Abdeen Jabara, co-founder of the American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee and longtime leader of the National Lawyers Guild. In the 1970s, he exposed the Nixon administration’s surveillance program against Arab Americans and forced the NSA to admit it had been spying on him, Abdeen, since 1967. We spoke to him in 2013 about his groundbreaking case.

ABDEEN JABARA: I had been very, very active in Palestinian support work. And one day I read in Newsweek magazine, in the Periscope section, that 26 Arabs in the United States had been targeted for surveillance, electronic surveillance. So, I thought, surely, some of those had been clients of mine or had talked to me on the phone about issues and so forth. And that’s when I brought the lawsuit. …

I was surprised, after all the revelations about the Snowden-NSA brouhaha, that nobody had looked back at what had occurred back in the — in the ’70s to show that at that time it came out in the press that over 1,600 Americans had been surveilled by the NSA.

AMY GOODMAN: So, that’s Abdeen Jabara, former head, founder of American-Arab Anti-Discrimination Committee, and at the time, we had a lower third that said “friend of Alex Odeh.” Rozina, explain.

ROZINA ALI: So, Alex Odeh was one of the vice presidents of the ADC for the West Coast chapter. And in 1985, there was a bomb in that office that killed him, unfortunately. And his murder was never solved, although at the time the FBI did suspect the Jewish Defense League, and there was actually a lot of conversation about the rise of terrorism in the U.S. against Arab Americans coming, emanating from the JDL. Unfortunately, what has happened in these intervening years since then is that terrorism has become more and more aligned with Islam, and we forget that terrorists can be from any group or any ethnicity or any religion. But really, what this long history shows us, that how we think about terrorism and Arabs and Muslims has been a problem much longer than 9/11.

ANJALI KAMAT: And where do you see — I mean, your book is called Seasons of Fury, and you trace the kind of changing Islamophobia both through the institutions and practices and bigotry of people, but also different administrations. Where are we today, 25 years later? I mean, this is also a time of the rise of so many Muslim politicians, outspoken Muslim politicians, including our own mayor, Mayor Mamdani, who is once again facing Islamophobic attacks.

ROZINA ALI: I would say we’re probably at a really — a worse place than we have ever been, because it is so accepted, and policymakers are peddling anti-Muslim rhetoric. But just even take the example of Giuliani. It’s funny to me that he apologized to Talat Hamdani, because, years later, he’s essentially doing the same thing over again towards Mayor Mamdani by saying Muslims cannot be victims of 9/11, right? A Powerball ticket sold at a gas station in western Illinois was the sole winner of the $1 billion jackpot, ending a three-month drought without a top-prize victor.

More than 3 million tickets won lesser cash prizes.

Trump administration officials earlier this year killed a federal criminal investigation into the coal empire owned by Sen. Jim Justice, a Republican from West Virginia and a close ally of the president’s.

The investigation examined potential criminal violations of the Clean Water Act by the multistate mining operations largely run by Justice’s son, Jay, according to current and former officials familiar with the matter.

The criminal probe was a significant escalation in the yearslong effort to police serial pollution offenses by Virginia-based Southern Coal and dozens of affiliated mining operations controlled by the family. In the past decade, Southern Coal and other Justice corporations have racked up tens of thousands of alleged violations of the Clean Water Act and have been sued repeatedly by state and federal prosecutors over their failure to properly follow environmental laws at their mining sites.

The investigation shuttered by the Trump administration was a joint effort by prosecutors and investigators with the Environmental Protection Agency, the Department of Justice’s Environmental Crimes Section and the U.S. Attorney’s Office of the Western District of Virginia to probe whether the incessant violations of antipollution laws had risen to the level of criminal behavior, people familiar with the matter said.

People familiar with the investigation told ProPublica that prosecutors believed they had a strong case. They initially had the blessing of Robert Tracci, President Donald Trump’s top official in the Western District of Virginia, to move forward.

But in recent months, as prosecutors battled the Justice companies in court over subpoenas for records, the Office of the Deputy Attorney General shut down the probe. At the time, Todd Blanche still headed the office, before assuming the role of acting attorney general in April.

“They were told ‘pencils down,’” a person familiar with the investigation said.

That prosecutors were even conducting a criminal investigation is noteworthy, people said, because the DOJ only charges a dozen or so criminal Clean Water Act cases each year. It is rare for top DOJ officials to derail a criminal investigation initiated by career officials at such an early stage, people familiar with the case said.

“I’ve never heard of that happening before,” said former federal prosecutor Rick Mountcastle, speaking generally about DOJ protocols. Mountcastle spent 24 years as a prosecutor in the Western District of Virginia. “There shouldn’t be some sort of untouchables list of people who are immune from enforcement.”

The move is part of a pattern of behavior at the top echelons of the DOJ to push cases against Trump’s political adversaries and ease up on allies.

Environmental enforcement against large polluters has plunged under the second Trump administration. Just days after inauguration, the administration reassigned top career environmental lawyers at the DOJ, including those overseeing the Southern Coal case, to work on the president’s immigration crackdown. At the beginning of the year, Blanche personally ordered prosecutors to stand down from cases against diesel emissions cheating.

We’re still reporting. If you know more about this case or other instances of the Trump administration shutting down criminal investigations, please contact our reporting team.

Molly Redden

Send me tips or documents about lawyers getting special access to the Trump administration, the DOJ rewarding Trump’s supporters and pursuing his enemies, the administration’s legal strategy, and the White House’s judicial appointments.

Steven Ruby, an attorney for the Justice companies, said they became aware of the criminal investigation earlier this year.

“Ultimately the finding of the inquiry by the government was that there wasn’t any evidence to pursue criminal charges,” Ruby said. “There’s never been any intentional wrongdoing by the companies.”

While objecting to the subpoenas in court, the company simultaneously convinced the DOJ to drop the case, he said.

“The Justice companies — because Sen. Justice has been governor and because he’s now a senator — are singled out and put under a microscope, and there’s news coverage of violations and consent decrees and compliance actions,” Ruby said. “But the fact of the matter is that those kinds of issues exist throughout the industry.”

Current and former government officials familiar with the companies’ environmental record called them routine bad actors.

Spokespeople for the EPA and the Western District of Virginia referred questions to the DOJ. Justice’s senate office did not respond to questions.

“There is no case to be made here for a criminal investigation,” Emily Covington, a DOJ spokeswoman, said in an email. “Any career prosecutor who would paint a criminal case as strong is simply a deep state prosecutor continuing to push the priorities of the Biden administration.”

The deputy attorney general’s office is routinely involved with reviewing cases, she added. The office determined that this case was not consistent with the Trump administration’s priorities, she continued, and it was more appropriate to resolve it through the less punitive civil process. “The bottom line is that this was a politically motivated prosecution for a case that can and should be resolved civilly,” she wrote.

The Justice family runs a sprawling coal mining enterprise that extends across the South. Estimates of its fortune fluctuate. Forbes tallied Jim Justice’s net worth to be as much as $1.9 billion until 2021; more recently, it declared him “broke” and facing $1 billion in debt. But environmental groups have accused his companies of misrepresenting their assets to avoid paying environmental penalties.

Ruby said company finances seesaw because coal is a “boom and bust” industry.

Justice, who was first elected governor of West Virginia as a Democrat, announced he had become a Republican at a Trump rally in 2017. Trump backed Justice’s bid for Senate in 2023, amid a contested GOP primary. Justice went on to win the seat, helping Trump clinch a GOP majority in the Senate.

Coal mines often leach dangerous chemicals like arsenic into waterways and are required to strictly monitor pollution discharge and keep it under certain limits. The family’s companies have settled many accusations of environmental violations by agreeing to pay fines and invest in better pollution prevention without admitting or denying culpability.

In recent years, however, the company has repeatedly flouted regulators and the legal process. Jay Justice has been a no-show at court hearings involving Clean Water Act violations in the past, and in 2024 a judge in Alabama issued a civil contempt order against him for his repeated failure to respond to those lawsuits. Ruby, the Justice companies’ lawyer, attributed the violations in that case to surrounding facilities the family does not own. The case is now in mediation.

A number of recent legal proceedings have laid bare the extent to which the Justice companies may have knowingly violated environmental laws, a key threshold for bringing a criminal matter.

Such allegations surfaced in a 2023 civil case brought by the Justice companies’ former chief of environmental compliance Robert Fowler. In the suit, Fowler claimed that Jay Justice blocked him from spending the money necessary to comply with environmental laws, including making court-ordered payments and repairing equipment. As a result, according to emails disclosed in the lawsuit there were at times complaints of near-daily violations of permit water requirements.

In a resignation letter and in subsequent court filings, Fowler said he was concerned the circumstances exposed him to “potential civil and criminal liability.” Fowler declined to comment.

The Justice companies denied Fowler’s accusations. The Justice companies believe the government’s criminal investigation was based primarily on Fowler’s claims, which Ruby dismissed as the allegations of a “disgruntled” former employee.

Last month, a jury in Alabama found that the Justice companies had made false representations to Fowler about his role, but it did not award him the millions of dollars in damages he demanded in his lawsuit. The judge has yet to enter his final ruling.

In the DOJ’s aborted investigation of Southern Coal, prosecutors and federal agents had begun to gather evidence, scrutinizing testimony in the Justices’ various civil trials, and had approached former employees seeking information. Government attorneys also sent subpoenas seeking further documentation, said those familiar with the probe, a move that was opposed by the company’s lawyers.

People familiar with the case said Justice Department attorneys were ready to fight the Justices’ lawyers over the subpoenas.

But before they could move forward, Blanche’s office shut it down.

Sharon Lerner and Ken Ward Jr. contributed reporting. Kirsten Berg contributed research.

We recently covered the “essay wars” in Lightbulb, in which Tony Blair, Keir Starmer and Andy Burnham fired off long missives on the state of the nation. It seems Nigel Farage was feeling left out, for yesterday he published the “first of many” articles on his new Substack account, titled “Britain is a two tier state—against white people”. (It has slightly more likes than my own Substack interview with Yanis Varoufakis, though a far more negative comments section. No one, as far as I know, called our discussion “horse sh*t.)The “white British” ethnic identity has been an increasing point of emphasis on Britain’s populist right—see Ben Ansell’s column from October 2025, in which he criticised Tory MP Neil O’Brien and other right-wingers for using the term. “Let’s call this turn what it is: racist,” he wrote. “This is racism of a type that mainstream politicians have not encouraged since the early 1980s.”As for Farage’s essay, he claims that the British police have become functionally “anti-white”—something he was adamant on in his public statements about Henry Nowak’s murder. But Alan Rusbridger begs to differ. “Before this lie passes into history and becomes the truth,” he writes, we ought to remember various recent investigations, from Hampshire to Charing Cross, that have found serious accusations of racism within police ranks. With this in mind, Alan questions whether anti-racism efforts within the police are really so unfounded.As we approach the ten-year anniversary of Brexit, Alan notes an irony here too: by allowing disinformation and racism to spread unchecked on social media, we are “​​taking back control from the unelected Brussels bureaucrats and handing it to Elon Musk, JD Vance, Nigel Farage, Tommy Robinson and a handful of faceless crypto billionaires.” Ah, the pure air of sovereignty!Speaking of connections between debates about race in the US and UK, CBS News has hired British broadcaster Trevor Phillips, who was previously suspended then readmitted to the Labour party over allegations of Islamophobia. Alan and Lionel Barber speak to NPR’s media correspondent David Folkenflik on Media Confidential about what’s going on at CBS, as controversial editor-in-chief Bari Weiss causes ructions, including at its flagship programme 60 Minutes.Alan has also been busy penning a profile of conductor Nil Venditti for our latest issue. A 31-year-old Italian-Turkish maestro, Venditti likes to talk with audiences before, after and even during performances—and her innovative approach has landed “like a small benign bomb exploding in the world of classical music.”Finally, Keir Starmer has announced a social media ban for under-16s, with Meta, YouTube and Snapchat all arguing that the policy will push teens into even less regulated spaces. It’s a great time to revisit Ethan Zuckerman’s essay from our last edition—a nuanced take on how to balance the harms and benefits of social media for kids. WASHINGTON (AP) — A federal judge has dismissed the remnants of the government’s landmark case against far-right Proud Boys members who were convicted of seditious conspiracy for plotting to attack the Capitol to keep President Donald Trump in the White House more than five years ago.

The case’s dismissal late Friday became a foregone conclusion when Trump last year used his pardon powers to erase every case that the government prosecuted after a mob of his supporters stormed the building on Jan. 6, 2021. The judge who presided over the Proud Boys leaders’ trial saw no basis to preserve the convictions after Trump’s sweeping act of clemency last year.

U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly, whom Trump nominated during his first term, said there is “little mystery” about why the second Trump administration decided to abandon this case and every other Jan. 6 riot case.

“President Trump’s views about the prosecution of those who attacked the U.S. Capitol on January 6 — whether those views are based on fact or fiction — are well known, as is his intention to extend clemency to them,” Kelly wrote.

The judge stressed that his order should not be mistaken as an endorsement of the Department of Justice’s decision to abandon the case. He referred to the Capitol riot as “a perilous event” and an assault on the constitutional imperative for a peaceful transfer of power between presidents.

“Moving forward, if this Nation’s experiment in self-government is to last another 250 years, the American people — no matter their partisan preferences — will have to act together to preserve, protect and defend that miracle through our constitutional framework,” Kelly wrote.

Juries in the nation’s capital separately convicted leaders of the Proud Boys and another extremist group, the antigovernment Oath Keepers, of orchestrating violent plots to keep Trump, a Republican, in power after he lost the 2020 presidential election to Democrat Joe Biden.

A different judge has not ruled yet on the Justice Department’s related request to throw out Oath Keepers’ seditious conspiracy convictions.

Friday’s ruling applied to four of five Proud Boys members who were convicted after a jury trial: Ethan Nordean, Joseph Biggs, Zachary Rehl and Dominic Pezzola. Trump commuted their prison sentences, but they were not covered by the president’s mass pardons.

Former Proud Boys national chairman Enrique Tarrio was convicted at the same trial but received a pardon from Trump. Kelly had sentenced Tarrio to 22 years, the longest prison term in any Capitol riot case.

The Norway soccer federation said it will look to file an official complaint over Folarin Balogun's overturned red card.

The American's one-game suspension at the World Cup was wiped after pressure from US president Donald Trump.

Norwegian federation president Lise Klaveness said the complaint would be looked at on August 6.

US President Donald Trump's role in clearing Folarin Balogun from a mandatory one-game ban at the World Cup is set to provoke a formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators.

The Norway soccer federation said its board of directors will consider filing the complaint at its next meeting, likely on August 6.

"We need our leader in FIFA to say that this was an error," Norwegian federation president Lise Klaveness told The Times in an interview.

After Trump called FIFA president Gianni Infantino, a one-game ban for Balogun's red-card tackle against Bosnia-Herzegovina was deferred so he could play against Belgium with a quarterfinals place at stake.

Belgium beat the US 4-1 after a chaotic 36 hours at the World Cup. The Belgium players were seemingly fired up by one of the greatest controversies in tournament history.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino (left) with Crown Prince Haakon of Norway and Football Association of Norway president Lise Klaveness.  (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Trump called the referee's red card for Balogun after video review a "horrible" call and took credit for getting FIFA to review what should routinely have been a one-game ban.

"We all know that this verdict was influenced from external forces and did not have the proper process," Klaveness said of the FIFA ruling that was unprecedented in the past 60 years at World Cups.

"When you bend a rule like this, you're on a slippery slope that will put the whole game at risk," said the former Women's World Cup player for Norway, who is an elected member of European soccer body UEFA's executive committee.

Klaveness is a lawyer and judge who has positioned the Norwegian federation as a conscience in world soccer since her election in 2022.

"It is a worry for the game when you compromise fundamental rules of the game," she said about not enforcing Balogun's ban.

Norway previously joined a London-based NGO's complaint to the FIFA ethics committee alleging Infantino breached a statutory duty of political neutrality, including by creating a peace prize to award to Trump at the World Cup draw in December.

A group of European politicians launches a bid to begin an investigation into how and why a red card for an American football star was overturned at the World Cup.

The close personal and political ties between Trump and Infantino include the US president believing the soccer official could be a good pick as next secretary general of the United Nations, the New York Post reported this week.

The human rights NGO, FairSquare, also has filed an ethics complaint about the Balogun incident to the International Olympic Committee, where Infantino is an elected member, about breaching its rules on political neutrality.

FIFA and the IOC rarely acknowledge or provide updates on potential cases before their ethics bodies.

The independence of FIFA's process to handle complaints alleging unethical conduct has been questioned since the lead investigator and judge both were replaced in 2017, in the second year of Infantino's presidency.

FIFA has yet to publish documents explaining how its disciplinary judges reached verdicts about Balogun or other World Cup players.

nowak_police_treatment_explainer:
Analysis of evidence and interviews with experts suggests focus by rightwing critics on race misses reality of police failures

As the row over the police handling of the stabbing of Henry Nowak by Vickrum Digwa continues, critics on the right have suggested that a preoccupation with anti-racism played a significant role in the failure by officers at the scene to properly assess what had happened – and resulted in the appalling treatment of Nowak as he lay dying.

Criticisms have focused in particular on a document published by the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC) last year, the police anti-racism commitment. Critics have also claimed that there is a broader sense that the police’s instincts are now to side against white people whenever there is any doubt.

But an analysis of the evidence and interviews with policing experts suggest this account misses crucial aspects of the circumstances that led to a devastating set of failures.

The police anti-racism commitment was produced as part of the police race action plan. But it is not widely known: even some of those who worked closely on the race action plan have never heard of the anti-racism commitment.

It summarises what police chiefs will do to end racial bias. The part that has become controversial this week says: “It does not mean treating everyone ‘the same’ or being ‘colour blind’ (racial equality).”

The home secretary has said she believes the phrasing is “clumsy”. What it is supposed to mean, said one person with knowledge of police thinking on the matter, is that officers should take into account the context and historic experience of different groups with policing.

Someone who is Jewish may need reassurance that police are taking a claim of criminal damage seriously and that hate will be considered as a motive, for instance. A black person may need particular reassurance that a stop and search is for legitimate reasons and not racially motivated.

Ministers accept the document was not sent to officers to act on, but regardless it gives the wrong impression.

Sarah Jones, the policing minister, said: “I don’t think it forms the basis of any training or any police activity. We think the language is wrong, it gives the wrong impression. But I don’t think it affects how our training is done.”

The NPCC made clear the document was not formal policy or training for officers. One source went further, saying few senior officers, never mind those on the frontline, would know it existed, let alone be guided by it.

Police are supposed to treat claims of a racial motivation seriously. But that was different to automatically accepting any claim that an alleged crime was motivated by hate, said Britain’s former head of counter-terrorism, Neil Basu.

Basu, a former Metropolitan police detective who became Britain’s most senior ethnic minority officer, added: “When a victim says something you take it seriously, but that is different to believing it. The policy is supposed to stop police officers ignoring victims without investigating.”

The policy came out of the 1999 Macpherson report into the murder of Stephen Lawrence and was supposed to guide the recording of hate crimes and force better investigation of them.

There are no official figures on anti-white bias in operational policing, but the statistics that do exist show longstanding racial bias against ethnic minorities, and especially against black people.

Police use of force – such as Taser use – and coercive powers such as stop and search are greater against black people than white people, and police chiefs cannot explain why.

The police race action plan, launched after the murder of George Floyd in the US, was meant to tackle the enduring problems police have with race. But there has been little improvement.

An independent assessment of the multimillion pound plan concluded it had had no “meaningful impact”, with police chiefs lukewarm in their commitment.

As Basu points out, every independent report going back to the 1980s, including first by Lord Scarman, then Macpherson in 1999 and Louise Casey in 2023, has found police failing on race.

They made promises but little if anything improved, said Basu. He added that claims the police had overreacted to evidence of bias against black people by being biased against white people were laughable: “How can it be an overreaction to something that was barely reacted to in the first place?”

Officers are taught the national decision making model.

The College of Policing says: “Police decision making is often complex. Decisions are required in difficult circumstances and are often made based on incomplete or contradictory information.

“In addition … those involved [may] deliberately mislead or try to mislead them.”

It provides a framework for officers to justify their decision making. But it cannot protect policing from bad decisions, and that is at the centre of the Nowak case.

One frontline officer with 25 years experience said the “mindset” an officer had when they attended an incident affected how they reacted, and could be difficult to shake off.

This could be shaped by the details the officer was given by their control room. The officer added: “There’s a danger that this clouds judgment. It can fall into: ‘This is the problem I’ve been told to solve, so this is the problem I will solve’.”

The trial judge said that until too late the police were “in ignorance of the fact that [Nowak] had a serious chest wound”.

From the bodycam footage of Nowak’s arrest, it appears the police do not see any blood consistent with a stab wound.

As the judge noted in his sentencing remarks, Nowak’s clothing was dark, and the incident took place when it was dark. The bleeding that resulted from Nowak’s injury flowed into his chest cavity, the judge said.

Donna Jones, the Conservative police and crime commissioner for Hampshire, has asked for a review from the policing inspectorate of these issues, and “how officers are trained to triage competing accounts at the scene of a violent incident”. Her letter asks the inspectorate to examine how officers understand “the physiological presentation of serious internal bleeding”.

Every past and former police source who spoke to the Guardian said they believed “professional curiosity” by officers on the bodycam footage was lacking and questioned the decision to handcuff Nowak.

npr_fertilizer_hormuz:
By

Joe Hernandez

A worker spreads fertilizer after planting potatoes at Bluff View Farms on April 24 in West Jefferson, North Carolina. High fertilizer prices due to the war in Iran have hit farms already dealing with severe weather, tariffs and the high costs of fuel and labor.
                
                    
                    Allison Joyce/Getty Images North America
                    
                
                hide caption

When the war with Iran started, one of the top economic concerns globally was the slowdown of oil shipments. But there was another critical export that got stuck in the region when hostilities began: fertilizer.

Before the war, around one-third of the world's fertilizer transported by sea passed through the Strait of Hormuz, according to UN Trade and Development. The waterway has become a shipping chokepoint in recent months.

With the strait closed, fertilizer shipments from the Persian Gulf slumped and prices rose, affecting countries all around the world that import fertilizer. The war also created a global shortage of natural gas, a key component in nitrogen fertilizer manufacturing.

It caused a massive headache for U.S. farmers who were hit with higher fertilizer prices and limited availability just as they were deciding what to plant for the upcoming growing season.

But the costs borne by farmers don't necessarily get passed on to consumers, and food system experts say they're unlikely to have a major impact on the retail prices of fruit and vegetables.

"Consumers are going to see higher food prices come September to January, once harvests start coming in, and the few months thereafter," said Chris Barrett, a professor of agricultural economics at Cornell University. "Very little of that is going to be directly attributable to fertilizer."

That's because food inflation is generally driven by larger factors affecting multiple parts of the food supply chain, such as fewer workers and high fuel costs.

About one-third of the fertilizer used by U.S. farmers is imported, according to The Fertilizer Institute, an industry trade group. TFI Vice President of Public Affairs Christopher Glen said little of that comes through the Strait of Hormuz.

"But we get impacted in a big way because the fertilizer market is global," Glen said over email. "Even if those tons from the Mideast aren't coming to the US, they are still tons that have been removed from the market and need to be made up elsewhere. That's where the pressure comes from."

An American Farm Bureau Federation survey released in April reported that 70% of respondents said they couldn't afford all the fertilizer they needed this season.

Some farmers are more vulnerable to price swings than others. Producers of corn and wheat, which rely heavily on fertilizer, can spend around a third of their operating costs on fertilizer alone. Half of the farmers who responded to a survey released by the National Corn Growers Association in early April said they wouldn't apply the full amount of fertilizer to their corn crop this year, due largely to higher costs and limited availability.

Because farmers often secure their fertilizer stores well before a growing season begins, some weren't seriously affected by the price swings created by the war in Iran. (Iran said it closed the Strait of Hormuz shortly after it was attacked by the U.S. and Israel at the end of February. U.S. corn growing season typically begins in April.) But they are worried about the future: corn growers who responded to the survey were twice as concerned about the 2027 corn crop as they were about this year's.

This season, some farmers may opt to plant crops that require less nitrogen fertilizer than corn, such as soy beans, in response to rising costs.

According to USDA data, farmers are expected to plant 95.3 million acres of corn this year, down from 98.8 million acres last year. But the total acreage of soybeans is predicted to rise to 85.4 million acres this year from 81.2 million acres last year.

If higher fertilizer costs lead to smaller harvests, that could contribute to modest retail price hikes. A TD Economics analysis estimated that a 2-5% production shortfall in North America could grow food inflation by around 0.1-0.5 percentage points in 2027.

But experts say the costs of the fertilizer shortage will be largely shouldered by farmers.

The amount a farmer spends on fertilizer is a small fraction of the total cost to grow food and get it to grocery store shelves. Just 12 cents of every dollar U.S. consumers spend on food goes to farms, while the rest is received by transportation companies, processors, wholesalers and grocery stores, according to the USDA. And the USDA's National Agricultural Statistics Service reported that U.S. farms spent around 7% of their budgets on fertilizer, lime and soil conditioners in 2024 (though farmers growing crops more reliant on fertilizer such as corn would spend more).

Additionally, farmers don't have much bargaining power to negotiate with wholesalers for higher crop prices when their operating costs rise, according to Rob Vos, a senior research fellow at the International Food Policy Research Institute. "Those buyers will go to other farmers to try and get it cheaper," he said.

But there are factors other than the fertilizer crunch that are more likely to cause food prices to jump. Barrett said the global food industry is facing a "really unpleasant layer cake" of pressures, from tariffs and extreme weather to higher prices on labor, fuel and fertilizer.

"No one of those by itself is especially painful," he said. "But when you add them all up, they become quite painful together."

In parts of Africa and Asia, the effects of the fertilizer shortage could be far worse. Jorge Moreira da Silva, Executive Director of the UN Office for Project Services, said in April that the reduction of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz may prove "very significant and severe" for poorer countries. Less-developed countries that rely heavily on fertilizer from the Persian Gulf include Sudan, Sri Lanka, Tanzania and Somalia.

Some fertilizer prices have begun to fall again in recent weeks, after the U.S. and Iran reached a deal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz last month.

The Trump administration has also taken steps to lower fertilizer costs for American farmers. This week, Trump temporarily suspended "countervailing duties" on certain phosphate imports, which are added to some imported goods to cancel out subsidies provided by foreign governments.

Still, it will be a while before the fertilizer sector returns to normal. Vos estimated that it could take weeks or months for fertilizer manufacturing plants to come back online and return to previous production levels. If high prices stick around, that could snarl the plans of U.S. farmers preparing to plant cool-season crops this autumn, he added.

Barrett said the trouble with the fertilizer industry has also gotten farmers thinking about how they can protect themselves from these kinds of supply-chain disruptions in the future and looking for other ways to replenish their soil, such as manure, compost and cover crops.

"Just like we're seeing more people interested in electric vehicles because the price of gasoline and diesel has gone up, you see more farmers interested in other ways of replenishing soil nutrients as the price of fertilizer has gone up," he said.

by Andrea Hsu, NPR's labor and workplace correspondent

Kwame Crockett started working at the plant a few days a week but now he works full-time hours.
                
                    
                    Julie Holder for NPR
                    
                
                hide caption

Flexible work is something that I've followed closely since the pandemic. Remote work exploded, then was rolled back. The tantalizing idea of a four-day workweek has become a reality in pockets of the country.

But through all this reporting, seldom do I hear about flexibility in a blue-collar job. In fact, I often hear quite the opposite. In 2022, freight railroad workers nearly went on strike as they protested strict attendance policies that kept them away from family events and even doctors' visits. United Auto Workers President Shawn Fain's pitch for a four-day workweek for assembly workers was brushed aside as a pipe dream.

So I was intrigued when I heard from folks at GE Appliances that they had opened the doors to part-time, flexible work at a couple of their plants. It sounded so unusual that I had to go see it myself. I traveled to the company's kitchen appliance plant in LaFayette, Georgia.

Tony Gabbert, director of manufacturing operations, told me the idea began during COVID when workers were staying home just as demand for ovens and ranges was soaring. Some days, Gabbert himself had to work on the line to keep things moving. Amid this crunch, he learned about a staffing company called MyWorkChoice, which recruits part-time workers who could fill in as needed, picking their own shifts through an app.

His boss thought the idea was crazy. Letting outside folks just drop in for a few hours at a time was unheard of in an industry that runs on consistency. But it paid off. Today, about 450 flexible workers join full-time employees on the assembly line each week. Together, they keep the factory humming.

Gabbert says they've discovered that there's an entire population of people out there who don't want to work the traditional 40-hour workweek and don't need or don't care about the benefits that come with full-time jobs. They're often retirees, mothers with young children and people with other jobs or passion projects.

With a push to bring more manufacturing back to the U.S., the workers have to come from somewhere. For GE Appliances, this has proven to be a viable solution.

Warning: Graphic content

When Carly Richardson’s mental health hit a crisis point, she tried to seek help. She asked her community mental health team for more intensive therapy, but was told the resources weren’t available. She was then sent to hospital after she self-harmed, but was discharged after little more than a week, despite telling staff what she was planning.

Before she’d arrived home, she attempted to end her own life.

“I was on the train tracks,” the now 21-year-old said of the incident 18 months ago. In a state of distress, she said police pulled her away and bent back her wrists to move her forward, with a level of pressure that left bruises.

“I was crying from the pain and they didn’t seem at all fazed,” she said. “It was really triggering because I’d been trying to tell myself that the world is a safe place, but it’s so weird when you’re met with responses like that when you’re suffering.

“I felt like a criminal just for being unwell. It was really dehumanising. I didn’t feel like a person anymore – I just felt like an animal.”

Richardson’s story is not in isolation. Last week, 21 prominent mental health and justice organisations released a joint statement calling for systemwide reform, including the implementation of a health-led response to mental health emergencies, with police deployed only when the safety of health workers is at risk. This change is supported by a major 2024 inquiry, cross-bench agreement and the NSW Police.

“Mental crises aren’t a crime,” said BEING Mental Health Consumers chief executive Giancarlo de Vera, who led the statement.

De Vera pointed to the 52 people in mental health crisis who were killed by police in the five years to 2023, and the variable risk of police escalating a situation, rather than providing support.

When a motion on the subject was raised in NSW parliament last Wednesday, Minister for Mental Health Rose Jackson said reform around police first responders remained a “key priority” for the government, but she acknowledged it was “taking time”. In a statement, she said consultations were still ongoing “and we will have more to say soon”.

De Vera said the government had “wasted their term” with talk and sentiments: “You can pave the road with good intentions, but until we see action, nothing’s going to get better.”

Mental health measures announced in the NSW budget did not truly represent a new funding boost, de Vera said, with $108 million of the $112 million promised a re-announcement of previous commitments.

Key to the joint statement – which was also signed by the Royal Australian College of General Practitioners, the college of psychiatrists, law organisations and People with Disability Australia – was a request for the public release of a government-commissioned gap analysis report, which is expected to highlight the funding and staffing gap in each local health district, to allow for better resourcing.

Jackson denied the report was being withheld and said that initial research had been released in collaboration with the Mental Health Alliance over an extended period: “It’s not fair to characterise it as though there’s a document sitting there that hasn’t been released,” as the approval process to make the data publicly available was ongoing.

De Vera said previous releases were “piecemeal updates” and said “the government needs to lay out the full facts so we can get on with the urgent work of fixing the system and saving lives”.

The release of a detailed analysis will assist the health coalition’s call for appropriate funding of mental health services in NSW, de Vera said.

Dr Pramudie Gunaratne, CEO of the Australian Society of Psychiatrists, said the system was “not functioning”.

She said demand for mental health support in NSW emergency departments was at “an all-time high, whereas resourcing seems to be dwindling”.

Gunaratne said community mental health services were “like a desert”, with people unable to access the therapy they needed, leading them to resort to ED admission.

“Something has to change,” she said. “We would never accept this level of under-resourcing for any other part of our health system.”

While Richardson has now found trauma-focused therapy helpful, she said her previous crisis could have been prevented through better access to quality care. She remembered feeling as though she was “hitting a wall” as she oscillated between being turned away for not having a serious enough presentation, and then later being sectioned when her health deteriorated.

“A lot of the times that I have become really unwell, it’s not out of isolation,” Richardson said. “I have tried to get more help, and the resources just aren’t there because the system’s designed in a way where it can only really respond to you once you’re at a breaking point. It’s traumatising.

“You’re either treated like you’re not suffering enough or you’re crazy – there’s no in between.”

Crisis support is available from Lifeline on 13 11 14.

By Hamish Cole

Topic:Renewable Energy

The Crudine Ridge Wind Farm is one of many renewable energy projects within the Central-West Orana Renewable Energy Zone. (ABC Central West: Lauren Bohane)

Penny Sharpe says the development of renewable energy needs to occur "quickly", which will lead to mistakes.

It follows the destruction of an Aboriginal heritage site earlier this year within the Central-West Orana REZ.

The minister says a grant funding program for farmers within the REZ will open in the coming months.

New South Wales Energy Minister Penny Sharpe has conceded mistakes will occur with the rollout of renewable energy projects but says it is necessary to speed up their development.

In March, renewable energy consortium ACEREZ destroyed an Aboriginal heritage rock shelter near Mudgee during the construction of transmission infrastructure for the Central-West Orana Renewable Energy Zone (REZ).

An investigation conducted by the company concluded "failures in site design and on-site construction protocols" led to the irreparable destruction of the site.

Ms Sharpe made the admission after announcing a grant program for producers within the Central-West Orana Renewable Energy Zone at the National Renewables in Ag Conference in Orange on Wednesday.

The Aboriginal rock shelter was demolished during construction of a renewable energy zone in central west NSW. (Supplied: Kylie Manson)

Ms Sharpe said she was "appalled" by the actions of ACEREZ.

"We cannot say to First Nations communities that we will look after your heritage and then have something like that happen.

"You cannot build trust with communities if we don't do what we say we're going to do."

Ms Sharpe said the rollout of the Central-West Orana REZ "has been way too slow" with the state racing to meet its energy targets.

"This infrastructure needs to be built … We are doing it very quickly and when you do things quickly, things go wrong," she said.

"We are seeing more projects being approved and coming out of the system, which is very welcome."

Penny Sharpe made the funding announcement to the National Renewables in Ag Conference in Orange. (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

Dubbo mixed farmer Emily Blackburn implored the state government to ensure producers' concerns were properly considered.

"I really encourage the government to pause, plan and treat landholders fairly and listen to communities.

"I can feel the fear, the angst in my local community."

Ms Sharpe announced at the conference that farmers within the Central-West Orana REZ would soon be able to receive grants to purchase agricultural technology under a state government initiative.

The Wellington Solar Farm generates enough power for the equivalent of more than 140,000 homes. (ABC News: Jess Davis)

The $1.4 million Smart Funding Program will see 70 per cent of the cost of eligible technologies covered by the state government, up to a maximum value of $35,000.

The tools must assist with improving productivity, safety and business resilience, such as drones, water sensors, livestock and crop monitoring devices.

"It will help people with the up-front cost of smart tech on their farms," Minister Sharpe said.

Karin Stark says the funding is a "great start". (ABC News: Hamish Cole)

Karin Stark is a wheat, cotton and barley producer near Narromine, with her property falling within the Central-West Orana REZ.

"Having these types of funding programs is a way of trying to help others within an REZ to ensure that they can see some of the benefits of the money coming in," said Ms Stark, who organised the National Renewables in Ag Conference.

"A lot of communities feel like it has been very rushed, we need to ensure that people understand why the transition is happening and what are some of the benefits.

"It is a great start … But I think a lot more can be done."

Applicants will be required to have completed an Agtech Fundamentals workshop, delivered by the Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development, either online or face-to-face.

Grant applications will open in the coming months, with more than 900 products available for farmers to purchase.

This lab is still trying to identify 9/11 victims. Not everyone wants to know

Inside a lab in Manhattan, forensic scientists in white lab coats are still diligently working to keep a promise made 25 years ago.

They're extracting DNA from thousands of pieces of human remains recovered following the terrorist attacks on the World Trade Center, trying to match them to samples from toothbrushes, razors and other sources provided by family members of victims.

What has changed is the science they're using to draw out the DNA from the remains, and the evolving forensic investigative techniques that didn't exist in 2001.

"When … after years of pushing that science, you're finally able to figure out who it is and return that loved one to their family … that's powerful," said Mark Desire, assistant director of forensic biology at the New York City Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

Forty per cent of the 2,753 people who died at Ground Zero have not had their remains identified, including approximately 10 of the 24 Canadian victims.

Last month, the lab announced it made its first identification of previously unknown remains using a breakthrough technique.

The woman's family chose to keep her name private. It's the first identification the lab has made in a year.

The technique combines DNA testing with genetic genealogy — which uses family tree research conducted by members of the New York City Police Department.

"I think it is sort of a new frontier," said Dr. Jason Graham, New York's Chief Medical Examiner.

"We had really found a breakthrough innovation that's going to open the door, I hope and I believe, likely to many other identifications."

Sharing story of 9/11 'only way I can survive,' says first responder visiting Gander

How Gander, N.L., took care of ‘the plane people’ on 9/11

For Monica Iken-Murphy, whose husband Michael Iken died in the collapse of the south tower where he worked as a bond trader, this development brings renewed hope.

"I didn't get a ring, I didn't get an ID. People got cards. They found papers with their names on it," she said. But for her, "it's like he went to work and that's it. Nothing."

Desire was a rookie scientist in the New York crime lab back on Sept. 11, 2001, and was sent to the scene to preserve evidence soon after the second tower was hit. He had never worked on a mass fatality before.

"One of the … first victims I saw die that day landed right in front of us."

Soon after Desire and his colleague arrived, he heard a sound he described as a "crack," and he realized they were far too close to the south tower as it began to collapse.

Trump's 9/11 statements come under scrutiny again

Amid trade tensions, Americans visiting Gander for 9/11 distance themselves from their president

He sprinted toward a nearby building to take cover and barely made it in time. Debris fell on him just as he was escaping into the building through a broken window.

"It just fell across my legs, shattered my foot — the most violent moment of my life."

He survived, and made it his mission to keep the promise made by then-chief medical examiner Dr. Charles Hirsch to preserve and identify the remains of all the victims.

The World Trade Center was reduced to a 21-metre hill of debris that for visual reference, if spread out, could cover approximately eight city blocks.

Plans were made to excavate debris from the site and move it for sifting and sorting at a landfill site on Staten Island in hopes of preserving whatever remains they could.

"Everything that destroys DNA was present at Ground Zero: the fire, the water to put out the fire, the jet fuel, the diesel fuel, the chemicals in the building, the chemicals on the ground, sunlight, mold, bacteria," said Desire.

'We'll never be able to finish this project': the difficulty of IDing 9/11 victims

Reporting on 9/11: The day the world changed

Excavation work officially ended in 2002, but scientists continued to search for DNA in the remains they had.

Four years later, more debris was found on the roof of a nearby Deutsche Bank building, where more than 700 bone fragments were recovered.

That led to reopening searches in the area that lasted until 2014, leading to approximately 2,000 additional bone fragments being recovered.

At first, the remains were preserved by freezing them.

Later, as best practices for handling remains for forensic purposes changed, they began drying the bone fragments out to preserve them longer.

Nearly 22,000 pieces of human remains have been recovered since 2001.

During the early years, victims were identified using fingerprints, dental records and what was then considered cutting-edge DNA technology.

Since then, science has advanced such that more DNA can be extracted from bone fragments. But it still hasn't advanced far enough.

Bone, Desire says, is the toughest material to get DNA from.

"Blood and hair and skin cells — easy. Bone … you have to pulverize it."

He says thousands of samples that still need to be identified haven't even had DNA extracted because they're so badly burned.

Inside the lab working to identify 9/11 victims

One of the challenges scientists face is whether to keep testing a sample. Each time remains are tested, some of the material is consumed and can't be re-tested. Doing too many tests on one sample risks losing it altogether before a match can be made.

"It's very stressful, because we have remains today that we've tried 10, 15 times over the years," said Desire.

That's why this new technique brings so much hope.

The process involves sending DNA from unidentified remains to an outside lab that can generate a whole genomic sequence.

Then, similar to genealogical methods that have been used to generate new leads in cold cases, New York police conduct family tree searches. If a prospective match is found, it would come back to the medical examiner's office to confirm a relation through DNA testing.

Genetic genealogy is cracking cases once thought unsolvable. Not all police forces can afford to use it

5 Canadian cold cases solved with help of genetic genealogy

Desire noted that there were 47 sets of remains for which they have full DNA profiles that don't match any of the 17,000 reference samples provided by family members.

So the individuals may have relatives that never contacted the lab or provided samples.

"Using genealogy to help identify them, that was an excellent next step."

The chief medical examiner's office is renewing its call to families to provide samples — in hopes it can help make more matches.

Despite the lab's ongoing work, many families of victims whose remains have never been found don't want to know if a match is made.

"That can be very traumatic," said Jennifer Odein, the World Trade Center anthropologist at the New York City Medical Examiner's Office.

She is the direct line between families and the lab, and says some families are contacted multiple times because their loved one has been matched multiple times to their remains.

"And if they've already had phone calls in the past they might have said, 'OK, we've had enough, we've had our ceremony … we're OK with not getting the notification.'

U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra to visit Newfoundland for 25th anniversary of 9/11

Canada-U.S. ties 'so much stronger' than trade war divisions, Manitoba premier says ahead of 9/11 anniversary

Long ago, Abigail Carter, a Canadian expat whose husband Arron Dack died while attending a trade show at Windows on the World in the north tower, decided she didn't need to know if his remains were ever found.

"I know he was there," said Carter. "He called me and that was good enough for me."

She has found her own way to honour him.

Canadian recalls losing her husband on 9/11

At their daughter's wedding this past summer in France, where Carter now owns a chateau, they placed a framed photo of Dack on a chair, and later added a martini — shaken, not stirred, just as he liked it — to make sure his presence was felt.

"He was very funny and very charismatic. He had different personas a little bit. He had a very, very silly, silly side," she said.

Iken-Murphy understands that complexity of grief. She hopes that one day, her husband Michael's remains will be matched to samples provided to the lab, but says she wouldn't want to keep them herself.

"I want to remember Michael as a whole human. With his beautiful face and his blue eyes and his smile."

Instead, she says they'll stay at the repository in the 9/11 Memorial and Museum at Ground Zero where all the unidentified remains are stored by the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner.

The nor’easter took the Big Apple by storm — again.

A 1-year-old boy and 7-year-old girl were among four people hurt by a falling tree in Brooklyn, it surfaced Sunday — as round two of the region’s deadly weekend storm battered the city.

The wet-and-wild storm sent hapless ocean fish swimming through driveways and hungry seagulls diving for dinner in city streets — while prompting a waterlogged NYPD cop to deem it the worst flooding in his Queens neighborhood since 2012’s Hurricane Sandy.

“I mean, there’s horseshoe crabs all the way here up to Broad Channel Drive,” said rubber-boot-wearing off-duty Officer Matt Langdon, 48, standing in the water pooled outside his Beach 84th Street house.

“I moved here to Far Rockaway when I was 10, and this is the worst it’s been since Sandy.”

“Our crawl space is flooded up to the joists,” the cop told The Post on Sunday. “At its highest, it was coming up to my thigh, it was 2-and-a-half-feet deep at my house. My kids are stuck in the house.”

Millions of New Yorkers hunkered down as the storm unrelentingly continued to pummel the area since Saturday with inches of soaking rain, tempestuous winds and rising floodwaters.

Nearly 40,000 people across the Empire State on Sunday morning were left without power, including 19,800 alone in Suffolk County on Long Island, according PowerOutage.us.

A whopping 3.16 inches of rain fell in Howard Beach, Queens, with most city neighborhoods seeing at least an inch since Saturday, National Weather Service data show.

Up to 56 mph winds were recorded in JFK Airport in Queens, with Midtown seeing gusts as high as 47 mph over the storm’s two days, according to the weather service.

The punishing winds felled scores of trees citywide, including one that killed beloved NYCHA repairman Leighton Brown, 56, on Saturday.

Four other New Yorkers — including the little boy and girl — were also nearly flattened by another falling tree Saturday in Kelly Park Playground in Homecrest, Brooklyn, police said.

The tree struck a 40-year-old woman and 41-year-old woman in addition to the kiddies when it crashed down around 5:30 p.m., cops said.

Miraculously, all four were left with minor injuries.

The baby suffered a cut to his cheek, the little girl was left with a broken arm, the 40-year-old woman had a head and wrist injury and and the 41-year-old hurt her head, authorities said.

The near-miss coincided with a “missing” Long Island swimmer who turned out to be alive and well.

The still-unidentified swimmer sparked fears Saturday when he was spotted jumping — and apparently vanishing — into 18-foot waves near Field 3 on Fire Island’s western tip.

But after learning he was the subject of a search off Robert Moses State Park, the man contacted authorities to inform them he was fine, according to a joint statement from New York State Police and New York State Park Police.

“The individual was located alive and well, and no further assistance from the public is needed at this time,” the statement reads.

Beyond dangers of life-and-limb, the storm also yielded downright surreal scenes across the city.

Bewildered Queens mom Fadela, 40, said she woke up Sunday morning to find fish swimming in her driveway.

“Look at the little fish!” said Fadela, 40. “The fish swimming in the driveway, a whole crew of the little ones! Look! This is a first for us.”

A happy seagull also swooped down apparently to try to catch fish swimming along a flooded Far Rockaway street Sunday, video taken by The Post showed.

The seagull’s dive was unsuccessful, as the shorebird’s feet were empty as it lofted back above the water.

The fishing expedition unfolded Sunday as water inundated Beach 84th Street and Beach Channel Drive.

The flood not only brought schools of bait fish onto what’s normally dry land but also prehistoric-looking horseshoe crabs.

Switch between CA and NY editions here.
