The presence of an El Niño will likely bring less rainfall and warmer temperatures to parts of Australia. (Supplied: Taryn Seccombe)

The US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says an El Niño is now underway in the Pacific Ocean.

In Australia, the presence of an El Niño can intensify drought, bushfires and heatwaves.

There is a 63 per cent chance this year's El Niño could be one of the largest events since records began in 1950.

The US meteorological agency says an El Niño has now formed in the Pacific Ocean that could reach record-breaking intensity in coming months.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) officially confirmed the existence of the El Niño, which is a warming of the Pacific near the equator that affects weather patterns across the globe.

The NOAA's announcement said there was a 63 per cent chance the El Niño would get so intense over the Southern Hemisphere's spring and early summer that it "would rank among the largest El Niño events in the historical record going back to 1950".

Experts said the El Niño, a natural warming cycle, should further heat a globe already warming from fossil fuel pollution and would likely turbocharge extreme weather across the planet.

It was Peruvian fishermen, hundreds of years ago, who first noticed and named El Niño. Little did they realise they had named one of the most consequential climate drivers on Earth. This is how it works.

Meteorologists forecast it will rival or exceed a record El Niño that began in 1997 and helped trigger billions of dollars in damage from heat waves, floods, droughts, tornadoes and wildfires.

Clark University climate scientist Abby Frazier said the warm, deep waters of an El Niño affected weather patterns by bringing "a lot of extra heat to the surface, fuelling a lot of extreme events for a lot of places around the world".

She said, especially in the Pacific, that "it can get dire very quickly".

United Nations secretary-general António Guterres described El Niño as an "urgent climate warning."

"El Niño conditions will pour fuel on the fire of a warming world," Mr Guterres said in a video message.

Forecasters use a region of the Pacific Ocean to determine whether an El Niño or La Niña is underway. (Supplied: NOAA)

The weather pattern's effects vary by region. El Niño often dampens but does not eliminate Atlantic hurricane season activity, but increases the chance of cyclones and typhoons in the Pacific.

In Australia, the climate driver can intensify drought, bushfires and heatwaves.

So while the US East and Gulf coasts may get a break, Hawaii and other islands are more in danger, Ms Frazier said.

Meteorological rhetoric in Australia, including from the media, can at times be inaccurate, misconstrued or just completely fictitious.

The drought-stricken Middle East could benefit, climate scientists said. Other places were looking at more danger.

Parts of western South America, where the first El Niños were noticed decades ago, often get heavy rain and floods, along with an extra warm summer.

India faces more intense heat waves, and has already experienced 45 degree Celsius days this month.

Columbia University climate scientist and El Niño expert Muhammad Azhar Ehsan said north-eastern Africa was likely going to get weather whiplash from intense drought to dangerously heavy rains.

In the US, El Niños can cause more intense storms with heavier rainfall in the South, but they also tend to generally benefit the US agriculture industry, said Jon Gottschalck, operational branch chief at NOAA's Climate Prediction Center.

Michael Ferrari, meteorologist and head of research at the investment research firm Moby, said conditions for grains and seed, especially soybeans, look favourable in 18 major growing states, but were more mixed when it came to dairy and cattle.

There is a 63 per cent chance this El Niño could be one of the strongest on record. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

The northern Rockies and south-west, where there was an "off the charts" snow drought, could get some strong summer rains, Mr Gottschalck said.

The biggest effect in the US is often in the winter, when the south can get wetter and the Pacific Northwest warmer and drier.

But overall, temperatures raised by the weather pattern could dampen American economic growth, said Stanford climate economist Marshall Burke.

Several climate scientists forecast that 2027 will be the hottest year on record because of lagging effects of this El Niño, which is expected to peak in the fall or winter.

"We have pretty clear evidence that the US economy grows more slowly when temps are above normal," Professor Burke said.

The weather extremes caused by an El Niño also depend on when it develops.

Usually El Niños form in the Northern Hemisphere's summer, peak in the late fall or early winter, and peter out the next spring, scientists said.

However, Dr Ehsan's team forecasts that this El Niño will peak a month or two earlier based on strong early signs from recent weeks.

Princeton University climate scientist Gabriel Vecchi said large El Niños like these also tended to last longer.

The early indications, including warmer water pushing toward the surface of the Pacific, have been so strong and noticeable that forecasters have all been predicting the same ultra strong El Niño, Professor Vecchi said, adding that El Niño forecasts often were all over the place at this time of year.

Scientists predict stronger El Niños as the world warms from the burning of coal, oil and gas, Dr Frazier and others said. But she said it was too early to say if this El Niño was part of that.

Even before it officially formed, this El Niño has gotten nicknames ranging from "super" to "Godzilla."

"Instead of scared, we can ask people to be prepared," Dr Ehsan said.

Portraits of Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai are shown on the screen as they are awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm, Sweden, on Oct. 7, 2026.
                
                    
                    Fredrik Sandberg/TT News Agency via AP

STOCKHOLM — Henri B. Kagan and Kenso Soai won the Nobel Prize in chemistry Wednesday for their discovery of non-linear effects and autocatalysis in asymmetric organic synthesis.

"Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai have provided a solution to a chemical mystery that is over a century old: how homochirality can emerge spontaneously," Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry, said in a news release. "The chemical reactions they have developed are spectacular."

The duo's discoveries, the news release said, "have been decisive for chemists who design reactions for the manufacture of pharmaceuticals."

Kagan, born in France, is affiliated with Université Paris-Sud in Orsay, France, and Soai, 95 years old and born in Japan, with the Tokyo University of Science.

The so-called "Soai reaction" is named for the scientist's experiment.

The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the winner in Stockholm.

Last year, three scientists won the chemistry Nobel for their development of new molecular structures that can trap vast quantities of gas inside, laying the groundwork to potentially suck greenhouse gases out of the atmosphere or harvest moisture from desert environments.

This year's prizes began with the Nobel for medicine, awarded Monday to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award Tuesday recognized a scientist's efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos.

The literature prize is set to be awarded Thursday. After Friday's peace prize is awarded, the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, a small group of laureates or an organization.

Is Trump choosing North Korea over South Korea? | About That

South Korea's presidential office condemned North Korea's launch of more than 10 short-range ballistic missiles on Thursday and ordered its military to maintain full readiness during ongoing joint ​exercises with the United States.

The presidential office convened an emergency ​security meeting attended by officials from the Defence Ministry and military authorities after North Korea fired the missiles from the Pyongyang area toward the sea to the east of the ​Korean Peninsula, it said in a statement.

"The ballistic missile launch is a grave act ⁠that violates UN Security Council ⁠resolutions," it said, calling on North Korea to immediately ‌halt such actions.

Officials reviewed South Korea's response posture, assessed the security implications of the launches and discussed necessary measures, the office said.

The missiles flew around 300 kilometres toward the sea, South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff said.

The missile barrage comes the day after the South Korean and U.S. militaries said they were scaling back their 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, set to conclude by the end of Friday.

U.S. President Donald Trump ordered the Pentagon to "substantially reduce" the exercise just before it began Monday. Trump cited what he said was a good relationship with North Korean Leader Kim Jong Un as well as South Korea's refusal to support the U.S. in its war in Iran.

Asked by reporters Wednesday if he would be meeting with Kim this year, Trump replied, "Yeah, I will be."

Trump added that North Korea possessed 57 "very powerful" nuclear weapons, the first time he's cited that figure. South Korean officials have said they believe the number is between 80 and 120 nuclear warheads.

Trump orders Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea

Kim Yo Jong, Kim Jong Un's sister who has emerged as a spokesperson for the regime in recent years, dismissed Trump's overture later Wednesday.

"The provocative, aggressive nature of the drills won't change even though their duration and size were reduced," she said. "If the U.S. calculates that it can propagate its recent measure as the one of so-called good faith, they will not get the desired answer."

She also cited a series of other military drills carried out by the U.S. and South Korea earlier this year and South Korea's push to introduce nuclear-powered submarines.

Kim Yo Jong said personal relations between her brother and Trump are "still excellent," but denied Trump's claim that the North Korean leader had responded to his request for a conversation.

Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University ⁠of North Korean Studies in Seoul, said the launch appeared aimed at underscoring that Kim Yo Jong's warning ⁠a day earlier was "not mere rhetoric."

He said the launch likely served multiple purposes, including signalling opposition to the ⁠South ⁠Korea-U.S. military exercises, expressing displeasure over recent ​discussion of North Korea's nuclear arsenal, and warning outside powers against speculation about Pyongyang's security affairs.

"It is a message that ​matters concerning North Korea's security are ⁠for North Korea to decide," Yang said, adding the launch could also have been used to test improved missile systems.

During Trump's first year as president in 2017, North Korean missile tests infuriated him, and he threatened the regime with "fire and fury." He would later meet Kim three times — to the chagrin of advisers like John Bolton — setting a precedent for a U.S. president but without achieving any substantial diplomatic breakthrough.

Trump, dating back to his first term, has repeatedly questioned the cost of maintaining roughly 28,500 U.S. troops in South Korea while insisting that Seoul remains an important ally.

The allies have a cost-sharing agreement covering 2026 to 2030, under which Seoul will contribute about 1.52 trillion won ($1.1 billion US) this year toward the upkeep of American troops. Nevertheless, Trump has continued to argue that South Korea pays too little.

Japan's government and coast guard also said North Korea appeared to ⁠have fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Thursday. Japan's coast guard said the projectile had already fallen.

The missile appeared to have landed outside Japan's exclusive economic zone in the sea, NHK reported.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi, who visited Seoul this week, urged South Korea not to take sides between Beijing and Washington, saying the U.S. should abandon its "hostile" policy toward North Korea.

"China would be glad to see the peninsula move toward peaceful coexistence between South Korea and North Korea," Wang told his South Korean counterpart.

China and North Korea have appeared to reinforce their ties recently, with Kim and Xi Jinping meeting twice in the past year.

“Seeing that the polls of President Trump are the highest in my country, so Macedonian citizens are supporting very decisively President Trump’s administration, and when I’m saying that the polls are highest, I’m meaningful because I’m following the polls, and I know that his credibility among Macedonian citizens is absolutely huge, and without any doubt, keen to invite him,” Mickoski said. “I will be very keen to host him at the highest level. He will enjoy the support of Macedonian citizens. When he will have available time slot in his schedule we will be very keen to host him if he decides to visit the region, because as I said, like not so many allies in Europe, we are the country without any doubt for support when it comes to the President Trump administration, even much more longer time ago and prior to him becoming president officially, when there were not too many countries in Europe believing that he would defeat Kamala Harris during the presidential race.”

North Macedonia was also one of the first countries to negotiate a trade deal with the United States after Trump’s Liberation Day tariffs, and Mickoski said he hopes more deals can get signed in the coming weeks when he visits the United States for the United Nations General Assembly in New York. He said he hopes to visit the White House to see Trump or to see him on the sidelines of the UNGA in New York.

“Yes, we negotiated one year ago, I think it was, when we started our negotiations with President Trump’s administration, and we reached we reached a compromise,” Mickoski said. “We impose zero custody rate for the United States products for importing in the territory of my country, and so vice versa. We’ve got zero tariffs when it comes to the exporting Macedonian products to the United States. So practically, more or less, we have common ground, and I think that soon from now, probably there is a chance now during the UNGA to have an official meeting, either in White House or wherever, to sign this bilateral treaty between both of countries. So I think that this will add a value on the relations of both countries.”

He is hoping for even more cooperation between the U.S. and North Macedonia in the coming months.

“Since I’m traveling for UNGA this year—for the United Nations General Assembly—maybe it will be a good opportunity to sign this bilateral treaty either in the White House or in the Department of State, whichever works,” Mickoski said. “For us, it’s very important, and I think that for the United States it is very important because through us, by increasing our economical cooperation, this will increase bilateral cooperation as well. Even our bilateral cooperation is at the highest point ever, historically speaking. But by signing this bilateral treaty, everything will be much more easier for both countries. So, the United States has a very strong ally in the Balkans. I know that they appreciate very much what we are doing for our partnership. But with this bilateral treaty, we will make our bilateral partnerships much more stronger and much more feasible in terms of economical cooperation in the future, and this will open the gates for U.S. exports and investors to have a much more ambitious and much more meaningful role not only in the Balkans but also in Europe generally speaking.”

Both Grenell and Guilfoyle, top Trump officials, spoke highly of Mickoski ahead of the Breitbart News interview with him—and Mickoski likewise spoke highly of both of them. Mickoski made clear that North Macedonia very much so backs Trump and the United States on key matters even when it’s politically inexpedient to do so—including voting lockstep with the United States at the United Nations.

“When America needed allies to take positions practically, my country did not hide in the crowd, which is very important,” Mickoski told Breitbart News. “We stood with the United States very quickly, clearly, and consistently, including when practically doing so carries a political cost. That was for us very important because friends are when some others are not such devoted friends as they are pretending to be in the peaceful times. So practically, when President Trump needed our support in United Nations voting declarations, which are based on the interests of the President Trump’s administration, we gave our no-doubtless support without any reservations unlike with some other stakeholders. So that was a clear message of support, and we will continue to do so in the future.”

“Every day American Air Force aircraft are landing and departing from our airports,” North Macedonia’s Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski said during an exclusive interview with Breitbart News last week. “We have an open sky for American aircrafts, military aircrafts, and we are proud to and we are on disposal to provide such support for the American Air Force.” (Photo Courtesy the Prime Minister’s office in North Macedonia)

It is not just bureaucratic institutions where the Macedonians are providing support. United States Air Force jets are using North Macedonia’s airports—in the heart of the Balkans in Eastern Europe—as a strategic location near the Middle East. Mickoski told Breitbart News he is proud to lend support to the United States in the war with Iran.

“The American Air Force is using our airports, so every day American Air Force aircraft are landing and departing from our airports,” Mickoski said. “So some of them are using our airports for parking, for taking a rest a little bit, and going back to the Gulf. We have an open sky for American aircrafts, military aircrafts, and we are proud to and we are on disposal to provide such support for the American Air Force, of course.”

North Macedonia is just north of Greece, and just south of Serbia, right in the heart of the Balkans—Albania borders North Macedonia to the west, and Bulgaria to the east.

Mickoski described his nation as being on the “front line” of an “invisible battlefield” in an emerging economic war between the west—the United States and Europe—and the far east, in China.

“I will try to describe a little bit the geo-strategical position of my country, which is unfortunately a landlocked country—which might be considered as a small disadvantage,” Mickoski said. “We are a couple of tens of kilometers far from the sea, but unfortunately we are not exposed to the sea since something from the past. However, we are a crossroads of two very important pan-European corridors, but not pan-European only. They are important for the world as well. I’m talking about corridor eight and corridor ten. What is the purpose of both corridors? Corridor eight is connecting the Adriatic and Ionian Sea with the Black Sea, and corridor ten is connecting the Mediterranean and Aegean Sea with Central Europe. Corridor eight is very important due to the fact that immediately when the war in Ukraine will be over, and when the reconstruction of Ukraine will start, this corridor eight will be very important for the supply chain, and practically this will make a shorter supply chain and the cost of delivery will be much lower. When it comes to the corridor ten, it’s worth mentioning that corridor ten, as I said, is connecting the Mediterranean, although I mean Aegean Sea with the Central European countries like Hungary, Austria, and so on and so forth. Practically, we are here, hypothetically speaking, we are at the front line of this invisible battlefield. When I’m talking about an invisible battlefield, I’m talking about the Chinese interest in this part of Europe, European interests on their own soil, and the American interests. Why we are at the front line of the invisible battlefield? Because now everything that comes from the east, all raw materials, all products, are used in two ports in Europe, the ports of Rotterdam and Hamburg. China acquired two ports in Greece, Piraeus port, and they are a shareholder into the Thessaloniki port as well. When I’m talking about Piraeus port, I’m talking about complete ownership of the port. So practically, they’re expanding the capacity of the port. Why? Because they will need, they want to use Piraeus port for harboring vessels—and practically they would like to connect these Piraeus ports with Central Europe which will make the supply chain shorter between 18 and 22 days. So you can imagine what 18 and 22 days nowadays means in terms of costs and in terms of increasing the competitiveness and increasing the maneuvering space and decreasing of a price.”

The Macedonians have formally made clear to the world they side with the United States, and they are also trying to gain entrance—a decades-long goal—into the European Union. Mickoski warned of China’s rising influence in the region, particularly through its efforts to buy and fund ports in Greece—particularly the Piraeus port. As Breitbart News has previously reported, Chinese President Xi Jinping visited Piraeus port in Greece just outside Athens and called it China’s “dragon’s head” in Europe. Greek Health Minister Adonis Georgiadis and Guilfoyle, the U.S. Ambassador to Greece, spoke in interviews for that story laying out how the United States has responded by funding a port of its own in Greece—but Mickoski warned that the long-term goals of the Chinese are to “swamp” the markets of western countries with companies controlled by the Chinese Communist Party. He cited as an example Chinese electric automaker BYD’s growth in Hungary.

“China will use Piraeus port to export products and raw materials and to deploy all of them to Central Europe, for example, BYD,” Mickoski told Breitbart News. “I don’t know whether you have this information. BYD commissioned a production facility in Hungary worth $10 billion, and literally now BYD swamps up competition when we are talking about electric vehicles in the European market. So the number one seller in the European market now is BYD. Imagine what will happen in the future if we allow China to connect Piraeus with Central Europe. Literally, they will swamp up competition from the European market, and they will dominate, and they will conquer the European market. So the only puzzle which is missing in the mosaic is the territory of my country. Why? Because they are building a fast railway which is connecting Budapest via Belgrade with the northern border of my country with Serbia and an important fast railway in Greece, so practically the only section which is missing in the mosaic is the section which is crossing on the territory of my country, connecting the northern border with Serbia and southern border with Greece. So that’s why I’m saying that we are at the front line of an invisible economical battlefield.”

North Macedonia does not seek hostilities with China, and respects China’s One China policy, but Mickoski explained that the priorities of his country are working with the United States to advance freedom on the world stage.

“We respect the principle of one China without any doubt, but at the meantime, our strategic partner is the United States, together with our allies in NATO and with our partners in the EU,” Mickoski said. “But our utmost priority are relations with our strategic partner, the United States, and the current President Trump administration. So this is our pathway forward, and we will follow our pathway forward in the future.”

North Macedonia has also been trying for many years to join the European Union, and has faced issues with disputes between North Macedonia and both Greece and Bulgaria with French President Emmanuel Macron even vetoing its induction at one point. Mickoski said the “second milestone for my country” after working with the United States as a first priority “is to be a part of the EU.”

“To be a part of the EU is good for plenty of reasons for my country and for the citizens of my country. Why? Because we are talking about increasing the security and increasing the resilience of the region overall,” Mickoski said. “We started our journey two and a half decades ago. It was 2000 when we signed a stabilization and association agreement with the European Union. Then, together with Croatia in 2005, we’ve become officially candidate countries to be a part of the EU. In 2008, from the European Commission, we’ve got the first positive report for starting the negotiations but unfortunately since then our hurdles and our challenges started. So practically, it was first the name dispute with our south neighbor Greece, and now we have a dispute with our eastern neighbor Bulgaria, and all those disputes are somehow connected with our identity. I don’t know whether you knew that information, but we are facing a lot of challenges since we’ve become an independent state from the former Yugoslavia. So if we go back three and a half decades ago, I must flag out a couple of very important pieces of information. We changed our flag. We changed our currency. In the meantime, we changed our constitution two times, and finally we changed our constitutional name. According to a lot of, I would say, bureaucrats from Brussels and from all over the world, it’s supposed to be the last thing that we did. But unfortunately they betrayed us and they lied to us. Immediately after our change of our constitution, French President Macron imposed a veto. He requested a change of methodology of negotiations, and when the new methodology for negotiations was adjusted, then unfortunately our eastern neighbor came to the scene and they asked from us to change our constitution. So practically, we are now in a very, I would say, critical situation, and very funny situation. In one multilateral organization, we are allies with Bulgaria, with our eastern neighbor. I’m talking about NATO. And in another multilateral organization, European Union, we have the same allies from NATO imposing constraints for us and imposing a veto, which is not a very, I would say, friendly gesture. Those are the double standards and unanimity rule within the EU itself. They can’t understand that our membership in the EU is strategical for NATO. As I said, from plenty of reasons, among them is resilience and security. So they are weakening the south and eastern flank of NATO by constraining us to become a part of the EU, because as economically much more stronger is my country that makes much more resilient the eastern flank of NATO—and we will be able to modernize in a much quicker way our armed forces and invest more into the corridors which are important for logistical purposes of NATO. So there are plenty of reasons why we need to be a part of the EU, and this is the reason plus for the United States and President Trump’s administration to support us in this manner.”

“We want to turn the strategic dialogue into the present Trump-style diplomacy, with fewer bureaucratic processes and more concrete deliverables in security, energy technology, and infrastructure, trade, and investments,” North Macedonia’s Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski said during an exclusive interview with Breitbart News last week. (Photo Courtesy the Prime Minister’s office in North Macedonia)

North Macedonia earlier this year signed a “strategic dialogue” with the United States, and Mickoski is hopeful this will expand beyond that into even more concrete economic cooperation between the two nations.

“We want to turn the strategic dialogue into the present Trump-style diplomacy, with fewer bureaucratic processes and more concrete deliverables in security, energy technology, and infrastructure, trade, and investments,” Mickoski said. “This is our milestone, and we signed a lot of MOUs. I think that there is big progress. DFC [the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation] is financing one very important project, a mine project. We we have probably the biggest depot of antimony. So there is a big Australian and Canadian investment in the country, and the U.S. is financially supporting that kind of investment. So practically, we will excavate antimony in my country, and we will deploy that critical mineral to the United States. Later, the United States will use this critical mineral for producing military equipment. So practically, we have very, very, very strong ties created with the strategic dialogue.”

North Macedonia is also, Mickoski said, very supportive of Trump’s efforts to get NATO allies to spend more on their national defense. He said North Macedonia is already north of 2 percent of its GDP on defense spending with a plan to get as high as 3.5 percent—with an additional 1.5 percent of GDP spending on critical infrastructure projects to be used by NATO forces.

“Yes, you are absolutely right, and practically we are in the first half of the group,” Mickoski said, the groups referenced being most of Europe which is already spending more on defense versus a small minority which is not. “We are now above the threshold of 2 percent when it comes to the military expenditures. We are, I think, that we are in the first half of the group, and we prepared a scenario on how to reach 3.5 percent up to 2032. On top of that, we have 1.5 percent of our GDP investments into our critical infrastructure, which will be used by NATO South and Eastern flanks. So practically, this is the exact idea of President Trump: 5 percent overall, 3.5 percent military, typically military expenditures, and 1.5 percent investments and expenditures into critical infrastructure which will be used by NATO forces, like railways and highways and so on and so forth. So practically, we are fully aligned with this idea of President Trump, and we strongly support this idea.”

Mickoski said he was very proud of the speeches that both Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio delivered to Europeans early last year and early this year, respectively. He also referenced a speech Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick gave as well with similar warnings for Europe. Mickoski said he may have been the only European leader clapping for Vance’s speech to the Munich Security Conference.

“I was in the room during both speeches but also for the not officially revealed speech of Howard Lutnick, Secretary of Commerce, during the official dinner at the Davos World Business Forum this year. So practically, the two of them had similar speeches conveyed by a different tone, but more or less the messages were the same,” Mickoski said. “Let me start from Vice President Vance’s speech at the Munich Security Conference back in early 2025. So, according to my humble opinion, I’m not flattering here. But I think that that was a very sovereign and very straightforward speech with a lot of frank messages, real policy-making messages, and very realistic messages. Absolutely, you’re right—probably, I was the only person in the room who was clapping with the hands and trying to support the messages that he conveyed during his speech, and I strongly believe that that kind of sovereign speech is the future of humanity. Otherwise, we will lose our identity and credibility, which is something in the contrary of our policy-making process and probably in the contrary of the United States and President Trump’s policy-making process. More or less the same was rhetoric delivered this year with Rubio, but as you said, with a different tone, and maybe the situation among the European allies is changed a little bit. Now, according to my humble opinion, I think that the messages that are coming from the other side of the ocean are considered much more seriously, and I think that our allies in Europe are trying to remain with very close ties with the President Trump administration nowadays, because to be honest and frank, the United States Armed Forces and administration of President Trump is providing the security umbrella for our continent. I think that you can’t play double games and you can’t enjoy double standards. So practically, either you are a liar or not. So this is not a buffet breakfast table. ‘I would like this to eat and that to eat, not that, I don’t like this and I would like that.’ So practically, this is a process. Either we are all together, or we are alone. It’s like a chain. The chain is solid enough and strong enough, as much as the weakest part of the chain is strong. So practically, if one part of the chain is destroyed, then probably the chain will not exist anymore. So this is the way how, according to my understanding, this is the way how our allies in Europe are thinking at this moment, so we must be together and we must stay together with the President Trump administration because as I said President Trump’s administration is providing too many reasons to support that administration. For us, this is inevitable process as a country, but I think that most of our European allies consider that this is inevitable process as well.”

North Macedonia is also going to be a huge part of the so-called “Vertical Corridor” which will ship American LNG up from Greece through pipelines into Central Europe and Ukraine. Mickoski said there are multiple inter-connectors his country is currently building on its southern border with Greece and on its northern border with Serbia, to help move the project along quickly.

“Now we are building inter-connectors that will connect my country with the south, in Greece, and practically that pipeline will leap all over to the LNG terminal Alexandroupolis,” Mickoski said. “We have four slots reserved at the LNG terminal in Alexandroupolis. So practically, in this inter-connector, this pipeline, this Alexandroupolis terminal will become more effective, but it will not be enough. That’s why we are investing into the northern inter-connector pipeline that will connect our national pipeline with the Serbian national pipeline. In that regard, Alexandroupolis—from Greece to Macedonia and Serbia, all over to Central Europe, to Hungary and to Austria. The capacity of the pipeline is between three and six BCM [billion cubic meters] annually, which will make this pipeline real, tangible competition to the Russian assets in the region. So practically, this is the only project which is the transit-able competitor of the Russian assets in the region, and this is the project that might make doable the ambitions of the President Trump administration for exporting the LNG through Alexandroupolis terminal to Central Europe, and we are developing northern inter-connector by our own financial resources from our budget. But when it comes to the south inter-connector, we are using European funding. So practically, at the beginning of 2028, if everything goes according to the plan that we have foreseen, we will connect Alexandroupolis terminal with Central Europe.”

Mickoski is also trying to build multiple hydropower plants to help generate lots of electricity that and to help water flows in North Macedonia.

“Those two hydropower plants are very important for all of us, but not only for the country and not only for producing electricity,” he said. “Bearing in mind climate changes and global heating, I think that the region will need the additional two reservoir supporters. My country has a wonderful perspective, and this is a magnificent, amazing environment for developing those kind of hydropower plants with the high dams, with a big installed capacity, and this is the only reason why we would like to develop those two hydropower plants first to secure our water supply for the region, and second for the irrigation, and then as a third priority producing electricity—although we are talking about one terawatt hour electricity annually, which is a super big amount of electricity for the size of a country like ours. This is a super big amount of electricity.”

The extra electricity, he said, will help North Macedonia build data centers to harness the power of artificial intelligence and he is holding meetings currently with the CEO of Rumble—the major video streaming platform—Chris Pavlovski, whose ancestors are Macedonian, to talk about building them in his country.

“Everybody now is talking about AI, about artificial intelligence, and practically artificial intelligence without data centers—it’s so you can’t drive your data centers without having a sustainable supply of electricity,” Mickoski said. “This is the only way we are able to drive data centers and how we are able to work on artificial intelligence. Chris is investing a lot with his partners in Europe. I know that they acquired one big company in Germany, and since he has super big patriotic feelings for the country of his roots, of his family’s roots, he wants to invest in Macedonia, and I will meet him this weekend, so we will be able to talk more about his potential investments and the investments of his colleagues into the data centers and what we are able to provide for them. So, practically, when we are talking about with those two hydropower plants, we are talking about the project with the amount of $1.5 billion, and also when we are talking about data centers, we are talking about complete American investment, and we’ll be working to provide all necessary incentives what we are able to provide for them to make that investment doable in the future.”

The American's one-game suspension at the World Cup was wiped after pressure from US president Donald Trump.

US President Donald Trump's role in clearing Folarin Balogun from a mandatory one-game ban at the World Cup is set to provoke a formal complaint to FIFA ethics investigators.

The Norway soccer federation said its board of directors will consider filing the complaint at its next meeting, likely on August 6.

"We need our leader in FIFA to say that this was an error," Norwegian federation president Lise Klaveness told The Times in an interview.

After Trump called FIFA president Gianni Infantino, a one-game ban for Balogun's red-card tackle against Bosnia-Herzegovina was deferred so he could play against Belgium with a quarterfinals place at stake.

Belgium beat the US 4-1 after a chaotic 36 hours at the World Cup. The Belgium players were seemingly fired up by one of the greatest controversies in tournament history.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino (left) with Crown Prince Haakon of Norway and Football Association of Norway president Lise Klaveness.  (Getty Images: Jean Catuffe)

Trump called the referee's red card for Balogun after video review a "horrible" call and took credit for getting FIFA to review what should routinely have been a one-game ban.

"We all know that this verdict was influenced from external forces and did not have the proper process," Klaveness said of the FIFA ruling that was unprecedented in the past 60 years at World Cups.

"When you bend a rule like this, you're on a slippery slope that will put the whole game at risk," said the former Women's World Cup player for Norway, who is an elected member of European soccer body UEFA's executive committee.

Klaveness is a lawyer and judge who has positioned the Norwegian federation as a conscience in world soccer since her election in 2022.

"It is a worry for the game when you compromise fundamental rules of the game," she said about not enforcing Balogun's ban.

Norway previously joined a London-based NGO's complaint to the FIFA ethics committee alleging Infantino breached a statutory duty of political neutrality, including by creating a peace prize to award to Trump at the World Cup draw in December.

A group of European politicians launches a bid to begin an investigation into how and why a red card for an American football star was overturned at the World Cup.

The close personal and political ties between Trump and Infantino include the US president believing the soccer official could be a good pick as next secretary general of the United Nations, the New York Post reported this week.

The human rights NGO, FairSquare, also has filed an ethics complaint about the Balogun incident to the International Olympic Committee, where Infantino is an elected member, about breaching its rules on political neutrality.

FIFA and the IOC rarely acknowledge or provide updates on potential cases before their ethics bodies.

The independence of FIFA's process to handle complaints alleging unethical conduct has been questioned since the lead investigator and judge both were replaced in 2017, in the second year of Infantino's presidency.

FIFA has yet to publish documents explaining how its disciplinary judges reached verdicts about Balogun or other World Cup players.

An Albanese government minister has doubled down on his claims Liberal icon Sir Robert Menzies was a “Nazi appeaser,” saying he would “absolutely not” withdraw his comments after being asked to apologise for the incident.

Fronting media on Friday, Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy said he would “absolutely not” apologise for relaying “a historical fact” during a speech he made at the National Press Club this week.

“Labor is the party of national security … We’re proud of our record, and I’m not going to take a step back,” Mr Conroy told Nine’s Today.

When asked if he had been engaging in needless culture war back-and-forth, Mr Conroy accused the Liberals of blowing the comments up, saying they are “a party that has no relevance and they’re desperately trying for it right now.”

“They’re the ones who interrupted parliament with this hysterical stunt,” Mr Conroy said.

“In the end, you can’t argue with history in the history.”

Liberal frontbencher Dan Tehan called the “Nazi appeaser” comment an “utter, utter disgrace” as parliamentarians filed out of the House of Representatives shortly after parliamentary question time on Thursday.

Mr Tehan attempted to have Mr Conroy “sanctioned” over his comments only hours earlier, though a suspension of standing orders to move the motion was swiftly quashed by Labor’s massive majority.

Mr Tehan claimed another MP went on to brand Sir Robert – the founder of the Liberal Party and Australia’s longest-serving prime minister – a “coward” and called for whoever made the statement to withdraw it.

During Mr Conroy’s National Press Club address earlier in the day, he declared his “great hero” was Labor wartime prime minister John Curtin.

“I consume his biographies. I’m very interested in disclosing what really happened before World War II and during World War II, where it was a choice between John Curtin and Nazi-appeaser Robert Gordon Menzies,” he said.

“This is really important stuff that the Left needs to embrace more fully.”

The Australian reported that while Mr Tehan and Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke argued over the motion, Mr Conroy stood ready to table a letter from Sir Robert to Australia’s high commissioner in London eight days after committing Australia to war supporting negotiations with German leader Adolf Hitler.

The September 11, 1939 letter was released in 2001.

In it, he urged for talks with Hitler and said “nobody really gives a damn about Poland”.

He said the war would not be sustained “by the cry of ‘Down with the Nazi government’ for it is really quite indefensible for us to be dictating to the German people what sort of Government they shall have”.

“The cry then must be, in effect, `Law and order and an end of terrorism in Europe’,” it said.

“I don’t underestimate this cry, because I believe it is true and a good one.”

Sir Robert served twice as prime minister between 1939-1941, as war got under way in Europe, and again as the dust settled between 1949 and 1966.

Menzies Research Centre executive director David Hughes said it was unfair to “reduce complex history to partisan attacks”.

“Apply that method to (former British Prime Minister Winston Churchill) and even the man most associated with defeating Hitler can be distorted by selective quotes,” he said.

“Serious history looks at the whole record, not convenient fragments.”

He noted that Sir Robert was the prime minister who broke the news to Australians that the country was at war with Nazi Germany.

“In that address he described Hitler’s ambition as the subjugation of European nations by force,” Mr Hughes said.

He said Mr Conroy “is right to admire John Curtin”, calling Mr Curtin “a great wartime prime minister”.

“But Curtin’s own pre-war record was more complicated than Labor mythology allows,” he said.

“He opposed Menzies’ compulsory training scheme and, like many leaders of the time, sought to avoid conflict with Japan for as long as possible.

“In 1941 he was still engaging privately with Japan’s minister to Australia, Tatsuo Kawai.

“None of that diminishes Curtin’s greatness. He rose to the moment history demanded. Pat Conroy needs to do the same.”

Labor, including Mr Conroy and Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, have repeatedly called for a “progressive patriotism” in recent months amid a surge in support for One Nation and renewed security challenges.

With it, Messi effectively completed soccer, winning the top titles for club, country and individually.

Since Qatar, he has moved to the United States to make Inter Miami the dominant force in MLS, winning the MLS Cup last year.

His status as the greatest player of all time is still debated, with Maradona and Pelé generally considered his main rivals for that title. But back-to-back World Cups — which Pelé achieved in 1958 and ’62 —would further strengthen his case.

Messi, however, has given Argentina a scare just two weeks ahead of the World Cup. The 38-year-old was substituted in an Inter Miami game on Sunday and diagnosed with “an overload associated with muscle fatigue in his left hamstring.” No timeline was given for his recovery.

Ronaldo is still waiting for the one trophy that has eluded him in his glittering, record-breaking career.

The Portugal star heads to the World Cup after leading Saudi club Al Nassr to the domestic league title this season. That trophy adds to league titles with Manchester United in England, Real Madrid in Spain and Juventus in Italy, along with five Champions League trophies (four with Madrid, one with United).

Cristiano Ronaldo celebra tras marcar un gol para Portugal en el partido contra Hungría por las eliminatorias del Mundial, el 14 de octubre de 2025, en Lisboa. (AP Foto/Armando Franca)

He has also won the European Championship with Portugal and two UEFA Nations League titles. His 143 goals is a record in men’s international soccer and nobody has scored more than his 41 in World Cup qualifiers.

Even at the age of 41, his hunger for trophies and records shows no sign of relenting.

Mbappé has long been considered the player to take over the title as the best player on the planet after Messi and Ronaldo.

Some would say the Real Madrid striker has already done that as a World Cup and multiple title-winner, but the fact that he has yet to win the Champions League or Ballon d’Or leaves a big question hanging over his career.

France’s Kylian Mbappe celebrates after winning a World Cup 2026 group D qualifying soccer match against Ukraine in Paris, Thursday, Nov. 13, 2025. (AP Photo/Christophe Ena, File)

He should have a good shot at this year’s Ballon d’Or — awarded annually to the best player in the world — if he can lead France to another World Cup title after topping the scoring charts in Spain and leading the way in the Champions League.

Mbappé is often judged on what he hasn’t won, rather than what he has. In two years at Madrid, he is still waiting for major titles in Spain.

The current Ballon d’Or holder could be a two-time Champions League winner by time the World Cup kicks off.

The France forward has reignited his career since joining Paris Saint-Germain three years ago, helping it secure its first Champions League title last season and reach back-to-back finals this year.

Having been touted as one of the brightest prospects in Europe earlier in his career, Barcelona bought Dembélé for $173 million in 2017. An underwhelming time in Spain led many to think he would never realize his potential.

No one is saying that now.

The Manchester City striker is playing in his first major international tournament after smashing records at club level.

Haaland, 25, is well on his way breaking scoring records in the Champions League and Premier League and has already surpassed benchmarks set by Messi in terms of the speed with which he’s amassing goals.

Norway is an outsider at this year’s World Cup, but in Haaland it has arguably the most lethal forward at the tournament.

Spain’s teenaged sensation was the star of its triumph at the European Championship in 2024 despite not turning 17 until the eve of the final. With mesmerizing speed and footwork, he became the youngest-ever scorer at a men’s Euros.

Yamal is earning comparisons to Messi, who was once photographed with the Argentina star when he was still a baby.

Yamal has arguably overtaken Mbappé as the man most likely to fill void when Messi and Ronaldo retire and an impressive World Cup could strengthen that argument.

He’s the midfielder virtually every top team wanted when Real Madrid sealed his signature in 2023. He went on to lead the club to its 15th Champions League title and the Spanish title in his first season at the club before driving England to the final of the Euros with one of the goals of the tournament on the way.

Bellingham is a matchwinner capable of unforgettable moments on the biggest stage and despite an underwhelming season at Madrid, he will be one of England’s biggest hopes as it aims to win a major title for the first time since 1966.

Brazil’s all-time record goal-scorer has carried the weight of a nation on his shoulders throughout his career.

Despite winning the biggest honors as a player, he is yet to lead Brazil to a record-extending sixth World Cup title.

The Egyptian icon is leaving Liverpool after a disappointing campaign, but remains his country’s talisman.

Salah scored 257 goals in 442 games and won a full set of trophies with Liverpool — including the Champions League and two Premier League titles.

With Egypt he has been runner up in two African Cup of Nations.

From an early age Pulisic was seen as capable of becoming American soccer’s biggest overseas star.

He has gone on to play for some of Europe’s biggest clubs in Germany, England and Italy, winning top honors along the way and none bigger than the Champions League with Chelsea.

Now at AC Milan the forward has discovered some of his most consistent form and will be an important part of Mauricio Pochettino’s hopes to go far with the U.S. Men’s National Team at a home World Cup.

by  Amy Fallon | 1 month ago

Micklin Korsuize, co-founder of The Queer Agenda, was busy preparing for an event at the world’s largest gender equality conference in Melbourne in April when, ironically, their Instagram platform was deleted without warning or explanation.

“It was kind of fitting, but then also so annoying, because we’re trying now to build a community here in Australia and in Melbourne,” said Korsuize, who moved from the Netherlands to the Victorian state earlier this year.

“We might post some things that are a bit edgy for the mainstream, but it’s still nowhere as close as things that are still up on Instagram that are related to child porn or harassment or right-wing hate, and it doesn’t hurt anyone, in fact, the opposite.”

The sudden censorship of their account by the tech giant was the second for the queer community account, the first having been in November. It’s part of a broader crackdown of nearly 400 documented censorship incidents involving LGBTQIA+ communities, artists, performers, nightlife spaces, sexual and reproductive health organisations, educators, activists, and cultural groups worldwide this year – almost double the number recorded last year – according to Repro Uncensored. The global nonprofit, based in the US and Europe, tracks censorship and reinstates blocked accounts among other things.

The accounts censored in Australia include those belonging to sex workers and local LGBTQ+ events, plus a national HIV group.

“Repro Uncensored has already documented dozens of censorship cases affecting organisations, creators, and community spaces in Australia, and we believe this represents only a fraction of the actual scale of the problem,” its founder and executive director, Martha Dimitratou, told Women’s Agenda.

“What we are seeing reflects the same broader pattern documented elsewhere: accounts being suspended, removed, restricted, or made significantly less visible, often with little explanation and limited opportunities for meaningful appeal.”

The scale, consistency, and timing of these reports make it increasingly clear that this is not simply a collection of isolated moderation errors and that Australia’s world-first teen social media ban could be to blame, said Dimitratou.

“Many of these cases emerged alongside expanded platform safety measures, increased reliance on automated moderation systems, and broader restrictions around content classified as sensitive,” she said.

“While protecting young people online is an important goal, many of the affected accounts provide legitimate health information, public education, community support, cultural programming, and civic engagement.”

Last month Dykotomy, a Melbourne-based lesbian event organisation founded and run by four sex workers, had their Instagram account followed by almost 5000 people deleted and was left with no other way of reaching their community.

Co-founder Amelia Abboud said that her personal account was removed about a week ago and that she had tried to appeal the decision involving it and the group’s. But she had been informed by Meta that they would be personally deleted. One of the women also had her business accounts for her hairdressing and cooking services – “very PG-rated stuff” said Abboud – permanently deleted. She too had been informed by the multi-million dollar platform that she would not be able to appeal the decision.

The group, providing another space for the queer community to gather online and physically, have now resorted to using an email list to communicate with people and have been unable to get in touch with any one at Meta about having the accounts restored.

“We don’t really know what to do,” said Abboud.

Meanwhile, Basjia, an award-winning queer artist of colour, has had Instagram accounts removed six times and has told Digital Rights Watch, a Melbourne-based NGO, that the censorship threatens her survival and has left her isolated.

Paisley Heart, a Sydney-based event producer, queer activist, DJ and facilitator, said they had received a lifetime ban from Meta in December. It has cost them an estimated $60,000 – $70,000 in business.

“The platforms have us in a chokehold where, because we make our money through them, it’s hard to take a stand,” they said.

The National Association of People With HIV Australia (NAPWHA) also told Women’s Agenda that they were unable to boost posts for a campaign for the National Day of Women Living with HIV a few months ago and received a notice about them containing political or social issues. Sydney Sauna’s account was disabled in March and they’ve also been unable to appeal.

What Were You Wearing?, a charity dedicated to ending domestic, family, and sexual violence, the LGBTQ+ NSW Community Arts Hub and Festival and Central Coast Pride have experienced problems with their accounts too, according to Repro Uncensored.

DRW said some of the reported content was often innocuous, for instance, photos of high heels, or details for upcoming dance workshops. The censorship was having “a chilling effect on online LGBTQ discourse,” said the charity’s founder and chair Lizzie O’Shea, with some content creators now forced to self-censor.

“It means we are missing out on valuable perspectives,” she said.

The removal and appeal process is opaque and difficult to navigate.

One account owner expressed feeling as though they were “being punished for being queer”.

Some account owners have resorted to scammers who promise to retrieve deleted accounts for up to $3,000 USD per account, but then hold them for ransom and continue to demand money from them, said DRW.

As Repro Uncensored and a coalition of Dutch queer organisations pursue landmark legal action against Meta over the removal of accounts in the Netherlands, they and DRW warn similar legal and regulatory challenges could emerge in Australia.

It was only on April 29 that The Queer Agenda had its Instagram account reinstated through Repro Uncensored. But even now back on the platform, “you’re not actually safe from the big scary Meta police”, stressed Korsuize, adding they were now effectively self-censoring so it wouldn’t happen again.

A post shared by The Queer Agenda (@thequeeragenda.ams)

Having been banned from the digital world twice, and to highlight the crackdown, The Queer Agenda, together with the NGO, staged a physical exhibition during April’s Women Deliver conference in Melbourne. It featured photos taken by Korsuize, documenting “bodies, intimacy, nightlife, desire and collective presence”, to emphasise that in the online world “simply being seen becomes political”.

“That was really lovely and empowering to see our community show up,” said Korsuize. “A lot of people support and are angry with us or for us.”

A spokesperson for Meta told Women’s Agenda: “We take action on accounts that violate our policies, and people can appeal if they think we’ve made a mistake.”

Ecuador looked stricken early, passing slowly, moving a little too carefully. It was a tactical choice that cost them dearly.

The first 20 minutes of play were a Mexican blitz. The team in green flew out of the blocks, applying massive pressure from the moment the first whistle blew. Attempt after attempt on goal was only barely thwarted by an Ecuadorian side denied any chance to build momentum.

Ten minutes later, Wolves striker Raúl Jiménez repeated the trick, his strike finding the top right of the goal and taking Mexico to a 2-0 lead.

When Ecuador trooped off to the dressing room, they looked for all the world like a visiting team at Liverpool's Anfield — rattled by the intensity of both the on-pitch attack and that of the fans in the stands.

When the second half began, Mexico went right back to work, their vision and passing among the best and most creative of the entire tournament. They'd changed up their tactics, however — with two goals in hand, the mission was now to protect them. Thus, Mexico parked the bus, free to sit back and let Ecuador come to them.

They did. Ecuador finally enjoyed a decent spell in possession at the top of the second half, provoking cacophony from the Mexican crowd.

Ecuador's Pedro Vite blew their best chance for the night, hounded down the right flank toward the penalty area before booting the ball into orbit.

Ecuador made their first change in the 58th minute, Kevin Rodríguez came on to replace Enner Valencia. For Mexico, it was Brian Gutiérrez swapped out for Gilberto Mora.

The Mexican midfield made themselves a wall, batting away any ball that came even close to their box. Again and again, Ecuador probed the defensive line in search of a way through. Only in the 73rd minute did Mexico display its first example of poor defending, a loose ball from Ecuador very nearly finding its way into the net.

Unfortunately, with 25 minutes of regulation time still remaining, it was clear that Ecuador was running out of ideas. Tasked with climbing a mountain higher than the 2,200m Mexico City plateau they were already playing on, no answers were forthcoming.

It boiled over three minutes into extra time when Piero Hincapie drew a red card for covering his mouth with his hand when speaking to an opponent during a confrontation. Such conduct has been outlawed by FIFA. Miguel Almiron of Paraguay met a similar fate only days ago.

An ignoble end to a difficult game for Ecuador. A moment of further vindication for Mexico.

Yes, it was a battering. Yes, Mexico had Ecuador outplayed and out-manoeuvred from the moment the match began. But what a treat to watch a Mexican team this good ply their trade. They look like a team that will be very difficult to stop as they move forward.

Kylian Mbappé scored twice, and Michael Olise was in scintillating form as France beat Sweden 3-0 at the World Cup on Wednesday to set up a Round of 16 clash with Paraguay.

Mbappé finished a superb move to break the deadlock just before half-time in the last-32 tie watched by 80,663 at the New York New Jersey Stadium, after France had already hit the woodwork twice — once through Mbappé and once through Olise.

The French were on top throughout against a limited Swedish side, utterly dominant in terms of possession and shots on goal.

Olise set up Paris Saint-Germain winger Bradley Barcola for the second on 53 minutes, and then delivered a delightful pass for Mbappé to complete a convincing victory.

Mbappé's strikes saw him move level with Lionel Messi on six goals in the all-star golden boot race at this World Cup.

The France captain now has 18 World Cup goals in total, meaning he is just one behind Messi's overall record of 19 — a mark which 27-year-old Mbappé will keep chasing.

Olise released Mbappé through the middle to put the ball in the net in the 20th minute, only for a tight offside call to cut short the celebrations.

However, that sparked an intense spell of French pressure which eventually resulted in the opening goal.

Some of their football was mesmerising, as Mbappé hit the post from a Jules Koundé ball across the face of goal and Adrien Rabiot fired narrowly over.

Olise then struck an upright with a breathtaking overhead bicycle kick before Dembélé put the rebound wide.

The opener came right on half-time, after an Olise effort was tipped behind by Swedish 'keeper Jacob Widell Zetterstrom.

Dembélé and Olise combined at the resulting corner before finding Mbappé, and he did the rest.

He celebrated his first goal by running across to embrace coach Didier Deschamps, who missed France's final group game against Norway to travel home for his mother's funeral.

Deschamps will step down at the end of the competition after 14 highly successful years in charge.

Going out in the Round of 32 would have been an anti-climactic way to depart for Deschamps, who captained the first France team to win the World Cup in 1998 and coached them to glory in 2018.

In 1998, France's run to victory on home soil included a 1-0 last-16 win over Paraguay, when Laurent Blanc scored a golden goal in extra time.

Sweden have quality in attack too, with the Premier League trio of Viktor Gyökeres, Alexander Isak and Anthony Elanga. But they couldn't get enough of the ball to create chances, and Graham Potter's team now go home.

Sweden needed the interval to regroup, but they conceded again eight minutes after the restart as the magical Olise threaded a pass through the legs of Gustaf Lagerbielke for Barcola, who lashed in.

Olise couldn't score when clean through, but soon after he delivered an exceptional assist for Mbappé to curl in again on 74 minutes.

Getting this far should really be seen as a success for Sweden, however, after they only made it to North America through the back door of the play-offs.

Les Bleus will face the South Americans in the Round of 16 again this time, on Saturday in Philadelphia.

France will be fully expected to win and march on. Freshly-minted giant killers Paraguay, riding high on their win over Germany, may feel differently.

Erling Haaland scored a late winner as Norway set up a Round of 16 showdown with Brazil at the World Cup after taming the Côte d'Ivoire 2-1 in Texas on Tuesday.

The Manchester City striker prodded in from close range, the ball dribbling in on 86 minutes for his fifth goal of the tournament.

It was the first time that Norway had won a knockout game in the history of the competition.

A match between two physical teams was tepid to begin with at the impressive air-conditioned home of the Dallas Cowboys.

Côte d'Ivoire had a sight of goal after 20 minutes, defender Ghislain Konan bursting into the Norway box from the left but finding the side netting.

Côte d'Ivoire players and fans were irate just before the drinks break when the livewire Yan Diomandé was brought down on the break just inside his own half.

Referee Jesús Valenzuela surprisingly did not even book defender David Møller Wolfe.

The 19-year-old winger Diomandé, who appears set to join European champions Paris Saint-Germain from RB Leipzig, was growing into the game.

The African side, one of the youngest at the tournament, were on top and particularly threatening down Diomandé's left-hand side of the pitch.

Haaland had little to feed on but might have done better with a tame header that bounced into the hands of goalkeeper Yahia Fofana.

Then came a moment of genuine class as Nusa, fed by captain Martin Ødegaard, cut inside and bent the ball wonderfully into the top corner.

Ødegaard put his hands on his head in disbelief at the strike by the 21-year-old, Diomandé's Leipzig team-mate.

Ståle Solbakken's Norway finished the first half on the hunt for a second, and Haaland was denied by a last-gasp block by Ibrahim Sangaré, who celebrated as if scoring a goal.

Côte d'Ivoire, into the knockout rounds for the first time, won their 10th corner to start the second half.

Nicolas Pepe was denied by the legs of Norway stopper Ørjan Nyland as Côte d'Ivoire piled on the pressure.

Norway, runners-up to France in the group stage, were inches away from a second when Diallo blocked the ball on the goal line following a corner.

The Norway fans, sensing the next round was close, began their now-famous rowing in the stands.

Almost as soon as they stopped, Diallo danced into the box past two challenges for a spectacular leveller.

Then up popped Haaland to break Ivorian hearts, with goalkeeper Nyland pulling off a flying stop from Diallo's well-struck free kick at the death to send Norway through.

Mexico pledged Monday to buy more American goods and curb Chinese imports as it sought a trade deal with the Trump administration.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum said that Mexico planned to increase purchases from the U.S. while reducing imports from other countries as Washington pressed Mexico to shrink America’s trade deficit, according to Reuters. Mexico was seeking an agreement over the future of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA) as negotiations between Washington and Canada remained stalled following a tariff fight.

JUST IN: Sheinbaum announces Mexico will buy more U.S. goods & reduce imports from other countries as part of the USMCA review.

“The United States is asking for its so-called trade deficit to be reduced,” Sheinbaum said during her Monday press conference, according to Reuters.

Mexico has also moved to curb imports from China. The country imposed tariffs of as much as 50% on a range of products from countries with which it does not have free-trade agreements, including China, at the beginning of 2026. The duties cover products including automobiles, auto parts, textiles, steel and appliances.

The tariffs align with a broader U.S. effort to reduce China’s role in North American supply chains. U.S. and Mexican officials began the USMCA review process in March with an explicit focus on “reducing dependence” on imports from outside North America and strengthening regional supply chains.

The two countries have since discussed economic security, rules of origin, steel, aluminum and automobiles. U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said following a July negotiating round that the two countries were seeking to strengthen North American manufacturing and address “free-riding” by countries outside the agreement.

Mexico’s approach stands in contrast to Canada, where Prime Minister Mark Carney’s government broke off trade negotiations with Washington in August after the two sides failed to reach an agreement.

The U.S. subsequently imposed 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion of Canadian products, while Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs that took effect Sept. 8.

Sheinbaum said Friday that her government was still “working towards” a trade agreement with President Donald Trump. Mexico was seeking lower U.S. tariffs on Mexican steel, aluminum and automobiles as part of the negotiations.

The Trump administration declined to renew USMCA in its current form during the agreement’s July 1 joint review, but the pact remains in force while negotiations continue. Greer said the administration would continue negotiating with Mexico and Canada over the agreement’s shortcomings and U.S. trade deficits with both countries.

A Monday analysis from the Center for Strategic and International Studies identified increased Mexican purchases of American agricultural, energy and manufactured goods as one potential concession Washington could seek to reduce the bilateral trade deficit.

The analysis also identified Mexican alignment with U.S. tariffs, investment screening, export controls and other measures targeting nonmarket economies, particularly China, as potentially more consequential demands that could reshape Mexico’s trade relationships outside North America.

Trump negotiated USMCA with Mexico and Canada during his first term to replace the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). The three countries signed USMCA in November 2018, and Trump signed its implementing legislation in January 2020 with the agreement taking effect on July 1, 2020.

michigan-upper-peninsula-tariffs:
By

Russ McNamara

Sault Ste. Marie, Mich., is connected to its sister city, Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, by the International Bridge. Both cities are facing economic challenges due to President Trump's imposed tariffs.
                
                    
                    Education Images/Universal Images Group via Getty Images
                    
                
                hide caption

SAULT STE. MARIE, Mich. — The escalating trade war between the U.S. and Canada is particularly tangible in Michigan's rural Upper Peninsula, regionally known as the UP, where many residents rely on the regular exchange of goods and tourists that cross over several times between the two countries.

While Michigan is home to a competitive U.S. Senate race, this region has most recently voted for Republicans. The last Democrat to represent the UP in Congress was Bart Stupak, who left office in 2011.

Now, President Trump's decision to impose a 50% tariff on nearly $20 billion in Canadian goods could influence a race that could be pivotal to the balance of power come November.

UP residents, affectionately known as "Yoopers," are already facing high costs on goods and groceries. Part of the problem is that the UP is difficult to get to — accessible by two bridges and a land border with Wisconsin. That also means higher shipping and transportation costs during a time of record-high diesel fuel.

Ben Rahilly owns an appliance store, a gift shop, a furniture store and a concrete business in Newberry, a faded logging town about 60 miles west of the Canadian border. The village's largest employers are a prison, a hospital and a mill that makes wood siding.

Rahilly says running a small business in a county that has around 5,300 people is tough work.

Downtown Newberry, Mich. The single-screen Tahqua Land Theater plays new movies, while the neighboring drugstore has closed.
                
                    
                    Russ McNamara/Michigan Public Radio
                    
                
                hide caption

"Prices are going up. Our shipping charges are getting more and more every day. The cost of just goods is going up, so it's making it tougher on our profit margins," Rahilly said. "Trying to keep it small town, small prices … so people can afford to keep shopping with us."

Marquette, the largest town in the UP, has the big-box stores that compete with a host of local businesses, but it's 100 miles to the west.

Rahilly can feel the added costs throughout his businesses and is baffled by the trade war.

"You got, right now, our president in a pissing match with Canada. Well, we do a lot of business with Canada, surprising enough."

Rahilly leans conservative but refuses to rule out voting for a Democrat.

"Yeah, I voted for him [President Trump], but I don't think everything he's making right on his decisions," Rahilly said. "Yes, we need goods made in America, but we don't have a workforce either, so we're not going to get it. So we have to bring in some stuff. We just have to be able to work with them countries."

Tony Haller is the executive director of the Sault Area Chamber of Commerce in Sault Ste. Marie, Mich. He has no choice but to work with its sister city, Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario.

"Yeah, I think there's certainly a sense of frustration between both communities," he said.

Haller thinks the local economy has been as steady as it can be.

"Basically, never at the highest of highs or lowest of lows," Haller said.

The two sister cities are connected by the International Bridge, and commercial and passenger traffic is down by about a quarter since Trump's second term. The International Bridge Administration, using per-trip estimates from the Canadian government, believes businesses on the Sault Michigan side are missing out on $62.7 million in lost revenue.

"Speaking from Sault Michigan's point of view, you know we're pretty solid all year round, but because of the bridge traffic being down, I know our businesses aren't quite as busy as they should be, and so we're hoping that when this all gets settled, that we'll go back to some sort of normalcy," Haller said.

The federal government says over a third of all Michigan exports go to Canada. That equaled more than $21 billion last year. That makes the state uniquely susceptible to a trade war.

And tourists to the region are also weighing in. Todd Campbell and his wife, Debbie, were watching the Algoma Harvester, a Canadian carrier, make its way to Thunder Bay, Ontario, upstream through the Soo Locks, the shipping channel that allows freighters to bypass the rapids of the St. Marys River. He believes the president's talk of making Canada the 51st state is just rhetoric, but he says he does not like the tit-for-tat tariffs.

"I'm not real happy about that. I'm a more conservative person, but I'm not happy with the way that's going, to be honest with you," Campbell said.

Campbell owns a trucking company near Knoxville, Tenn. He says business is good and that he likes most of the GOP's policies.

Todd and Debbie Campbell of Knoxville, Tenn., visit the Soo Locks in Sault Ste. Marie, Mich.
                
                    
                    Russ McNamara/Michigan Public Radio
                    
                
                hide caption

"That doesn't mean I'm lockstep with every decision they make, to be honest with you," Campbell said. "I think both sides are really out for themselves, and we all get caught in the middle. And this is a good example of it."

Despite his concerns over the Trump administration's tariffs, Campbell insists he wouldn't "vote blue," saying he thinks the Democratic Party has been "hijacked" by the far left when it comes to other issues, like abortion rights.

Homer Coleman, who lives in metro Detroit, is a trucker vacationing in the UP with his wife and friends. He's an Independent voter and against abortion rights. He's totally baffled by the president's actions.

"I mean, Canada and the United States are sort of like I would say brothers, you know," Coleman said. "He [Trump] seemed like he wants to pick a fight with everybody, and he shouldn't be picking a fight with Canada of all people."

Retired engineer Don Laban from the west Michigan town of Muskegon considers himself a middle-of-the-road voter. He applauds the president for evening out trade with Canada and is critical of the left for not being more policy-forward.

"What did the Democrats have to offer me, other than Orange Man bad? That's all they could say last time. You know, don't tell me who not to vote for. Tell me why I should vote for you," Laban said.

Still, Coleman figures there's not a lot he can do at the ballot box and that the record-high cost of diesel fuel he puts in his big rig is driving up costs for everyone.

"Just gotta just keep going, you know. Everybody gotta just work as hard as they can and just … try to get along with people, you know."

Canada is set to impose countertariffs on the U.S. later this month.
