When so much of your financial life lives online, protecting the device you use to access your money deserves some extra thought. Nancy from Baton Rouge, Louisiana, recently wrote to us asking whether keeping banking and investments on an entirely separate computer could provide another layer of protection.

"I've had several clients tell me they have bought a computer that is only used for online banking, financial institutions and anything to do with their investment accounts. Is this a good strategy for protecting some of your assets? What are the upsides and what are the downsides?"

Nancy, yes. Using a separate computer only for banking, investments and other financial accounts can add a meaningful layer of security. I especially like this approach for someone with substantial savings or retirement assets. It can also make sense if you simply want to keep your financial life separated from everything else you do online.

However, buying another computer will not make your accounts untouchable. How you set it up and how you use it are what make the strategy worthwhile.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

CYBERCRIME LOSSES NEAR $21B: 5 WAYS TO PROTECT YOUR MONEY

A dedicated computer used only for banking and investments can reduce exposure to many everyday online threats. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

Think about what happens on the computer you use every day. You open email, click links and shop online. Maybe you also use social media, download documents or install browser extensions. All of that creates opportunities for malware, phishing attempts or malicious software to reach your device. A dedicated financial computer removes much of that exposure.

On this computer, you would skip email and casual web browsing. Online shopping would happen on another device. Ideally, you would install very little software beyond what the computer needs for security and accessing your financial accounts. That gives attackers fewer opportunities to reach the device you use to manage your money. Our guide to safely viewing your bank and retirement accounts online also explains why protecting the device you use is an important part of financial security.

The biggest advantage is isolation. If malware gets onto the laptop you use for email or everyday browsing, your dedicated financial computer remains separate.

There are several other benefits worth considering:

For people who do not need to check investments constantly, that separation can be especially useful.

FAKE PASSWORD-MANAGER ALERTS COULD PUT YOUR VAULT AT RISK

Keeping your financial computer updated and limiting what you do on it can help strengthen its security. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

This is where you need to be careful. A banking-only computer can reduce certain risks, but it cannot protect you from every way criminals may try to reach your money.

If you reuse a password that later appears in a data breach, having a separate computer will not solve the problem. Every financial account should have its own strong password. A password manager can help create and securely store unique passwords for you.

Many financial institutions still use text messages to send security codes. Criminals may try to hijack a victim's phone number through SIM swapping or an unauthorized number transfer. If that happens, they could potentially receive verification messages without ever touching your banking computer. Our guide on how to avoid a malicious SIM swapping scam explains how protections such as a carrier PIN or number-transfer lock can help reduce that risk.

Suppose you receive an alarming text on your phone claiming someone transferred thousands of dollars from your account. You walk over to the dedicated computer and type the website address included in that message. If the address leads to a phishing site, the separate computer cannot protect you from entering your login information there. That is why I recommend bookmarking your financial institutions' legitimate websites and using those bookmarks rather than following addresses sent through unexpected emails or texts.

A computer that spends most of its life sitting unused can create another problem. It still needs security updates. Operating system and browser updates regularly fix vulnerabilities that criminals may try to exploit. Keep automatic updates enabled and restart the computer when necessary. If you have not used the financial computer in several weeks, let it finish installing updates before signing into your accounts.

Strong passwords, secure authentication and account alerts still matter, even when you use a separate computer for your finances. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

If you decide to take this approach, keep the computer's purpose very narrow. The less you do on it, the more useful the separation becomes.

Keep Windows, macOS or ChromeOS updated automatically. Your browser should stay updated too. Do not keep postponing restarts when an important security update requires one.

Reserve it for your bank, brokerage accounts, retirement plans, credit cards and other important financial services. Avoid email and social media. Do your online shopping and everyday browsing on another device.

I would also keep strong antivirus software running on the dedicated computer. Look for protection that can detect malware, phishing attempts and other online threats in real time. Even on a computer with limited use, antivirus software adds another layer of protection in case a malicious website or other threat reaches the device. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android & iOS devices at Cyberguy.com

Go directly to your financial institution's legitimate website and save it as a bookmark. Then use that bookmark whenever you need to sign in. Be especially careful with financial links that arrive through text messages or emails, even when they appear urgent.

Never reuse your banking password somewhere else. If another website suffers a data breach, criminals may try stolen usernames and passwords on financial accounts. A password manager can create strong, unique passwords and remember them for you.

Enable multi-factor authentication on every financial account that supports it. If your institution offers a passkey or physical security key, consider using it. An authenticator app may also provide stronger protection than receiving a verification code by text. For more on the differences, see our guide to whether bank text codes are enough to protect you.

Do not wait until your monthly statement arrives to discover suspicious activity. Set alerts for logins, withdrawals, transfers, new payees and password changes whenever your financial institution offers them. These notifications can give you an early warning when something happens that you did not authorize.

No. You can safely manage financial accounts from a well-maintained everyday computer if you follow strong security practices. Keep the computer updated. Protect each financial account with a unique password and use strong authentication whenever possible.

For many people, those protections combined with careful online behavior will provide strong security. However, I look at the equation a little differently for someone managing significant retirement savings or investment assets. The cost of a basic computer may be relatively small compared with the amount of money you are trying to protect. You also do not need an expensive machine for banking and investment websites.

If you decide the extra separation makes sense for you, take a look at my best laptops for 2026 and best desktop computers for 2026 at Cyberguy.com to compare current options. A dedicated machine can create a cleaner and more controlled environment for accessing your financial accounts. Just remember that the separation only works if you maintain it. Once the "banking computer" becomes the computer you also use for email, social media or general web browsing, much of that security advantage disappears.

Nancy's question gets at something I wish more people thought about before a scam or account takeover happens. A separate computer for online banking can be a smart additional barrier, particularly when you are protecting significant savings or retirement assets. Keeping email, downloads and everyday web activity away from that machine reduces the opportunities criminals have to reach it. Still, I would never rely on the computer alone. Your passwords matter. Your phone number needs protection. Strong authentication can help stop someone who gets hold of a password, while account alerts can warn you when something suspicious happens. So, if buying a dedicated computer gives you greater control over how you access your money, I think it is a sensible strategy. Treat it as another layer in a larger financial security plan rather than a replacement for the protections you already need. And if protecting your money is top of mind, you can still watch the free CyberGuy LIVE replay, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, at CyberGuyLive.com. Black contrasted this to an inquiry about the removal of so-called nuisance tariffs (tariffs that don't raise much revenue and cost more to administer than they're worth) that ran for nine months.

"I think the fundamental challenge that we've got in terms of these reforms and the process so far is the timing associated with the way in which it's proceeding," he says.

Dozens of young people, masked and dressed in black, are burning bins in the street and thick black smoke fills the air.

The sound of sirens grows louder as fire crews and ambulances arrive.

A woman is shouting through a letterbox to friends inside a house: "The pastor is here, I promise you it is safe."

This is north Belfast on a rainy Tuesday night, and it is chaos.

The same scenes are playing out in other parts of Northern Ireland, where anti-immigration protests are being held.

Many of them are peaceful but others have been hijacked by people intent on violence and destruction.

I was part of the crew sent to the Crumlin Road, a predominately loyalist and working class part of Belfast, to report on the situation there.

When we arrive, the police are keeping a bit of distance, watching but also trying to avoid becoming a target.

We had been holding back from approaching the trouble until it felt safer, having been told at the other end of this long stretch of road to "leave, or you'll be next".

Being a journalist, particularly a BBC journalist, this is nothing new during times of heightened tension.

We move up towards the two streets of terraced houses which have become the focal point of the disorder.

Two cars have been set alight, and homes are also burning. There's real concern about potential injuries, and the risk of a gas explosion.

The torrential rain forces many of those who had gathered to disperse.

Our team is trying not to get in the way, as we step over the fire hoses while also avoiding debris and broken glass.

Fire officers want us to keep a distance, but we need to document what is happening on the streets of Belfast.

I speak to the woman who is shouting through the letterbox of a house with smashed windows. She tells me her friends are inside, and they are trapped, terrified. The house behind theirs is on fire.

A group of African women are led to safety - one of them collapses into the arms of firefighters. The ordeal of the last few hours has taken its toll. She is placed into the back of a waiting car; the others are able to walk to the vehicle.

Pastor Jack McKee, from the nearby New Life City Church, is part of the rescue mission. As he is tending to those members of his congregation he has helped to safety, I take the opportunity to speak to him. He is furious.

"These members have been with us for 20 years. They've been put out of their home," he tells me.

"They are good Christian people and they are getting put out just because they are black.

"You are hurting innocent people here. There are men, women, and children living in fear.

"I am angry. I am disappointed that this is the response of people in our community."

McKee doesn't expect them to return to the place they've called home for many years.

I have covered disorder in Northern Ireland for more than a decade now, including last summer when rioting erupted in Ballymena.

I have watched the police come under attack, a leisure centre being set on fire, and I have heard racist language used by people of all ages.

This week was the first time I witnessed people fleeing from their homes after being targeted because of their ethnicity.

The disorder was sparked after footage of a knife attack in north Belfast on Monday night was shared widely on social media.

Hadi Alodid, a 30-year-old originally from Sudan, appeared in court on Wednesday charged with attempted murder over the attack which left the victim, Stephen Ogilvie, with serious injuries.

I was also sent to Antrim and Ballymena this week to cover the protests there and it is important to say that they passed off peacefully.

The disorder was restricted to pockets of Belfast and other towns, but the whole of Northern Ireland suffered with schools and shops closing early, and public transport shutting down.

I return to the Crumlin Road on Wednesday - it is quieter but the air is still toxic from all the burning.

An end-of-terrace home has been completely gutted, the ceiling has collapsed and even from a distance, you can hear the water running through this shell of a house.

It became clear to me that only certain houses on these north Belfast streets had been the target of arson and criminal damage.

I knew from colleagues reporting from other parts of the city that masked men had gone door to door, intent on targeting those they believed to be from other countries.

I am invited into the house of an Indian man who has lived in the UK for 25 years; the last four in Northern Ireland.

He apologises for the mess inside, as he packs up his life to leave this place. He was too afraid to let us identify him.

The car outside his home was targeted and he tells me he didn't sleep on Tuesday night.

"It was horrible, it was like a war zone. Everything was burning," he said.

"I work full-time. I pay my taxes. I do everything for this country. I am British."

In the short term, he is not sure what to do. If he and his family stay in the house, he is afraid the rioters will come back, but he is also scared in case they are stopped as they make a run for it.

"We are trying to leave Northern Ireland, to take the ferry to the mainland and hopefully we are safe there as we have friends and family there," he adds.

"I have never, ever experienced this."

Over the past week, schools have reported fewer pupils attending, as families from ethnic minority communities keep their children at home.

Healthcare staff have been threatened. One nurse was confronted by masked men and chased while she was walking into work.

Her union said she had done nothing wrong apart from having a "different colour of skin" to the majority of people who live in Northern Ireland.

Despite this, the union said, she "bravely" continued with her shift at the hospital.

A Sudanese woman who came to Northern Ireland as a refugee in 2016 says her community is "terrified".

Twasul Mohammed and others have been helping some of the families who were forced out of their homes.

"When the attack happened on Monday night, we knew this would be coming," she said.

"Everyone is terrified, we are keeping our kids at home. I haven't sent my kids to school since it happened and everyone is worried and tearful."

Those responsible for causing this fear, and forcing people out of their homes, may be in their own homes now.

Those victims who do not have a place to call home this weekend are wondering where to go next.

Economy minister says projection is "beyond what we would see in the course of a normal August".

Fleadh Cheoil na hÉireann, hosted this year in Belfast for the first time, runs from 2 to 9 August.

The eight-day festival, running until 9 August, is the world's largest celebration of Irish music and culture.

The Northern Irish author has sold more than five million books globally and been translated into 40 languages

A litter of 12 unexpected puppies were reunited with their golden mom and dad to celebrate their first birthday as a family.

The humans, crucial to this dog family, were also there, reminiscing about when sister Rhian was babysitting her brother Meirion’s pregnant yellow Labrador, Tilly, while he was away on holiday last year.

Veterinarians assured them that Tilly would have six or seven puppies and were confident she was unlikely to go into labour while her owner was traveling.

But over the course of 15 hours, Rhian, her husband Steve and their two children helped deliver a staggering dozen puppies.

Rhian from Wales couldn’t bear to let the smallest female pup go, so she officially adopted her, while Meirion adopted one of the boys.

One year later, the proud parents Tilly and Lolo, were reunited with all 12 pups for a birthday celebration complete with party hats and dog-friendly cake.

“Looking back at that night, it was a complete rollercoaster of emotions—and pure panic,” Rhian told SWNS news service.

“We completely lost count of how many puppies were arriving.”

“Having all 12 pups back under one roof with Tilly and Lolo was beautifully chaotic, but it just shows how much love has come out of that one crazy night.”

And the night they were born was just the beginning. Meirion said they all set up a WhatsApp group to support each other through the puppy stages.

“It has turned into a real extended family.

“Our house is constantly full of dogs now, as we pet-sit for the other owners—it’s like running a dog hotel!

“Seeing the whole pack back together, healthy, happy, and turning one, is just wonderful.”

Meirion was on holiday for two weeks in August 2025 when pregnant Tilly began hiding under the bed in the spare room, scratching the carpet.

Both Rhian and Steve sat at the kitchen table with their laptops on—facing the pen to watch Tilly.

“We knew she wasn’t going to wait for my brother to return from holidays.”

9-11-families-target-saudi-arabia-nuclea:
Switch between CA and NY editions here.

See more of our coverage in your search results.

Anguished families of 9/11 victims are preparing to go nuclear – by gumming up Saudi Arabia’s push to build civilian nuclear reactors with Trump administration approval.

“How do you give a country nuclear weapons that [is] responsible for murdering 3,000 people and they’ve never owned up to it? They’re not trustworthy. They’re not honest brokers,” 9/11 Families United chair Terry Strada fumed to The Post, dismissing the Kingdom’s claims about its nuclear power program.

The advocates are hoping to use the approval process for the nuclear agreement, which would allow US companies to work with the Saudis on nuclear energy projects worth billions, as leverage to force Saudi Arabia’s government to admit what they say is its complicity in the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.

The emerging pressure campaign comes as senators push the White House to release concealed “side agreements” on the civilian nuclear power cooperation plan negotiated with the Saudis – in a deal that Congress has the capacity to try to block through a joint resolution of disapproval.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), who for years has pressed for declassification of documents on Saudi Arabia’s role in 9/11, recently said he would oppose or at least question the nuclear agreement until 9/11 family claims against Saudi Arabia are resolved.

In a decades-long case, a coalition of victims’ families sued the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia seeking punitive and compensatory damages in federal court that could total billions of dollars following enactment of the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act. Fifteen of the 9/11 hijackers were Saudi nationals.

A bipartisan group of senators this week called on the White House to release the “side letters” to the so-called “123 Agreement” for civil nuclear cooperation, opening up a new dispute.

President Trump said last week said he was “going to look at” releasing 9/11 records on Saudi Arabia’s role after Strada delivered an impassioned speech at the ceremony marking the 25th anniversary of the attacks.

The Saudi government has strenuously denied complicity in the attacks and says its nuclear program is peaceful and transparent.

Strada, who lost her husband Thomas, a bond trader for Cantor Fitzgerald, in the terror attacks, says she doesn’t want records. She wants Trump to pressure the Kingdom to stop denying its responsibility.

“Don’t continue covering for them or providing them cover . . .  He can be the one that stops that pattern,” she said.

“President Trump is leading the most transparent administration in history, which is why he authorized the declassification and release of hundreds of pages of documents related to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001,” said White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales, when asked if Trump had made a decision on the request.

“The President will always pay tribute to the American heroes we lost in the tragic attacks, their beautiful family members, and to the acts of heroism that defined that fateful day when the unbreakable spirit of the American people prevailed.”

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Twenty-five years ago today, a terrorist attack changed American life forever. Four planes were hijacked by al-Qaida; two struck the World Trade Center in New York, one struck the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. The 9/11 attacks killed at least 2,977 people, and a Brown University study found that an additional 7,000 U.S. service members died in post-9/11 wars, while thousands more suffered from illnesses linked to toxic debris after the collapse. Today, communities across the U.S. are gathering to remember, honor and grieve.

The Sept. 11 attack was the most monumental event of my lifetime and still shapes the world to this day. I was based in Jerusalem on 9/11, and when the second plane slammed into the World Trade Center, I immediately suspected al-Qaida was responsible. I'd reported extensively from Afghanistan in the 1990s, including the rise of the Taliban and previous al-Qaida attacks, marked by simultaneous strikes.

Within days, I was in Pakistan and would soon drive the rutted roads deep into Afghanistan, all the way to Kabul, as the U.S. military and its partners ousted the Taliban and pursued al-Qaida.

Afghanistan was otherworldly, a land frozen centuries in the past, all of it clouded in dust and poverty. The country had already endured two decades of war and been abandoned by the world. Yet at that moment, Afghanistan seemed to have a ray of hope, with the U.S. and its allies promising at least a measure of stability and sustenance.

That hope faded over years of grinding conflict. And almost as shocking as 9/11 itself is the way events have unfolded over the past 25 years. What was unimaginable then is today's bitter reality.

The Taliban are back in power, imposing their repressive rule on Afghans, women in particular. For most of the past quarter-century, the formidable U.S. military has fought three wars in three neighboring countries: Afghanistan, Iraq and Iran – all proving far more costly and complicated than expected. These countries have suffered terribly, while the U.S. still struggles to grasp why its overwhelming military might hasn't generated the outcomes predicted with such confidence. Sept. 11 happened 25 years ago. The consequences are still playing out.

It is a global phenomenon that voters are looking for change. I have to ask, change to what? In this increasingly challenging world, on recent experience, it’s best to be careful what you wish for.

Presumably the desire is for better government. Hence, the approach should be to vote for the team that is capable of good and effective governance, with the experience and the policies to make a real difference. It should not be simply a popularity contest or a protest – the objective should be beyond simply expressing disappointment or grievance.

The new Liberal Party president, Tony Abbott, and leader Angus Taylor have recently focused heavily on this “need for change”, to get rid of what they call this “rotten Labor government”. Ironically, they share a record of election losses. Their time in government failed to address the big issues effectively, with their party preferring to kick the can down the road.

The presidency of Donald Trump in the United States and the prospect of a Nigel Farage prime ministership in the United Kingdom should serve as warning against a drift to the fringes. This is becoming a particularly relevant concern in Australia with the surging popularity of Pauline Hanson and One Nation and their tendency to get ahead of themselves in assuming a capacity to win government. There is little to suggest they will have the competence or the policies to form an effective one.

Trump must serve as the most concerning example of incompetent government. When he was emerging as a potential candidate, I expressed concern that his claim to the position was as a property developer and a reality TV star with The Apprentice. I argued a property developer mostly uses other people’s money, such that if the project is a success, the investors will profit, but if it fails, they lose. The nonsense propagated in his book The Art of the Deal was the basis of his election pitch to bring a “business approach and experience” to deliver better government – in his words, “to drain the swamp”, to “shake things up”, and so on. All this under the emotive pledge to “Make America Great Again”.

It is sad that the Liberals prefer a government led by the far right than by Labor. I guess some are dreaming of a coalition with One Nation rather than the spent force of the Nationals. The Coalition’s standing will continue to erode…

Trump has certainly not lived up to the heady promises he made. He now sits on top of an oligarchy that has mostly governed to the benefit of himself and a cabal of obscenely wealthy family and friends.

He has undermined the public service, preferring to appoint sycophants rather than qualified or experienced advisers. His domestic policy responses have been erratic, based on his prejudices rather than evidence-based analysis. He has undermined the congress and the justice system, and developed his own militia, in the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who have caused the deaths of innocent Americans. He has compounded the cost-of-living crisis with his ill-conceived tariffs, deportations and budgetary initiatives. This also resulted in job losses and constrained growth.

It has been estimated that in his first administration alone he added $8.4 trillion to the national debt – a 39 per cent increase. He has added another 7.6 per cent increase in this term so far. There’s nothing really “great” in any of that. His performance has the hallmarks of irresponsible government, to the detriment of average Americans and to the US’s standing in the world.

On top of this domestic disaster, Trump’s ignorance and unpredictability has undermined what had been the global rules-based order. He ignored trade deals, alliances and national sovereignty, seriously destabilising the world economy, geopolitics and the essential global energy transition – making this an even more challenging time for all governments around the globe.

Farage in the UK has been operating as a “mini Trump”, running a particularly divisive strategy “to take our country back” with strong racist overtones and claims that “Britain is Broken, Britain needs Reform”. His popularity and thrust comes from his campaign, similarly race-based, to ensure the UK exited the European Union – Reform UK is a rebadging of the Brexit Party from 2019. This is not much of a base to demonstrate a capacity for competent government. Indeed, his Brexit campaign ignored the voluminous policy warnings concerning the possible trade and financial consequences – like Trump, he would pursue populism and prejudice rather than evidence.

Nevertheless, the polls suggest he leads the fastest-growing political movement in the UK. Farage has been most active signing up a host of former and sitting MPs, mostly from the Conservative Party, including cabinet ministers and backbenchers. It is a basket of scoundrels, most excited not at the prospect of real reform but of being on a winning team.

Like Trump, Farage is also very open to accepting large donations from wealthy individuals, conspicuously a £5 million “personal gift” from Christopher Harborne, a Thailand based cryptocurrency billionaire who claimed no strings were attached. The money, which Farage said was to cover the cost of his personal protection, was given before he became an MP after seven failed attempts. It was not declared in Farage’s register of members’ financial interests. Farage has not handled the controversy well, claiming a leak of personal information (that his phone was hacked by Russian spies), then exploitation by the “deep state”.

Harborne also made a £9 million donation to Farage’s Reform UK, making him the largest single living donor in the history of British politics. The Art of the Deal indeed.

The UK branch of Transparency International has reported the huge donations from Harborne are part of a trend that’s evolved over the past decade. In 2015, just 1 per cent of donations to political parties from individuals or companies were for £1 million or more; by the last general election in 2024, the proportion had climbed to 35 per cent.

The past year has seen the advent of an even more right-wing party, Restore Britain, led by Rupert Lowe, whom Farage kicked out. Lowe has attracted considerable financial and editorial support from tech mogul Elon Musk, via his platform X, at the expense of Farage.

The surge in support for Pauline Hanson and One Nation is a reflection of the Trump-Farage phenomena. Indeed, it seems Hanson has adopted their model. Although she claims hers is the party for working Australians, she too has her controversial billionaire backer, Gina Rinehart. Hanson has also sought to attract sitting and former MPs, and her emerging electoral strategy seems to be to win seats from both the Coalition and Labor.

According to recent polls, One Nation has overtaken the government in terms of primary votes, which has encouraged some to claim the far-right party could win the next election. However, the challenge for One Nation is to convert poll standings to seats in what promises to be some pretty tough contests. Preferences are as important as ever, and it is noteworthy that Coalition preferences helped One Nation to win several seats in the recent South Australian election, and handed One Nation victory in the Farrer byelection.

The recent Australian Financial Review, RedBridge Group and Accent Research poll has posited outcomes in terms of seats in the next federal election. It sees Labor with 76 seats, One Nation on 53 and the Coalition on 12. An allocation of preferences based on the South Australian election outcome would see an exchange of about 10 more seats to Labor from One Nation, with the Coalition unchanged at 12.

While Hanson and her colleagues have declared themselves “humble”, they have got ahead of themselves if they envisage Hanson after the next election actually leading the opposition, or even becoming prime minister. The party would be ill prepared for this elevation, to say the least, in terms of both policies and the skills and experience of their prospective team. The Coalition has lost the past two elections to Labor, as voters concluded they were not ready for government and had just been in government under Scott Morrison.

Despite their recent polling and electoral success, the organisation of the One Nation party is still subpar. This has been particularly clear in relation to candidate selection and vetting, where successful candidates in South Australia and Farrer have broken ranks on their key policy of immigration, and on some social issues. Most recently we saw a disagreement between Hanson and her new MP Barnaby Joyce over housing policy, showing a lack of understanding of policy positions.

I have no doubt much of the growing support for Hanson over the past 30 years has been because she provided a platform for protest and grievance over the broad performance of the two major parties. From the start, there was an undercurrent of racism in the support, particularly against Asian migration. This carried through into the resistance to the Voice referendum and anti-Muslim sentiment. People seemed to have assured themselves Hanson would never be in government and so agreeing with her grievances felt harmless – a vote for her was without serious consequence.

This surety of minimum consequences is fading as her popularity surges and trust in the major parties continues to wane. I suggest that as we get closer to the 2028 federal election, and she and her team are subjected to greater scrutiny, they will be found wanting on their proposed solutions to the many big issues that confront our nation. Poll popularity will not transfer easily to hard votes and seats.

In the meantime, the Coalition is panicking and Abbott and Taylor have committed to preference deals with One Nation, hoping to stem the tide. It is sad that the Liberals prefer a government led by the far right than by Labor. I guess some are dreaming of a coalition with One Nation rather than the spent force of the Nationals. The Coalition’s standing will continue to erode, opening opportunities that Hanson will try to exploit. Increasingly, though, I feel Australia will recognise she is not ready for government nor capable of the kind of global representation that Australians will want.

At least, this is my hope. May Ms Hanson never achieve her dreams.

ABC managing director Hugh Marks has faced questions from Radio National Breakfast show host Sally Sara over the resignation of former news director Justin Stevens.

Mr Marks said he and Stevens had a fundamental disagreement over the future of ABC News, and confirmed reports the process to replace Stevens was underway well before he tendered his resignation.

Stevens's replacement, Reuters deputy editor-in-chief Simon Robinson, will begin as news director in September.

ABC managing director Hugh Marks has confirmed former news director Justin Stevens was not aware a selection process for his replacement was already underway before he resigned from the ABC late last month.

Mr Marks revealed more details about the sudden departure during an interview with Radio National Breakfast host Sally Sara this morning, in which he also addressed the controversy surrounding the hiring of former Australian of the Year Grace Tame to host an ABC podcast series.

Asked why the ABC had thought it necessary to seek a new director of news, Mr Marks insisted Stevens's exit was a resignation, but said it had occurred in the context of a fundamental disagreement between the pair over the future of ABC News.

The national broadcaster is facing a number of challenges around resourcing live news and exploring different formats, he said, and "maybe we felt there were different directions to pursue".

Stevens announced his resignation on May 27. His replacement, Reuters deputy editor-in-chief Simon Robinson, was announced the following day.

Mr Marks also confirmed media reports that a formal process to find a replacement for Stevens was underway well before the news director tendered his resignation, saying he had engaged a recruitment firm as part of "general sort of succession planning" once he came to believe Stevens's resignation was likely "inevitable".

Justin Stevens (centre) resigned suddenly last month. (AAP Image: Mick Tsikas)

Pressed on whether Stevens had been informed of the process, Mr Marks said the former ABC News boss was unaware the search was taking place.

ABC managing director Hugh Marks says he did not "make threats" to terminate departing news boss Justin Stevens, as senators question his sudden departure.

"Sally, I have to go about my role in the way that I see best," he said.

In a wide-ranging interview, Mr Marks also addressed rumours sparked by comments he made to ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler that a 40-year-old "legacy television show" on the ABC "may not be the sort of content that we want for the future".

Asked whether he had been referring to a specific program — 7.30 turned 40 in January, multiple media outlets have noted — Mr Marks said he had "definitely" been speaking hypothetically.

"A better [way of saying it] would have been: 'What got us to where we are today is not necessarily the things that are going to be successful in the future,'" he said.

The hiring of activist Grace Tame to host an ABC podcast was also raised by Sara during the appearance.

Ms Tame was criticised for leading chants of the phrase "globalise the intifada" during a visit to Australia by Israel's president earlier this year.

The former Australian of the Year, who has spoken proudly of her support for Palestinian independence, hosts the four-part series Autistic AF on the ABC's podcast platform, going into depth on her experience growing up with undiagnosed autism.

Grace Tame is hosting a four-part podcast series for the ABC. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Asked whether her previous comments factored into the discussion to hire her for the project, Mr Marks clarified that the decision to hire Ms Tame occurred before those comments were made, but stood by the decision regardless.

"Obviously, I understand why people feel Grace shouldn't have a program on the ABC given the controversy … but I think if you look at the program itself, you know, it's a great podcast," he said.

"She's done a great job on a topic that I'm sure will be of real interest and real importance to many Australians who suffer from those conditions, and particularly young Australians and young Australian women."

Mr Marks said the ABC needed to be able to strike a balance to ensure it brought great content to air, while also "acknowledging that with some people we work with, sometimes there will be controversy".

Mr Marks also came to the defence of the ABC's Melbourne Drive host Charlie Pickering, who criticised Tame's hiring as "problematic" during an impromptu interview with far-right influencer Avi Yemini.

He said Pickering's remarks had been looked at by ABC management, but pointed out the comments had been "a little bit on the hop" and Pickering had made it clear that they were his own view.

"I think we felt comfortable that we were able to accept that his comments weren't a breach of the ABC code of conduct," Mr Marks said.

The accused ringleader of a cocaine trafficking operation run out of two Penn State frat houses fist-pumped his attorney as he was hauled into a Pennsylvania court Wednesday morning — where his team argued that his main alleged henchman was too drug-addled to be reliable.

Long Island-native Agostino Abbatiello, 24, arrived at the courthouse clad in a red prison jumpsuit with his hands shackled — but it didn’t stop the frat bro from pounding fists with his lawyer.

His alleged accomplice and main dealer in the drug ring, Thomas Robinson, his attorney father Paul Robinson, and several other alleged conspirators in the case were also among those who appeared at Centre County Courthouse in Bellefonte.

The group faces a slew of criminal charges after authorities discovered that members of the Penn State fraternities, Sigma Chi and Delta Upsilon, reportedly coordinated with cocaine suppliers in New York and Philadelphia.

Thirteen of the frat bros were busted for running the cocaine trafficking ring that forced young pledges to cut and bag the drugs, which were then peddled to students, according to prosecutors.

Abbatiello, the accused ringleader of the illicit operation, claimed in a motion on Monday that he was being unfairly held without bail and asked for the hearing to be postponed.

A Court of Common Pleas in Centre County said that Masorti’s motion was “moot” and allowed Wednesday’s hearing to continue as planned, according to court records.

His attorney said he was withdrawing the request for a continuance and was ready to proceed.

The younger Robinson was the first to take the stand, and detailed for prosecutors cocaine transactions of varying sizes orchestrated by fraternity members dating back to the fall of 2023.

It was then that he first discussed selling cocaine with alleged co-conspirator Mohammed Huraibi, 22, including conversations about “pricing, supplier and splitting the profits.”

Robinson said he knew Huraibi had a supplier, whom he identified in court as Abbatiello, prompting no reaction from the alleged ringleader.

Many of the larger deals, ranging in size from 4 to 8 ounces of product, were arranged over social media platforms like Snapchat.

Robinson said the group favored Snapchat because messages would auto-delete after 24 hours.

He said his first purchase from Huraibi was in August 2023 for 100 grams of cocaine, which he bought for $4,000 and packaged into half-gram baggies sold for $80 apiece.

Robinson told prosecutors that the proceeds from the illicit sales were split between him and Huraibi, and by November he was selling smaller amounts as demand skyrocketed.

The duo made similar transactions almost monthly until January 2024, when Huraibi said he was no longer interested in selling coke and suggested Robinson deal with Abbatiello from then on.

Robinson said his first deal with Abbatiello was in February 2024, when he purchased 250 grams for $15,000 using cash and Venmo.

The following month, Robinson said he again purchased cocaine from Abbatiello — this time a half-kilo — for $22,000.

He said the two met for another deal that July, and that he purchased a full kilo each in September and November of that year, also for $22,000

In total, Robinson detailed $120,000 worth of drug transactions, during which he bought approximately 5.6 pounds of cocaine in total.

During Robinson’s testimony, Abbatiello’s attorney Philip Masorti insinuated that drug use had damaged his ability to accurately recollect the details of their alleged dealings, but the line of questioning was shot down by the judge.

Next Huraibai took the stand, and referenced many of the same drug deals taking place between himself, Robinson and Abbatiello.

He said the operation had grown to the point that Delta Upsilon pledges had been recruited to bag up product for sale sometime around November 2023.

However, he said he grew weary of the grind at that point in the semester and “decided to walk away from everything going on.”

He told Masorti he was using cocaine while selling it, as well as other drugs, which he admitted could interfere with his ability to recollect with perfect clarity.

The inquest began on Tuesday. (ABC News: Dean Faulkner)

Christine Wyld, 61, died in a South Australian care facility in 2022 after she slipped and was strangled by her wheelchair's lap belt.

The court heard two workers assumed the other was with Ms Wyld at the time.

The coroner said there was a suggestion the supervisor on the shift was responsible for allocating carers to clients and that they should be able to respond.

A woman who died after slipping from her wheelchair and being strangled by its lap belt had been left unsupervised due to a staff shortage at an Adelaide care facility, a court has heard.

Christine Wyld, who had Huntington's disease, died on April 28, 2022, at a Department of Human Services-supported residential facility at Felixstow.

The facility's disability services officer Utpal Adhikari was working on the day of her death.

He told the Coroners Court she was immobile, could not speak and had "violent" involuntary movements.

Mr Adhikari described the 61-year-old as "difficult to handle", but recalled her love of TV and said the workers were saddened by her death.

"She was in pain … she used to cry out and shout all the time," he said.

"When you work so long with people, we grow close to them and you never want to lose somebody."

Utpal Adhikari told the court improvements had been made since Christine Wyld's death. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Counsel assisting Rebecca Schell said the inquest would examine whether Ms Wyld was left unsupervised and for how long.

She also said Ms Wyld's wheelchair may not have been in an optimal condition and had ongoing repair needs that required numerous visits from technicians.

Ms Schell said the foot plates of the wheelchair were not on on the day of Ms Wyld's death,

She said the inquest would investigate whether Ms Wyld's death was preventable.

Deputy State Coroner Emma Roper asked Mr Adhikari whether he understood that there must have been a period of time when nobody had eyes on Ms Wyld, and asked why she was left on her own.

He replied that the team was "short of staff on that day" and said other clients needed to be showered, medicated and fed during the time she was left unsupervised.

"Could it also be that nobody was allocated to Christine that day?" Magistrate Roper asked.

Emma Roper is presiding over the inquest. (ABC News)

Mr Adhikari said he was working with another client that day and was on his lunch break when Ms Wyld died.

He said there were five staff members on shift but one had been sent to another site.

The inquest heard that two other support workers assumed the other was with Ms Wyld near the time of her death.

They had heard a sound from her and assumed it was normal vocalisation.

But when one of them checked they discovered Ms Wyld "white" and unresponsive, with the lap belt of the chair across her neck.

Emergency services were called but Ms Wyld's care management plan stipulated that she was not to be resuscitated.

Mr Adhikari said a lanyard system had been introduced since Ms Wyld's death so that carers knew who was supposed to be looking after each client at all times.

He said staff needed to log when they were on a break or went to the bathroom.

Mr Adhikari also said there had been additional training and instructions about the definition of one-on-one care.

Ms Roper said that there had been a suggestion that the supervisor on that shift had been responsible for allocating carers to clients and that they should be given an opportunity to respond in case there were adverse findings.

A spokesperson for the Department of Human Services said it had made a number of changes to its safety systems, governance and staff training since 2022, and would carefully consider any findings or recommendations the coroner made.

"DHS will not be commenting further while the inquest is active," the spokesperson said.

The inquest will continue on July 24.

Far from a river or water source a large blue truck rolls into Esonorua Primary and Junior School, hours south of Nairobi.

Carrying thousands of litres of cargo, as it arrives the faces of students light up.

As the truck stops, a hose is connected to a large tank … and water begins to flow out the top.

Students try to capture the overflow.  (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

As it trickles down, dozens of boys and girls stand underneath it with cups, bowls and plastic water bottles trying to capture what they can.

A young girl enjoys a sip of water.  (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

It's a sweltering hot day, and it's hardly rained here for months.

With 275 students and staff, Esonorua school is reliant on having water trucked in for drinking, cooking and washing.

According to headmaster Patrick Mwangi, they only have the funding to fill one of their four tanks.

Each one of these water tanks holds roughly 10,000 litres of water. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Being unable to provide water and food to students is a key barrier to education in Kenya.

"Some of them [the students] do not have meals, do not have food at home and when they come to school there is no food."

Headmaster Patrick Mwangi addresses students at an assembly. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

But today, support has arrived, with Australian charity OpBlue providing two truckloads of water, which is used for drinking, cleaning and making porridge.

"When we have the food, attendance increases," Mr Mwangi said.

Students line up for porridge. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

OpBlue supplies students with two meals a day. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

On each visit OpBlue staff collect data, including the number of water-borne diseases like typhoid, cholera and dysentery.

Their goal is to dramatically reduce the impact of these diseases across the country by providing clean water.

"That is something that I need to say we really need support in."

They also provide food and scholarships to students and staff in an effort to get more kids in school.

The charity runs more than 2,000 projects across Kenya, providing 430,000 meals a year.

William Muchiru and other OpBlue staff are away from home for up to 11 months of the year. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

The head of OpBlue's Kenyan operations is William Muchiru.

He grew up at an orphanage and knows the positive impact of education, as well as the barriers to succeed without it.

"I was given education for free … food for free, and I was able to go into my education," Mr Muchiru said.

It's that support which helped him to where he is today, and motivates him to expand the charity's reach across Kenya.

There's always time for a kick at lunch.  (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Eleven thousand kilometres away at an Adelaide Hills vineyard, OpBlue's founder Jack Wilson is monitoring projects, disease rates and meals as well as attendance.

The vineyard produces around 30 tonnes of chardonnay grapes a year. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Between trimming the vines with his brother Harry, the 28-year-old can see what is and isn't working.

"Data collection is the backbone of what we do, if we don't do it we won't know that our projects are working," he said.

From his ute in the Adelaide Hills, Jack is able to monitor the project via his laptop. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Jack and William met and bonded over their shared passion to improve the lives of future generations during Jack's visit to Kenya in 2017.

They agreed water was a priority, with Jack initially sending over 20 to 30 water filters every six months.

These water filters remove 99 per cent of bacteria. (Supplied: OpBlue)

It led to him establishing and registering the charity.

OpBlue co-director Fallon Roocke (middle) is an integral part of the charity's growth.  (Supplied: OpBlue)

"In our eyes no child should grow up without access to clean drinking water, and no parent should be put in a position to choose between clean drinking water and none at all for their children."

The team also provides clean water, educational support and food to four of the country's largest refugee camps, near the Somali border.

The UNHCR says war and climate-related disasters helped displace over 550,000 Somalis in 2024. (Supplied: OpBlue)

"These are projects where our team put themselves in harm's way to help others … it's incredibly dangerous," Jack Wilson said.

The charity is funded in part by corporate and individual donors, as well as Jack's Willow and Goose wine label.

The charity's annual gala at Golding Wines raised more than $75,000 in 2025. (Supplied: OpBlue)

Jack created the brand in memory of his family home, which was destroyed in the 2019 Cudlee Creek bushfires.

"Back then we crushed 500 kilos of pinot and made it with a bunch of friends in an old barn that we built on the ashes of our own home," he said.

The Cudlee Creek bushfire destroyed almost 100 homes in the Adelaide Hills. (Facebook: Eden Hills Country Fire Service)

By providing water, food and scholarships, school attendance at Esonorua has tripled.

Much to the delight of headmaster Patrick Mwangi.

"When I came here seven years ago [attendance] was very low, we had classes with three students," he said.

"The action taken by OpBlue has made a lot of learners come to school, for the first time we have a class with over 70 students."

The main source of income in the area is pastoralism. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

Attitudes towards education are also shifting in the pastoral area.

"Parents' acceptance of education has also changed … they can now pick out the positive points about education," Mr Mwangi said.

Back at the vineyard, Jack is hopeful the charity will continue to grow to support more schools and communities across Kenya.

Jack is looking forward to what the future holds for OpBlue. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

It's a hope shared by his great mate William Muchiru.

"Knowing that a kid in a very far-off county is having education, having porridge, is having a meal at lunchtime … there's so much inner joy," Mr Muchiru said.

"That makes me feel like: 'What if I can do more for another person?'

"[There's] so much desire, so much fire to keep helping other different communities."

It's never not smiles for William Muchiru.  (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

...and then you might not be able to ride a normal bike.

This story is a fascinating practical example of neuroplasticity (the ability of our brains to modify themselves, to change neural pathways). Destin has a Youtube channel called SmarterEveryDay where he makes various experiments to figure out how various things work. A recent one struck a chord with me: Welders at his workplace modified a bike. Nothing major (ha!), just this:

Youtube/Screen captureHere it is from the side:

Youtube/Screen capture

For those of you not familiar with how gears like this work, what this does is reverse how the handlebars operate. If you turn them left, the front wheel will turn right, and vice versa.

This might seem like an easy change to get used to, but it isn't, in good part because riding a bike is cognitively a lot harder than we realize. Consciously, it feels easy once you know how to ride, but under the hood, your brain it taking into account all kinds of factors and running them through a fairly complex algorithm to keep you going. If you change one of the variables, things stop working.

Destin has been challenging various people to ride just 10 feet on the backwards brain bike for a reward of $200, and, well... See for yourself. But make sure to watch to the end, because just as interesting is how Destin practiced riding this weird bike for eight months every day, and how after that he tried riding a normal bike again. Very interesting to see how our brains work!

Geelong has been handed a belated 'please explain' notice from the AFL after initially avoiding sanction over its controversial secret deal with defender Jake Kolodjashnij, a player with a history of concussions.

In 2024, Geelong struck a secret agreement with Kolodjashnij, who on Friday evening identified himself as the player in question, whereby he took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to exonerate the club and its medical staff from court action down the line.

The bombshell concussion case emerged on Thursday and pressure mounted on the league and Geelong after the AFL didn't hand down any punishment that night.

On Friday afternoon, Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking said he had signed off on the deal and confirmed the 'please explain' notice.

Geelong's Steve Hocking said the club would provide information to the AFL about Kolodjashnij's contract. (AAP Image: Erik Anderson)

"I take responsibility for the fact that we didn't lodge it with the AFL and the (AFL)PA," Hocking told reporters in Geelong.

"… I have received a letter of 'please explain' from the AFL in relation to this matter, so we'll deal with that over the coming days."

Hocking said not registering the deal was a "misstep" and was uncertain what consequences Geelong would face.

"We've got a 'please explain' letter, and at the appropriate time we'll work through that with the AFL," he said.

"We'll have to respond to that, and then it'll be up to the AFL, and whatever that is, we'll accept."

Later on Friday, Kolodjashnij issued a statement through Geelong, confirming he was the previously unnamed player.

"While I appreciate the efforts made not to identify me, the speculation has left me feeling I needed to address this personally," Kolodjashnij said.

"I participated fully in the AFL's independent concussion panel process, respected its independence, and was comfortable with the outcome. I have continued playing AFL football since.

"What disappoints me most is that my private medical information has been made public. Everyone deserves the right to keep their confidential medical information private.

"… I am healthy, feeling good, and focused on playing my role for the team for the remainder of the season."

The 2022 premiership defender, 30, has played 209 games.

Kolodjashnij's twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, retired prematurely in 2020 due to concussion.

On Thursday night, calling it a "complex and unique case", the AFL had insisted it was "satisfied that the letter was not used by Geelong to allow a medically unfit player to return to play".

Geelong also issued a statement, saying they would remove the waiver from the contract.

"The club was not attempting to vary the terms of the AFL standard playing contract, or attempting to avoid its responsibilities under health and safety laws," the Geelong statement read.

West Coast Eagles star Adam Hunter's mother Joanne Brown says AFL executive Laura Kane reached out to her, but the grieving mother says the phone call was "too little, too late".

New AFL Commission chair Craig Drummond was the president of the Geelong board when the deal was struck.

Drummond was not mentioned in the AFL statement.

Drummond did not front the media and issued a three-line statement on Thursday night calling concussion a "challenging medical and legal issue for all contact sports globally".

Many AFL players, including former Melbourne star Angus Brayshaw, champion West Coast defender Jeremy McGovern and former number one draft pick Paddy McCartin, were forced into retirement due to repeated concussions.

Several deceased players, including Danny Frawley, Shane Tuck and Graham 'Polly' Farmer, were posthumously diagnosed with degenerative brain disease Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE).

There is also a multimillion-dollar concussion class action against the AFL, led by former Geelong defender Max Rooke, in the Supreme Court of Victoria that is set to go to trial next year.

With a conviction for the 1996 murder of Tupac Shakur this week, pressure is now mounting on authorities to find The Notorious B.I.G.’s killer.

The Brooklyn rapper — born Christopher Wallace, also known as Biggie — was gunned down in a drive-by shooting on March 9, 1997, in Los Angeles; a murder widely believed to have been in revenge for killing Shakur.

That case came to a conclusion when Duane “Keefe D” Davis was found guilty at court in Las Vegas last week of murder for ordering his cousin, Orlando Lane, to kill Shakur then handing him a gun.

“The Tupac verdict doesn’t necessarily help solve Biggie’s murder, but it inevitably puts it under an intense microscope,” Justin Tinsley, author of “Biggie and the World that Made Him” told The Post.

Both murders were gang related, as Shakur was aligned with the Bloods street gang, while BIG’s manager, Sean “Diddy” Combs, has been alleged to have connections to their rivals, the Crips.

Multiple theories over who killed Wallace abound, from rumors of involvement by off-duty LAPD officers to the killer being a juicily nicknamed associate of Shakur’s manager, Suge Knight.

However, gangland lips are tightly sealed, and self-incrimination — as was the case with Davis, who boasted of his role as “shot caller” of Shakur’s murder in a book — remains unlikely. Almost 30 years later, nobody has been charged in the killing.

“What separates the two cases is that Biggie does not have a central figure who put himself inside the story [like] Keefe D,” Tinsley said. “The police need somebody to corroborate evidence. Biggie needs his Keefe D moment.”

Somewhat ironically, Davis — who was a leader in the Crips — had his first brush with law enforcement when he was hauled in by the LAPD and questioned about Wallace’s shooting.

That drive-by took place outside the Petersen Automotive Museum on Wilshire Boulevard where Wallace had just attended a party.  A Chevrolet pulled up alongside the GMC Suburban he was riding in and opened fire. Like Shakur, he was hit with four bullets.

Former LAPD detective Greg Kading, who investigated both the murders of Wallace and Shakur said he and others from the LAPD interviewed a woman, who was given the pseudonym “Theresa Swan.”

She told law enforcers about receiving orders to get an associate named Wardell “Poochie” Fouse to kill Biggie, who was traveling in a three-car caravan and had security with him when he was shot, after receiving threats warning him not to come to Los Angeles.

“Theresa goes and meets with Poochie,” Kading, who authored the book “Murder Rap,” told The Post. “They agreed on the amount of money Poochie was expecting; money was gotten to the girl and she paid him. Then the lone gunman, driving a green Impala, pulled up alongside Biggie and shot him.”

But that’s just one of many accounts. Randall Sullivan, in his books “Labyrinth” and the follow-up “Dead Wrong,” made a case that members of the LAPD — some of whom were alleged to be on the payroll of Knight’s Death Row Records label — had a hand in it.

“The most likely theory, which has not been proven to an absolute certainty … is that police officers working for Suge Knight coordinated the murder, with the actual assassin being a [hired] hit man – who had spent many years in prison for armed robbery,” Sullivan told The Post.

“It was made known that Combs was wanted dead, and Biggie was his biggest star. The hitman couldn’t get Diddy [who was in one of the other cars], so he got Biggie.”

Knight has never been officially named a suspect or implicated in Wallace’s murder, despite prosecutors suggesting he was, during the Shakur trial. He is presently in prison for an unrelated manslaughter.

In 2002, the year Sullivan’s book was published, members of Wallace’s family sued the city of Los Angeles and members of the LAPD. “It was going to be a billion-dollar wrongful death lawsuit,” he said of the legal action, which charged not enough was done to prevent Biggie’s death.

Perry R. Sanders, Jr., who represented Wallace’s late mother, Voletta Wallace, told The Post their suit against the LAPD went to court, but did not reach completion.

“Evidence was found in the lead detective’s desk drawer that indeed implicated police involvement,” Sanders told The Post, speaking of Biggie’s murder. “The judge ended up declaring a mistrial, making them pay seven figures in attorney fees.”

In 2007, another suit was filed which contended former police officers were involved in the shooting, but that case was dismissed.

Alleged gunman Poochie — also killed in a drive-by in 2003 — may not be a household name for most, but in Compton’s gang scene he was a well-known figure.

Recalling seeing him in the recording studio, singer Danny Boy said: “It was kind of eerie when Poochie came around.

“Do I believe that man was a killer? Hell, yeah. He was definitely a killer. He looked like it. He felt like it. You felt it when he came into the room,” he said on “The Art of Dialogue” YouTube series.

Kading, Tinsley and Sullivan agree that it is unlikely the murder of Wallace was a one-man operation.

“To kill somebody like Biggie [who had Crips bodyguards] you would need what is called a spotter,” said Tinsley. “Someone to tell you where he is, which car he’s in, what street they are turning down. I don’t think there’s any way you can pull off something like that without it being a joint effort.”

Tantalizingly, this means that, even if the gunslinger himself is no longer alive, there can be someone walking around who knows the particulars of Wallace’s killing — and maybe took part in it.

Some of the more conspiratorial thinking about the murder has even suggested Diddy, whose car was right in front of the one transporting Biggie, knows more than he’s let on.

In “Diddy: The Making of a Bad Boy,” Gene Deal, a former bodyguard to Diddy, addressed rumors about his boss. “Did he directly have something to do with it? He could have … The week [in] which Biggie was murdered he was acting real anxious and trying to get Big at this party,” Deal said in the documentary.

“And [what] was crazy was, Big was telling people he had to be in London. But Puff was telling people, ‘He ain’t going to London’ that whole week.’”

However, Deal didn’t offer any explanation as to why Diddy would have any reason to be involved in the death of his most famous and profitable star, who was also one of his closest friends. Diddy has explicitly denied any involvement, issuing a statement saying: “I was not involved in the murder of Christopher Wallace [Biggie Smalls].”

Diddy is currently in prison on prostitution-related charges, his team did not respond to a request for comment from The Post.

Kading hopes there will be a death-bed confession, or a resetting of someone’s conscience, or maybe a criminal arrested who realizes his knowledge of an old case is more valuable than he thought.

“There’s going to have to be some rock-hard evidence brought forward,” said Tinsley. “But the encouraging thing about the Tupac verdict is that it proves these cases are never too old to pursue.

“I don’t know how it’s going to happen; I don’t know when it’s going to happen; but I think there is somebody out there who’s going to talk. Then the dominoes will fall.”

A teenager joins an online video chat. Within seconds, artificial intelligence analyses their face and gives them a score out of ten for “attractiveness”. They are compared in real time with another user who scores higher and is declared the winner. The game is live-streamed, and the audience ridicule the loser in the chat.

This is one example from a growing number of websites and apps that rate people’s faces – sometimes comparing users, identifying supposed flaws or recommending ways to improve their score.

AI appearance-rating platforms present attractiveness as though it can be measured with scientific precision. But beauty cannot be captured by a mathematical calculation or a fixed set of programmed rules. What people find attractive varies between cultures and individuals.

AI systems also reflect the assumptions and biases in their training data and design. A critical comment from another person can often be recognised as an opinion. A precise score from a computer may carry an illusion of authority or objective fact.

AI appearance-rating tools form part of a wider online culture in which appearance is treated as something to measure, rank and optimise. This is particularly visible within the “looksmaxxing” subculture, where users share advice intended to make them more “conventionally attractive”.

Some of this advice concerns personal grooming, clothing or exercise. Other content promotes cosmetic procedures, extreme dieting or dangerous practices. The language of optimisation can encourage users to see their face or body as a problem requiring constant correction.

A 2026 study explored the vulnerability of young people to body image disorders, as appearance-focused content saturates their online feeds. For young men in particular, this can take the form of muscle dysmorphia, a condition characterised by the persistent belief that the body is not muscular enough.

Looksmaxxing is part of a wider online environment that can expose young people to narrow appearance ideals. AI ratings add a number, which may turn an insecurity into something that feels like an objective verdict.

My research examines how social media algorithms expose users to narrow societal body ideals, and how appearance-focused content on platforms such as TikTok may affect how users see and feel about their bodies. AI appearance ratings go a step further by scoring the individual user against these ideals. This could lead to restricted eating, over-exercising or other appearance-changing methods.

As I describe in my research, appearance evaluation, objectification and social pressure can contribute to body dissatisfaction and disordered eating. Online environments that amplify these pressures may make existing difficulties worse.

Researchers do not yet know the impact of receiving these scores on users’ behaviour. Eating disorders are complex conditions, and no single platform explains why somebody develops one. However, turning appearance into a competitive score may reinforce the idea that personal worth depends on measurable physical improvement.

My research during the COVID pandemic found that most participants with experience of eating disorders reported their symptoms had worsened during the UK lockdown. Participants described several pressures including disrupted routines and support, social isolation, and greater exposure to triggering messages online.

Although preceding the emergence of AI ratings, that study showed how appearance-focused online content can affect people who are already vulnerable. Eating disorders are also associated with a substantially increased risk of premature death, which is one reason potential new sources of appearance pressure deserve careful study.

A 2026 review of looksmaxxing research, which drew on a small body of academic research and grey literature – material published outside conventional academic journals, such as reports, theses and conference papers – identified concerns about body dissatisfaction, constant comparison and features associated with body dysmorphia and disordered eating. Some looksmaxxing communities discuss extreme dieting, steroid use and cosmetic interventions.

The review described “bone smashing”, in which people repeatedly strike their faces with hard objects in the belief that injury will produce a sharper jaw. There is no evidence that this improves appearance. The review also stressed that high-quality research on looksmaxxing remains scarce.

Read more:
      ‘Bone smashing’: broken bones, tooth loss and blood vessel damage are just a few of the harms of this bizarre TikTok trend

AI-rating tools could also be incorporated into coercive relationships. Body shaming is a recognised feature of coercive control. Abusers criticise their partners’ appearance, control what they eat or wear, and undermine their sense of worth.

Prosecutors in England and Wales recognise that changes in appearance, including weight loss, can indicate controlling or coercive behaviour. Research has also identified links between intimate partner violence and eating disorders.

Research shows that abusive partners use a range of technologies to monitor, harass and control victims. An abuser could use a low AI-generated attractiveness score to demean a partner. For someone whose confidence has already been worn down, the apparent agreement of a machine may make the criticism harder to challenge.

There is no direct academic evidence yet that AI appearance ratings are being used in this way. But research on technology-facilitated intimate partner violence suggests this possibility deserves attention. It is also something that frontline professionals working with domestic abuse should be alert to.

These risks are not limited to adults. Some AI-rating platforms which say they are intended for adults do not use robust age checks.

In the UK, social media, search and other online services covered by the Online Safety Act that are likely to be accessed by children must assess and reduce risks to them, including risks from content that encourages disordered eating, bullying and dangerous activities.

Regulators have not specifically classified AI appearance scoring as harmful content. However, competitive appearance rankings, contact with strangers and public commentary are potential risks that platforms should consider when assessing how their services may affect children.

An algorithm can turn subjective opinions into a convincing-looking number. But it cannot discover somebody’s objective level of attractiveness, because no such measurement exists.

Researchers and regulators now need to examine how users interpret these scores, and whether competitive rating systems expose users to avoidable harm.

Chartered Psychologist & Associate Professor of Digital Health & Wellbeing, Northumbria University, Newcastle

More than seven in 10 Brits believe AI will never replace advice from their elders.

A study of 2,000 adults found while 21 percent use these artificial intelligence tools for help several times a week, 92 percent believe some forms of wisdom can only be gained through lived experience.

In fact, 71 percent feel AI advice will never replace genuine human connection, with mums (39 percent), female friends (20 percent) and sisters (12 percent) ranked among the most trusted sources of advice.

It also emerged those polled go to older people for tips on how to make a relationship last (19 percent), coping with stress (19 percent) and navigate a career change (13 percent).

Older generations are also valued for their practical know-how, including weeding the garden (16 percent), bleeding a radiator (18 percent) and removing stains from clothes (25 percent).

The research was commissioned by Maltesers, the candy company, which is encouraging people to submit their questions to its ‘Age Intelligence panel’, a playful spoof on AI hosted by British actor Sue Johnston—as part of the malted milk ball confection’s 90th anniversary.

“AI is very handy for quick answers,” said the actress. ”But it can’t tell you what a real person would say, remind you to take a cardigan sweater, or confirm that you’re definitely not overreacting (when you probably are).”

“Real wisdom comes from living through life’s ups and downs – and from the people who’ve been there with you, armed with a story, an opinion and a cup of tea they insist you have before making any decisions.

The research also found 55 percent of those who believed that AI will never replace advice from older generations say it’s because they offer real-life experience that technology simply cannot replicate.

Almost half believe advice from older people is more authentic, with 43 percent believing they’re better able to understand the nuances and emotions behind a situation.

Additionally, respondents value the personal stories and life lessons they provide, according to the OnePoll findings.

Among the most valued pearls of wisdom cited by those surveyed were “save for a rainy day” and “treat others as you would like to be treated”, as well as “life is too short to hold grudges”.

However, 64 percent of AI users admitted they have sought help from a chatbot when they could have, instead, spoken to a real person.

Like many of us would, 4 in 10 chose AI because it provided immediate answers. 25% appreciated the anonymity they felt, and another quarter preferred AI because it can sometimes explain things more simply.

Despite this, trust remains a challenge when it comes to personal topics— with just 18% relying on AI-generated parenting advice and 17% for relationship advice.

By comparison, 77% prefer advice from real people on personal topics.

Claire Norgate from Maltesers, which is also celebrating its long-standing partnership with Comic Relief which has raised more than £8.5 million for charity.

Whether it’s a parent, sibling, friend, or someone from an older generation, sometimes the best advice comes from simply having a conversation.
